An MP3 file is a digital audio file usually containing a single song. Even in 1999, MP3 files were small enough for users to store many of them on a single computer, and they were also easy to make. Users would upload songs one at a time to their computer by using music CDs, and once they’d created the digital files, Napster could make them available to everyone.

figure.title:
Napster’s file sharing software allowed for rampant music sharing in the early 2000s.
Photo by OpenClipart-Vectors via Pixabay.

note.para: What followed was a bonanza of file sharing. The company grew to over 10 million unique users in the United States by the time it began allowing international users at the end of 2000, and at its peak Napster had around 80 million users (while those numbers may seem small compared to some of today’s social media websites, they were very large for the early days of the internet). These millions of users were sharing millions of songs with each other for free, from old radio hits to the most recent pop music by artists like Britney Spears, NSYNC, and Garth Brooks.Tom Lamont, “Napster: The Day the Music Was Set Free,” Culture, The Guardian, February 23, 2013, .

In retrospect the problem seems even more obvious than it did then: almost no one was paying for the music. In theory, a single person could buy an actual CD and then convert the songs to MP3 format, thus making them available to millions of people who now didn’t need to buy the same CD. Napster users ended up with hundreds or even thousands of albums of music and paid absolutely nothing.

Napster’s popularity grew like a supernova and began to dim almost as fast. The Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) filed its first lawsuit against the company before the end of 1999, alleging that Napster software allowed the transfer of copyrighted material and that therefore use of the service amounted to copyright infringement. Although Napster filed appeals and changed its service to protect up to 99.4% of copyrighted material, the RIAA refused to agree that the system could continue to run.

The RIAA not only sued Napster, however, but sued individual users as well. Although they didn’t know the real identities of most users, the RIAA took them to court and expected them to pay thousands of dollars in settlements.“How to Not Get Sued for File Sharing,” Electronic Frontier Foundation, July 1, 2006, . One user claimed to be involved in a multi-million dollar suit more than a decade later, even though she’d used Napster to download just 26 songs.Tom Lamont, “Napster: The Day the Music Was Set Free,” The Guardian, February 23, 2013, .

A court order shut down Napster’s primary service in 2001, just over two years after it started. Later on it went through various versions in an attempt to revive it, but despite inaugurating the era of streaming music on the internet, Napster never became big again.

listitem.para: Is it ethically permissible to share MP3 files or other digital media online? Why or why not?
In what ways has file sharing on the internet changed since Napster’s day? Has it moved in a more ethical or less ethical direction? How do we know?
In their lawsuit, one of the RIAA’s arguments was that each downloaded album was equivalent to someone walking into a store and shoplifting a CD. Is that true? Why or why not?
Should users of a piece of software be liable for the possibly illegal business practices of those who create the software?
The RIAA wanted to hold Napster responsible for how its users were sharing files with its software. Should software companies be liable for how their customers use their software?
Should large companies and groups with a lot of financial backing, like the RIAA, be allowed to sue small-time users of a product? What about users who leave more of a footprint? Why or why not?

section.para: What ethical principles can you discover in the Napster case? After some reflection—remember our method, reflect and test—you might get to this one:

listitem.para: End users are not liable for the way they use a piece of software.

section.para: This principle would help us make sense of the fact that it seems unfair to sue individual users of a computer program for the use they make of it. How in good conscience could the RIAA, with dozens of lawyers and millions of dollars, bring a lawsuit against a regular person?

The test part of our method might lead us to rethink this principle, though. To test our principle we need to apply it to other cases. What about social media companies? Depending on an individual’s actions, there may be cases where we do want to hold someone responsible for how they use Instagram, say, or YouTube. The principle we derived from the Napster case wouldn’t account for that, so we’d need to refine it, or introduce a new principle and argue for why we need a separate one for social media companies.

Fortunately, ethical theories can focus our attention on important aspects of a business situation and help us use our method! They’re tools for helping us solve problems, make good decisions, and act well. The Napster case study gives us a lot to think about, and it helps us see why it would be so useful to have an ethical theory to walk us through the particulars.
In the next section, we’ll see another case study, and then we’ll use that case study to learn about many different ethical theories for our business ethics toolbox.

section.title: The Ford Pinto: A Case Study for Ethical Theories
section.para: There are many ethical theories, and some look similar to each other. We’ll see that duty-based and rights-based theories, for example, have a lot in common.

Some of the differences between the theories will be apparent as we discuss them. We can see the contrasts better, though, when we apply the theories to a particular case—each theory will analyze the case in a different way, focusing attention on different aspects of the situation in order to suggest principles for action.

With that in mind, this section will introduce a case study about a car called the Ford Pinto. We’ll read the case study here, and as we go through each ethical theory, we’ll refer back to the Pinto case. We’ll see how each theory takes a different approach and so has advantages and disadvantages in reasoning about business ethics.
The case study, then: the Ford Pinto.

note.title: Case Study: Ford Pinto
note.para: Ford Motor Company is one of the oldest automobile manufacturers in the world. Headquartered in Dearborn, Michigan, Ford is known for its assembly-line approach to making cars and for famous vehicles such as the Model T, the Mustang, and the Thunderbird.

One of the less happy events in Ford’s history involves another vehicle, the Pinto. Ford released the first Pintos in the early 1970s, and the car came in various models, such as a two-door sedan and three-door hatchback. Ford created the Pinto to rival smaller vehicles of other manufacturers, such as the AMC Gremlin and Chevrolet Vega. Production topped out at over 540,000 units in 1974 and declined to 188,000 in 1978 and then 185,000 in 1980. Throughout its lifecycle, Ford produced over three million Pintos before it ended the production run in 1980.Dennis Gioia, “Pinto Fires and Personal Ethics: A Script Analysis of Missed Opportunities,” Journal of Business Ethics 11 no. 5/6 (1992): 379-389.

figure.title:
The Ford Pinto, produced in the 1970s.
Photo from Michael Dorausch, 26 February 2011, original source, CC BY-SA 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

note.para: Management fast-tracked both the Pinto’s design and its production—the entire process took only 25 months, when the national average at the time was almost double that, at 43 months. The short process was in tension with management’s goals for the vehicle—that it not cost more than $2,000 or weigh more than 2,000 pounds. Every step in the design and production process was subordinate to these goals. In addition, the timeframe altered the process in other ways: because management wanted the car to be finished so fast, Ford employees worked on steps such as product planning and engineering in parallel, when they normally do them one at a time.

Two of these parallel steps were tooling and preliminary crash testing. “Tooling” is the process of creating the tools necessary to build many units of a particular design, so once engineers have created the tools, the car’s design is more or less set—it would be time-consuming and expensive to redesign the car and re-make all the tools. As employees continued tooling with an already-fixed design, crash testers discovered that impacts near the Pinto’s fuel tank tended to rupture the tank. This was true even for speeds as low as 31 miles per hour, much slower than most cars travel on most United States roadways. Although the Pinto carried its fuel tank in an industry-standard location, between the rear bumper and rear axle, other features caused the impact ruptures, such as studs sticking out from the rear of the axle box.

Of 11 crash-tested vehicles, 8 suffered gas tank ruptures that could be catastrophic in the right conditions. For the 3 cars whose tanks didn’t rupture, engineers had modified them to protect those tanks using changes they didn’t intend to add to market-standard vehicles. Because more stringent impact testing laws did not start applying until 1976, Ford did not break the law in its testing practices.
Thus, before the Pinto ever hit the market, Ford knew about the problems with its gas tank.

There were various ways to fix the problem. The costliest in both money and time would have been to redesign the vehicle to change the gas tank location; Ford chose not to do this because of the expense and because the redesigned Pinto would have had smaller trunk space. Another option was to modify the tank in post-production, which would have cost $11 per unit. A third option was to do nothing, and sell the Pintos as they were.

Ford opted to run a cost-benefit analysis to justify its decision. Since testing had shown that impacts had life-threatening consequences, the cost-benefit analysis necessarily required that Ford attach a dollar value to potential (even probable) lost lives. The value they used for each life was $200,000. This led to the following calculation, later revealed in an internal Ford memo called “Fatalities Associated with Crash-Induced Fuel Leakage and Fires”:

listitem.para: 12,500,000 estimated units x $11 per unit to modify the gas tank. It would cost $137 million dollars to fix each Pinto in post-production.

180 estimated burn deaths, 180 estimated burn injuries, 2,100 estimated burned vehicles x $200,000 per death, $67,000 per injury, and $700 per vehicle. It would cost $49.5 million dollars to pay death and injury benefits to victims without changing the Pinto. Mark Dowie, “How Ford Put Two Million Firetraps on Wheels,” Business and Society Review 23:46-55, 1977.

note.para: Ford used these calculations to decide to do nothing about the Pinto’s problem. It reasoned that it would be cheaper to pay out death and injury benefits than to fix the vehicle.

Though the company began to receive reports of burning Pintos, those in charge of recall programs at Ford did not have access to the preliminary crash-test data. For this and other reasons, the recall supervisors voted multiple times against a product recall.

More reports of burning Pintos and dead or burnt occupants rolled in, such as that of Sandra Gillespie, a mother whose Pinto stalled as she tried to merge into traffic. Another car rear-ended her going less than 30 miles per hour. The car’s gas tank ruptured, the fuel ignited, and the fire killed Sandra and left her 13-year old son with permanent injuries.

In 1977, following an exposé by Mark Dowie, the National Highway and Transportation Safety Administration (NHTSA) began an investigation. A jury in one case awarded a Pinto burn victim $125 million, an amount later reduced to $6 million. In 1978 the NHTSA determined that the Pinto was defective and obligated Ford to begin a recall of all Pintos produced from 1971 to 1976 (models built after those years had a modified gas tank).

The culmination of the story came in August 1978, when three teenage girls died after a van hit their 1973 Pinto from behind. The car burst into flames and incinerated them. A grand jury then indicted Ford—the company itself—on the criminal charge of reckless homicide. A jury found in favor of Ford, and the company was not held criminally liable for its design, production, and recall decisions.
After the criminal trial, Ford stopped producing the Pinto.

listitem.para: Which events in the Pinto’s production process contain ethical problems?

Ford and other companies opposed crash-test legislation which, had it governed Ford’s decision-making, might have stopped the company from moving forward with the Pinto’s original design. To what extent should companies be able to lobby against safety regulations that might affect their products?
Is it possible to use cost-benefit analyses to make decisions that involve potential injury or death? Why or why not?
Should Ford have been held criminally liable for its decisions about the design, production, and recall of the Pinto?
To what extent do government agencies such as the NHTSA bear responsibility for stopping safety problems such as the Pinto’s?
Why do you think that management at Ford, at so many different levels, took such a callous attitude toward the possibility of human injuries and deaths in the Pinto?

section.para: The Ford Pinto is one of the most famous case studies in the history of business ethics. In the next sections, we’ll be looking at different ethical theories, and we’ll learn about how they work and how they differ from each other by applying them to the Pinto case.

section.title: Utilitarianism
section.para: UtilitarianismAn ethical theory focused on maximizing happiness. is an ethical theory focused on maximizing happiness. Its founders are Jeremy Bentham (1748–1832) and John Stuart Mill (1806–1873). According to utilitarianism, the right action in a given situation is the one that will produce the greatest amount of happiness for the greatest number of people. Utilitarianism says that right actions are right because they produce that happiness.

At the root of utilitarianism is the principle of utilityAn ethical principle that says that actions are right to the degree that they increase happiness, and actions are wrong to the degree that they decrease happiness. , an ethical principle about right action. This principle says that actions are right to the degree that they increase happiness, and actions are wrong to the degree that they decrease happiness.

figure.title:
Ice cream can provide utility in the form of pleasure.
Photo by Lukas via Pexels.

section.para: Utilitarianism can think of happiness in various ways. The most common is to see it as pleasure Feelings of enjoyment or gratification, including things like eating good food or going on a roller coaster, but also the feeling of meaningful conversations or the security of not worrying about where your next meal will come from. . Pleasures include things like eating good food or going on a roller coaster, but also include less-obvious contributions to wellbeing, such as the feeling of having a meaningful conversation or the security of not worrying about where your next meal will come from.

It will help to make three clarifications about utilitarianism before seeing some examples. First, the “happiness” we’re talking about here is not just immediate or short-term happiness, but happiness in the long run. For example, after first learning about utilitarianism, it might seem like the right thing for you to do is withdraw all your savings and spend it all to party non-stop for three months, since doing that would create a huge amount of happiness. But it would only be short-term happiness, since after three months you’d be either dead or broke and jobless. The longer-term misery outweighs the short-term happiness, and so utilitarianism says that, at least most of the time, the right thing to do is be responsible and keep your money in the bank.

The second clarification is about whose happiness matters. According to utilitarian theory, my happiness is not any more important than anyone else’s, and so I shouldn’t give it special consideration when I think about how to act. Suppose that I can create a lot of happiness for many people by taking a job I don’t like. If the happiness I create for others in my new job is significant enough, it will outweigh the unhappiness I experience myself. Utilitarianism would therefore say that the right thing to do is for me to take the job, even though I’m the one who will be miserable.

The third clarification is that the intention of the person acting is irrelevant to utilitarianism—all that matters is the outcome of the action. Suppose I’m a very inept supervillain who sets out each morning to destroy the world, but by the end of the day I always end up inadvertently doing something good, like giving everyone on Earth an ice-cream sandwich. Those sandwiches create a lot of happiness for a lot of people, and so even though I mean to do harm, utilitarianism still says I’ve done a huge amount of good. My intent to harm doesn’t matter; only the actual results I produce matter, whatever they are.

Cost-benefit analyses are important to utilitarianism. For this theory, doing ethics is like doing a math problem: you estimate the potential happiness (benefit) and potential harm (cost) of each possible choice. Then you see which choice has the highest net happiness. Utilitarianism says that choice is the right one.

As an ethical theory, utilitarianism has some advantages. The principle of utility is clear, and the theory is easy to understand. It can give practical guidance to individuals, groups, organizations, and governments. Many people already make many of their decisions in a utilitarian way anyway, so it’s familiar and useful. It can accommodate different conceptions of “happiness,” and gives us an explanation for why actions are right and wrong.

Utilitarianism also has some disadvantages. It can be easy to project the happiness or pleasure our actions will produce on a small scale, but when we involve many people or many organizations, estimating happiness becomes very difficult. In addition, the principle of utility may create tension for individual rights. Imagine a criminal trial, for example, where the defendant is innocent but everyone wants to see him in prison. If the net happiness created by finding him guilty is greater than the unhappiness or harm he would suffer in prison, then utilitarianism may suggest that the right thing to do is convict him, whether or not he is guilty. We could try to modify the principle of utility to fix problems with individual rights, but we might lose some of the principle’s power.

Another issue for utilitarianism is that it necessarily involves cost-benefit analyses. There is nothing wrong about those analyses in themselves, but the reality of some choices will force a cost-benefit calculation to involve very different units, such as when we try to balance employee satisfaction versus shareholder value.

In fact, the Ford Pinto case involves one form of utilitarian calculation. Management at Ford estimated that it would be cheaper to pay out death and injury benefits than to fix the car’s design. The calculation involved attaching a price tag to a human life: $200,000.

Clearly, though, a human life is worth more than $200,000, even if we adjust that value for inflation. In a way, it’s impossible to put a dollar value on any human life at all, since life cannot be reduced to money or spending power. Organizations and governments confront this problem all the time. Utilitarianism is easy to use, but is it ever appropriate to weigh lives against money? Could we find an ethical principle which might guide the way we reason about this?

Utilitarianism could approach the Ford Pinto situation in other ways. One is to modify the calculation by making human life more valuable. Say we quintupled Ford’s $200,000 and valued a life at $1,000,000 even. At 180 estimated deaths, our calculation would now suggest it would be more expensive to pay out the benefits than to fix the cars. It’s a grisly math problem, but it works.

Another utilitarian approach might stop considering the financial numbers and focus on the happiness of the individuals and families involved in accidents. The tragic, painful deaths of Pinto occupants caused enormous harm both to them and to their families and friends, and much of that harm would have continued for many decades. Saving money would have created some happiness among Ford executives and stockholders, but would it have been enough to outweigh the harm and misery on the other side? Again, the question is callous, but certain forms of utilitarianism would have to respond to it.

In applying utilitarianism to the Ford Pinto case study and asking these questions, we see the need for deeper analysis and more fundamental principles of corporate responsibility and the relationship between a business and its customers. We will explore many of these issues in future chapters.

section.title: Duty-Based Ethical Theories
section.para: Some people will be upset at the analysis we get when applying utilitarianism to the Pinto case. They will believe that Ford has an obligation to makes its products safer, regardless of what a cost-benefit analysis might say—does it really matter if paying out the injury benefits is cheaper? Others might believe that no amount of happiness among shareholders or executives could justify design decisions that knowingly put lives at risk.
If you share these convictions, you may be reasoning from the perspective of a duty-based ethical theory.

A duty-based ethical theoryAn ethical theory focused on the right action based on a person's responsibilites in a given situation. is one that focuses on someone’s duty—the right action is whatever your responsibilities are in a given situation. Not fulfilling an ethical duty is wrong. Different duty-based theories identify duties in different ways, but they are often the obligations people are referring to when they say that some action is just “the right thing to do.”

figure.title:
A lost wallet.
Photo by Emil Kalibradov via Unsplash.

section.para: Imagine you find a wallet on the sidewalk, for example, and it’s got some cash, a few credit cards, and a driver’s license. You’ve got bills to pay and would love to take your partner out for a nice dinner, so you could use that cash for a lot of good; you could also buy a few small things online with the credit cards and then never use them again.

Most people believe, though, that it doesn’t matter what you could do with the money, because the right thing to do is return the wallet. To do anything else would be dishonest, and at least in most situations, we have a duty to be honest. We can fulfill that duty here by returning the wallet. We do it not because we expect a reward or because we want to make the wallet’s owner happy by returning it—giving it back is just the right thing to do.

The crucial difference between utilitarianism and most duty-based ethical theories is the following: utilitarianism says that right and wrong depend only on the outcomes or consequences of our actions, while duty-based theories say that outcomes or consequences are almost or entirely irrelevant in determining what is right and wrong. Utilitarianism puts all the ethical weight on the consequences; duty-based theories put almost none. For these theories, duties themselves—not consequences or levels of happiness or anything else—are fundamental.

We find one of the most prominent duty-based ethical theories in the work of German thinker Immanuel Kant (1724-1804). Kant’s and other duty-based theories are sometimes called “deontological” theories. The word “deontological” comes from “deontology,” which comes from a Greek word meaning “to bind”—duties bind us to act in certain ways. Kant proposed a test to identify our ethical duties. When considering whether to perform an action, we first specify what we are going to do and what we hope to accomplish by that action. Next, we imagine a world where everyone does what we are considering doing—where everyone performs that action in that situation, so much so that our action and reasons for it become an ethical law in that imaginary world. Then we ask ourselves: if everyone acted like us, would it still be possible for them to get what they hope to accomplish? If it is, then the action is ethically permissible, and we have a duty to fulfill it.

figure.title:
Immanuel Kant.
Painting from Johann Gottlieb Becker, 1768, original source, PDM 1.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

section.para: Let’s look at a concrete application of Kant’s test. Suppose we have an exam coming up, and we are deciding whether to cheat in order to get an A. Kant instructs us to imagine a world where everyone, when they want an A, cheats on their exam. In that imaginary world, would it be possible for the cheaters to get an A? You might think it would be, since it’s possible for many people to cheat. But Kant had this insight: if the action of cheating to get an A really were an ethical law, then the people giving the exams would themselves know that everyone else was cheating, and so they wouldn’t award any A grades. The cheaters wouldn’t get what they hope to accomplish, and so the action of cheating fails Kant’s test. Cheating isn’t ethically permissible, and we have a duty not to cheat.Another action that fails Kant’s test is lying. No matter the reason, Kant thought, lying was always ethically impermissible—in other words, we have a duty to tell the truth all the time, regardless of the circumstances or possible consequences.

We’ve already hinted at how to apply a duty-based ethical theory to the Pinto case. Ford employees may have had an ethical duty to fix their unsafe products, no matter the cost. This duty might be independent of the financial or reputational cost to the company. Ford should therefore have fixed the Pinto design or installed a post-production fix for the gas tanks.

Notice how different a duty-based analysis of the Pinto case is from a utilitarian one. That’s why we’re going through these ethical theories—each is a tool in our toolbox. The more tools we have, the better we’ll be able to understand and act on the ethical aspects of a situation.

One advantage to a duty-based theory of ethics is that it often agrees with what we already think is right, as in the wallet example. Duty-based theories also emphasize the reasons a person has for acting, instead of the action’s consequences, which is important if ethics is about more than the outcomes of what you do.

While they have advantages, duty-based theories face a few challenges as well. There may be cases where duties appear to conflict, and we don’t know how to reconcile them. Another challenge is knowing what our duties are. Kant’s test and others don’t always give clear answers, and even if they do, others may argue that the suggested action isn’t a duty.

section.title: Rights-Based Ethical Theories
section.para: Rights-based ethical theories are similar to duty-based theories, in that they tend not to focus on consequences like happiness or pleasure. They differ in emphasizing not the duties someone has to act in certain ways, but the rights that person has to be allowed to act in certain ways, or to to be treated in certain ways.

A rightAn entitlement to do (or not to have to do) certain actions, or to experience (or not to experience) certain things. is an entitlement to do (or not to have to do) certain actions, or to experience (or not to experience) certain things.Leif Wenar, “Rights,” The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Spring 2021 ed., . Common entitlements thought to be rights include the right to free speech, the right to vote, and the right to religious freedom. There are many others rights—some more central to human life, others more peripheral.

In analyzing actions, a rights-based ethical theory considers two things: first, whether that action is within the rights of the agent (that is, the person acting)—in other words, whether it is a legitimate entitlement of the agent; and second, whether that action will inappropriately infringe on the rights of other agents. Let’s look at both considerations in the context of the Ford Pinto.

The first is whether the action is within the rights of the agent. Ford executives decided to leave the Pinto’s design unchanged even after they knew the vehicle was unsafe. Did they have a right to do so? In other words, did Ford executives have a legitimate entitlement to set aside questions of safety in favor of a financial calculation? The fact that the NHTSA has passed so many regulations about safety testing and other aspects of vehicle design suggests that the executives did not have this right. They were not entitled to promote or even allow the reasonable certainty of preventable deaths by rear-impact collisions in the Pinto.

Contrast Ford’s refusal to change the Pinto’s design with their opposition to vehicle safety legislation. While that opposition will strike some as disingenuous or unwise, the company is within its rights to advocate for what it sees as its best interests.

The second consideration for a rights-based ethical theory is whether an action will inappropriately infringe on the rights of other agents. We don’t normally think of the entitlement to safe vehicles as a “right,” but it may be—we may have a general right to reasonable safety and security in the society in which we live. If we have such a right, then Ford’s decision not to redesign the Pinto may have inappropriately infringed on it.

More reflection on the Pinto case will lead us to understand other rights that Ford had or didn’t have, or its customers had or didn’t have. What other rights might be involved in the Pinto case, and how would they impact an ethical analysis of that situation?

Rights-based ethical theories are the flip side of duty-based theories. Rights are ways an agent can act with the expectation that others either will not interfere, or will help promote the action. The “others” we’re referring to here will be agents who have duties to act or not act toward us in certain ways. For more discussion of the relationships between these theories, see Robert Audi, “Some Approaches to Determining Ethical Obligations,” in Honest Work: A Business Ethics Reader, 3rd ed., by . Joanne B. Ciulla, Clancy Martin, and Robert C. Solomon (Oxford University Press, 2014), xxv.

figure.title:
The Bill of Rights of the United States of America.
Photo from Davy Jones, September 7, 2008, original source, CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

section.para: An advantage of rights-based ethical theories is how common they are—they are the basis for much thinking about consumer behavior, business law, and government action. Rights-based theories are also easy to understand and can have a powerful impact on behavior when they are codified in law, such as in the United States’ Bill of Rights.

There are some disadvantages to these theories. One is the significant disagreement over what rights an agent possesses. While rights to free speech, free assembly, and free worship aren’t controversial in most places, rights to firearms, affordable health care, and high-paying jobs might be. There are also important disagreements about what counts as “inappropriate” infringement. Deciding what “inappropriate” infringement might be requires balancing rights against each other, just as we might have to balance different duties against each other in duty-based ethical theories.

section.title: Virtue Theories of Ethics
section.para: Most virtue theories of ethics find their roots in the work of Aristotle (384-322 BC), an ancient Greek philosopher. Aristotle’s moral theory focuses less on what is right to do (or what rights a person has) and more on the character of the agent. By “character,” we mean what kind of person the agent shows themselves to be, or becomes, when performing an action. A person’s character can have various virtues, or excellences, if they act in specific ways across time.

figure.title:
A bust of Aristotle.
Photo by Jastrow, 2006, CC0 1.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

section.para: Aristotle’s original list of virtues includes character traits like courage, temperance, generosity, patience, truthfulness, and friendliness. Modern virtue theories may add or take away from Aristotle’s list, but they share the emphasis on the kind of person an agent becomes. The purpose of an ethical theory, according to virtue ethics, is to develop morally virtuous people.

The key question that virtue ethics asks when we decide how to act is, in what direction will my action take me—toward being a morally virtuous person, or toward somewhere else? While we can still ask this question in terms of what is “right” or “wrong” for me to do, we do so with the idea that “right” and “wrong” are defined in terms of the virtues I will or won’t develop by doing something.

Most virtue theories allow that becoming a certain kind of person is a process that takes time. For example, if I always tell the truth but one day tell a single lie, then I’m not automatically a dishonest person. I’m just an honest person that told a lie. But if I begin to lie more, I’ll reach a point where my character crosses over from honesty to dishonesty. The same is true in reverse—if I don’t have the virtue of honesty, I can develop it by starting to be honest. Virtue theories in ethics urge this kind of moral development.

In the Pinto case, we can see where executives and other managers at Ford may have failed to exercise or develop certain virtues. Many theories, including Aristotle’s, see justice or fairness as a moral virtue. Ford does not seem to have treated its customers very fairly. It also may have been dishonest in its production of the vehicle or subsequent marketing. A virtue ethics approach to the Pinto concentrates on the characters of the people involved and how they could better live up to certain virtuous standards of conduct.

One great strength of virtue theories is their focus on character. For many people, ethics involves not only abstract reasoning but the real-world transformations we undergo as we make choices. Most business professionals will go through many such transformations as their careers unfold and they interact with colleagues, management, and customers.

A weakness of virtue theories, at least in business ethics, is that they have a hard time giving us a clear standard of right and wrong that we can then apply to many different decisions. We’ll find reasonable disagreement in all of the ethical theories we’ve discussed so far, but it will usually be easier to resolve a disagreement over, say, whether a business’s actions caused physical harm, compared to a disagreement about what virtues are the most important, and how to demonstrate them in action.

section.title: Feminist Theories of Ethics
section.para: Feminist theories of ethics arose in part as a response to some of the ethical theories we’ve already seen. Previous theories tend to seek abstract, general principles of right and wrong in order to universalize ethics as much as possible. In doing so, they tend to work with idealized examples, sometimes far removed from the real day-to-day experiences of human beings. In addition, to the extent that most ethical thinkers have been male, their abstract theories may consider only certain sets of experiences, or certain viewpoints on experience, rather than others.

Feminist approaches to ethics call attention to the resulting limitations in traditional ethical theories. For example, according to utilitarian theories, the right thing to do is to maximize the amount of happiness in the world. But who gets to decide what counts as “happiness,” and who gets to establish that standard for everyone else? Men have done this in the history of most societies, but the answers they have given to these questions are not the only possible answers, nor necessarily the best ones.

Ethical thinkers in feminist traditions give us many useful tools, especially for thinking about business ethics. One is the value of a multiplicity of voices in large-scale decision making. Ford has a history of privileging men and male-dominated groups at various organizational levels; For more background, see Brett Theodore Morritt, “Systems of Male Privilege: The Industrial Relations Policies of the Ford Motor Company in the 1940s,” and Wayne Lewchuk, “Men and Monotony: Fraternalism as a Managerial Strategy at the Ford Motor Company.” what effect might this tradition have had on the business culture which allowed the Pinto production process to move forward despite such obvious problems? What might have happened had the company been constituted in some other way?

figure.title:
Feminist theories of ethics strive to approach ethics from an alternate perspective.
iStock.com/simonkr

imagedata.fileref: images/2.8 Men in a board room.jpg

section.para: In asking these questions, we are not suggesting that, if more women had been managers or executives at Ford in the late 1960’s and early 1970’s, the Pinto debacle would never have happened. We have no way of knowing what would have happened, had the company been different. Feminist ethics does not give us magical insight into an alternative universe where women, as opposed to men, run things. The power of the feminist approach is in asking the question in the first place, or in seeing that the question could be relevant to thinking about the ethics of the situation. Sure, having more women on staff at Ford might not have prevented so many Pintos from rolling into dealerships—but there are many other situations in which female voices would make a difference. By training ourselves to consider that possibility, we’ll begin to see situations where these questions will help us make tangible ethical progress.

Another tool of feminist ethics is a focus on relationships of power, and how power imbalances can create situations which appear to be ethical but which may hide ethical problems deeper down. Take a company like Ford, which can marshal vast amounts of financial and legal resources to defend its interests. If the family of someone injured in a Pinto accident wished to sue the company, they would have the opportunity to do so. Since they may sue if they wish, it may seem that they and the company stand on level ground. But is it really fair for regular families to have to pay lawyers thousands of dollars to seek redress for something that isn’t their fault? Is it really fair that large companies can drag lawsuits out to an almost infinite extent, in the hope that the plaintiffs will give up and go home? A feminist approach to ethics helps us discern and understand the effect that these relationships and the resulting power differentials can have.

We should note that feminist approaches to ethics are not just for women. They are for anyone who understands that traditional ethical theories have limitations, some of which come from the limited people, viewpoints, and experiences that gave rise to the theories.
As you’ll see later, we’ll draw from these and other ideas of feminist ethics throughout our book.

section.title: Other Ethical Theories
section.para: We have now covered five major ethical theories: utilitarianism, duty-based ethics, rights-based ethics, virtue ethics, and feminist ethics. This coverage focuses on those theories that have been most prominent among Western thinkers and business professionals, both because of the book’s audience and because of the norm-setting influence that Western business conventions have on the wider business world.

These are not the only ethical theories, however. There are many others, including the ethics of care and theories that come from Eastern thinkers.For a discussion of these approaches to ethics in the context of business professions, see Virginia Held, “The Ethics of Care As Moral Theory,” Daryl Koehn, “What Can Eastern Philosophy Teach Us about Business Ethics?”, and Thaddeus Metz, “Toward an African Moral Theory,” in Professions in Ethical Focus, 2nd edition, chapters 4–6. Other theories provide other valuable tools as well, and make it possible to see situations or ask questions that may otherwise be invisible to us.

section.title: Ethical Theories and Our Method for Progress in Business Ethics

figure.title:
Examining an Ethical Toolbox
Photo by Artem Perez via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: An open toolbox filled with wrenches, pliars, and screwdrivers.

section.para: In keeping with this book’s practical approach to business ethics, we present these ethical theories as tools to add to our ethical toolbox. We use the tools for dealing with ethical problems. Each has a different use and emphasizes different aspects of a situation. Some theories will focus on one thing while others will focus on others.

The more tools a business professional has in her ethics toolkit, the more she’ll be prepared to identify and work toward resolving the ethical problems she encounters. Not all situations give a perfect fit for a utilitarian analysis; not all are best analyzed with a rights-based ethical theory, and not all have dimensions which call for feminist analysis. But where one theory may not give us what we feel we need, another can step in to help.

At this point you may be wondering which of the moral theories we’ve seen is the correct one. After all, we introduced the idea of a “theory” by talking about scientific theories, and some scientific theories are correct, while others aren’t. Is the same true for ethical theories? Is one of them true, while the others are false? If there is a true theory, why wouldn’t we just use that one, and ignore all the others?

These questions raise deep issues in ethical philosophy. The issues may become sharper when we learn more about the theories themselves. Kant, for example, who originated the most widespread duty-based theory of ethics, was adamant that any approach to ethics which looks only at the consequences of action—like utilitarianism—cannot be correct. He was explicit about his theory being a repudiation of any theory that looked at all like utilitarianism. At their core, then, certain ethical theories may simply be incompatible with each other; if one is true, it may be that one or more others are false.

We saw these problems in the first chapter as part of our discussion on making progress in ethics. There we introduced the ideas of realism and anti-realism. According to realism, there is at least one true ethical theory—ethical truths, whether utilitarian, rights-based, feminist, or of some other kind—really do exist. Anti-realism says the opposite—that there are no ethical truths, just opinions. If realism is right, then one or more ethical theories is true; if anti-realism is right, then none are. There are many arguments for and against both positions.

It may look like you need to take a stand on these issues in order to do business ethics. For example, if you use a utilitarian analysis to examine an ethical problem, it may look like that theory must be true in order for your results to work; on the other hand, if you consider yourself able to draw from many ethical theories, it may look as though none are true, since you’re using all of them.

In reality, though, business professionals don’t need to take a position on issues like realism or anti-realism in order to do business ethics. It is not your responsibility to resolve problems which philosophers themselves have argued about for thousands of years. Rather, your job is to become sensitive to the ethical dimensions of your professional life, and to become proficient at dealing with ethical problems in ways that satisfy many or all interested parties. You can gain the skills to accomplish these goals regardless of whether moral realism is true.

In any case, the answers to abstract philosophical questions do not change the fact that we often need ethical guidance for real-life situations. If all the ethical philosophy in the world vanished, we’d still face ethical problems in our professions. Ethical theories can tell us what to value and why, but only we can evaluate whether the reasons they suggest are good ones. Theories are always one step behind the world—the world is always more complicated than the theory, because we face new situations that the theory can’t account for until we’ve dealt with them.

After reviewing so many ethical theories, you might also conclude that they’re all very different from one another. They have a lot in common, in fact, as business ethicist Jeffrey Moriarty notes in his Business Ethics.Jeffrey Moriarty, Business Ethics: A Contemporary Introduction, (Routledge, 2022), 50–52. If many different theorists got together and developed principles for ethical business conduct, Moriarty asks, what would they give us? He suggests that they would agree about seven principles:

listitem.para: Abide by agreements
Avoid deception
Respect people
Recognize rights
Do what justice requires
Minimize harm
Promote welfare

section.para: In our reasoning about ethical problems, we’ve already seen and used some of these principles. In one way or another, many different ethical theories lead to them.

The ethical theories we’ve learned about will help apply our method of reflect and test in order to make progress on ethical problems. As a reminder, that method has three primary steps: reflect, test, and repeat. We can use our ethical toolbox at each step.

As we begin our method by reflecting, our goal is first to gather as much relevant information as possible. We do this by asking questions and getting answers. Different ethical theories can help here by pushing us to ask different questions: what about a customer’s rights? Did the business’s decisions have a disparate impact on one demographic group over another? These questions come straight out of different ethical theories, and we may not think to ask them if we weren’t aware of our tools. Likewise, ethical theories can also give us ideas as we then consider our ethical values and generate or identify ethical principles.

The second step of our method is to test our moral principles. We apply them to other cases beyond our own, and then refine them in response to our tests. Ethical theories help here by suggesting new possible cases or new ways of refining our principles. We may find that our principles need to give more respect to rights, or aren’t attentive enough to the moral virtues of the agents in our situation.
In the third step of our method—repeat—we continue to reflect and test, and our toolbox of ethical theories still has a lot to offer us as we deepen our understanding of a problem.

As you practice reasoning about ethical problems, you’ll get better at using the tools of ethical theories. Those tools are our best hope to make progress. Just like a wrench can do many jobs but not all of them, not all ethical theories will be useful in each situation. Once again, practice will help us develop a sense of the right way to approach something.

figure.title: Photo by Artem Podrez: https://www.pexels.com/photo/tools-in-a-box-in-black-and-white-8985610/

imagedata.alt: Photo by Artem Podrez: https://www.pexels.com/photo/tools-in-a-box-in-black-and-white-8985610/

section.title: More Case Studies for Applying Ethical Theories
section.para: We’ll finish this chapter on ethical theories with three more case studies. As you read them, consider how different ethical theories would handle these situations.

note.title: Case Study #1: Coca-Cola
note.para: Joya Williams was a secretary who worked for the Coca-Cola Company in Atlanta. As part of her position, Williams had access to a lot of high-level company information, including notes about strategy and even future products. Adapted from https://content.time.com/time/subscriber/article/0,33009,1211565,00.html.

In 2006, Williams and two colleagues, Ibrahim Dimson and Edmund Duhaney, developed a plot to steal secrets from Coca-Cola and sell them to rival drinkmaker Pepsi. She used her company access to steal information about products and the details of upcoming promotions. Williams also took a sample of a new drink that was still in production and was not yet available in stores.

Dimson then contacted Pepsi to see if the company was interested in the secrets. Without Williams or the others knowing, Pepsi contacted Coca-Cola, which then contacted police. When Dimson met with a man he thought was a representative of Pepsi, he was actually meeting with an undercover FBI agent. Dimson took $30,000 in cash for some of the information and promised to sell more at a later date. At the second meeting, authorities arrested Dimson, Williams, and Duhaney.

For her participation in the scheme, Williams received a prison sentence of eight years. Dimson was to serve five, while Duhaney received a reduced sentence in exchange for his help in prosecuting Williams.

listitem.para: Would utilitarianism consider Williams’ action to be wrong? What about a duty-based ethical theory? What about a rights-based one? What about virtue theory? What about a feminist theory?
One notable aspect of this case is that Pepsi did not wait to contact Coca-Cola once they became aware of the stolen information. Did Pepsi have an ethical duty to act that way? Why or why not?
What obligations do employees have to their employers to refrain from speaking about what they learn while at work?

What kind of prison sentence would you consider to be appropriate for Williams, and why? (Consider that, for example, Coca-Cola suffered no material harm from her actions, and neither did any other business or person.)

note.title: Case Study #2: Boss Drug Use
note.para: Won-Ji worked at Buttons, a small retail establishment in Duluth, Minnesota. Buttons sells gifts and travel novelties to tourists. Won-Ji had five coworkers with whom he got along well. He received good pay for his labor and was happy at his job.

Won-Ji’s manager was Nicole, a single mother. Nicole took the manager position after moving from another state, where she went through a difficult divorce and a custody fight over parental rights to her daughter. She moved far from her ex-husband and was grateful for the chance to start something new.

Nicole treated Won-Ji and the other employees at Buttons fairly. She was sensitive to the ways they worked and tried to create a welcoming, friendly atmosphere. She loved working with customers and was competent at the other aspects of her job. She was always on time and helpful.

One day Won-Ji came in early for a shift and overheard Nicole talking to two other employees in the break room. She was inviting them to come to her house to use illegal drugs. She explained that she used the drugs sometimes to help herself relax, as she still had a troubling relationship with her ex-husband. She told the employees that she never used drugs while her daughter was home and didn’t use them often.

After hearing what his manager said, Won-Ji didn’t enter the break room. Later that day and throughout his shift, he acted as though he hadn’t heard anything. A few days later, he was able to confirm with his coworkers that Nicole had hosted them at her house. They got high and watched a movie, and Nicole’s daughter wasn’t around.

After the incident, Nicole continued to do the same superlative work as before. Won-Ji never witnessed her high at work, and she did not treat the employees who used drugs with her differently from anyone else.

listitem.para: Would utilitarianism consider Nicole’s action to be wrong? What about a duty-based ethical theory? What about a rights-based one? What about virtue theory? What about a feminist theory?
Did Won-Ji have an ethical obligation to inform anyone of Nicole’s drug use? What about the drug use of his coworkers?
Using our method of reflect and test, what ethical principle should govern Won-Ji’s behavior with respect to Nicole’s drug use? Can we extend that principle to other cases? How widely does it apply?

note.title: Case Study #3: Justine Sacco
note.para: In late 2013, Justine Sacco, a 30-year-old director of corporate communications at the media group IAC, was traveling from New York to South Africa, her home country, to visit family. During the long trip she posted several tweets about the people she was encountering in the airports of New York City and London. Before she took off for the longest leg of the trip, 11 hours from England to Cape Town, she posted a final message on her Twitter account: “Going to Africa. Hope I don’t get AIDS. Just kidding. I’m white!” She had 140 followers. Sacco boarded the plane less than an hour later. Since she wasn’t able to use her phone on the flight, she went to sleep.Adapted from https://www.nytimes.com/2015/02/15/magazine/how-one-stupid-tweet-ruined-justine-saccos-life.html

A few hours into the flight, without her knowing, someone retweeted Sacco’s post and it came to the attention of tech blogger Sam Biddle. Biddle, known for controversial headlines and articles, retweeted the message to 15,000 followers and posted it online with the headline, “And Now, a Funny Holiday Joke from IAC’s P.R. Boss.”

Biddle’s amplification of Sacco’s joke brought it to the attention of many more people, and in the half-day she spent on the flight, Sacco became world famous. Thousands of people retweeted the post, denouncing it as racist, and many others began to call for some kind of punishment. Other IAC employees began declaring that they would not work for the company as long as Sacco was there; IAC itself tweeted that Sacco’s tweet was an “outrageous, offensive comment,” but that the company could not reach her because she was still on the flight. The hashtag #HasJustineLandedYet began trending, which meant that millions of people were tracking Sacco’s flight to South Africa and waiting for the moment when she would land and be able to turn on her phone again. Someone from Cape Town even went to the airport to take a picture of her when she arrived.

Sacco’s phone exploded when she had service again, of course, and the deluge of hatred was so overwhelming that a friend had to delete Sacco’s account for her because she couldn’t bring herself to do it on her own.
Three weeks after her trip to Africa, Sacco cleaned out her desk at IAC. The company had fired her.

In later interviews, Sacco explained that she meant the tweet as a critique of white privilege, rather than an expression of it. “To me it was so insane of a comment for anyone to make,” she said. “I thought there was no way that anyone could possibly think it was literal.” She also wrote that “Living in America puts us in a bit of a bubble when it comes to what is going on in the third world. I was making fun of that bubble.”

listitem.para: Would utilitarianism consider Justine’s action to be wrong? What about a duty-based ethical theory? What about a rights-based one? What about virtue theory? What about a feminist theory?
Many people found Sacco’s original tweet offensive, but many others didn’t. To what extent does that disagreement matter in determining whether she did something wrong?
Did Sacco’s message cause harm? In what sense, and to whom?
IAC fired Sacco over her message. Why do you think they did so? Did they have an ethical obligation to end their relationship with her? Why or why not?
Was any wrong done to Sacco herself? What moral theory could we use to justify our answer?
Without the help of Sam Biddle, the tech blogger, it’s unlikely that Sacco’s tweet would have become so famous. Does he bear any responsibility for what happened to Sacco?

Had Sacco told her joke to a friend in private instead of tweeting it, nothing would have happened. To what extent does Twitter bear responsibility for the damage done to individuals and groups from use of its platform?

In the age of Twitter, Facebook, and other social media companies, what is the proper response from individuals and businesses to the offensive comments that employees or colleagues make on the internet?

section.title: Introduction to Economic and Political Systems

listitem.para: Understand the similarities and differences among major economic and political systems.
Recognize the features of different economic and political systems in the United States and other Western democracies.
Appreciate both the strengths and weaknesses of capitalist economic systems for ethics in general and for business ethics in particular.

section.title: Why Study Economic and Political Systems in Business Ethics?

figure.title:
Trees Preceeding a Mountain Landscape
Photo by Sagui Andrea via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: An open toolbox filled with wrenches, pliars, and screwdrivers.

section.para: In this chapter, we’ll be discussing ethical issues that arise from differences in how economic and political systems function. Our primary focus will be on capitalism, but we’ll also look at communism and socialism, along with some government types that tend to accompany these systems.

We’ll start by discussing why we’re devoting an entire chapter to this topic. One reason is obvious: there is already great controversy over certain interactions between businesses and governments, such as planned economies or programs of wealth redistribution. These aren’t just controversies about how beneficial or even how ethical these interactions are—some people believe that such programs are evil, whatever they might mean by that. Anything that can inspire such disagreement in a business context is worth looking at.

There’s a more important reason to have this chapter, though. Business professionals of all levels and backgrounds rarely, if ever, think about the ethically relevant aspects of the economic and government systems within which they work. It does not usually occur to them to turn critical attention toward those systems, and in fact it may even be difficult for them to imagine anyone asking ethical questions about them at all.

The blindness of business professionals toward these possibilities of ethical critique is not surprising and is in some ways a benefit to their careers and organizations. This blindness isn’t surprising, because the features of the economic system in which these professionals run their businesses are so ubiquitous and so normal to their lives that these features fade into the background, becoming a permanent part of the landscape that professionals navigate at work. For example, if your living situation requires you to have a long commute, you might not enjoy it, but you probably don’t question the ethics of your drive to and from work each day. The commute is a part of life which can be enjoyed or tolerated, but not interrogated on ethical grounds—the commute is just a feature of your life, like the trees outside your window or the mountains in the distance. For many people, the economic systems they function within are like trees, mountains, or a long commute. They’re just what is. They are the given and the norm.

For some of these same reasons, it’s probably to the advantage of most business professionals that they don’t constantly stop to consider the ethical dimensions of the institutions and laws that make their work possible. They’re worried about the next project, the next interview, or the next sale or contract; most are paid to get work done, not dissertate on the goodness or badness of the system. In addition, even if someone does consider the ethics of their economic and political surroundings, a single individual can have virtually no impact in changing those surroundings. The institutional mechanisms at play are so expansive and so deeply built into the foundations of a country or region that even those who dedicate their lives to changing them find it difficult to make any meaningful difference.

So it isn’t surprising, and it may be somewhat beneficial, that business professionals don’t stop to consider the ethically relevant aspects of their systems. Here’s the thing, though: all that can be true, yet it can still also be true that economic and political systems are legitimate targets for ethical analysis. In fact, none of this changes the reality that, for example, despite the good that capitalist economies do, they tend to produce serious harms as well. We can recognize both the good and bad features, and we can ask about their ethics and what we can do to make things better. While it may not be in our power to fix income inequality at large, we can still inform our practical decisions with reasonable analysis.

More broadly, there is an overwhelming tendency among working professionals to assume that the current economic and political systems we have are good simply because they are the ones we have. After all, if they weren’t good, we’d have some other systems, right? Isn’t that how things work? And since we don’t have other systems, the ones we have must be the good ones. And from that argument, it isn’t much of a leap to conclude that anything a business can do (or get away with) within a system must be ethical, because if it were unethical, we’d already have a law against it, of course.

It doesn’t take much thought to see the fallacious reasoning of the previous paragraph. There is no magical Ethical Seer guiding the development of economies and governments, making sure they stay on an acceptable course. Rather, we have the systems we have because the people and institutions who are able to form them have formed them, and because the people and institutions who have an interest in maintaining them have maintained them. Whether they are good, right, moral, or ethical is a question entirely separate from the reason for their existence—one we’ll have to ask for ourselves.

When we understand that we can ethically analyze even the foundations of an economic system, we’ll begin to see that things which always seemed to be part of the background will jump to our attention. We’ll want to ethically analyze them as well, in order to know whether there are better principles for guiding the actions of our professional lives.
That’s why we have this chapter! Let’s get started.

section.title: John Rawls and the “Original Position”
section.para: We’ll begin with a famous thought experiment from political theorist John Rawls. In his book A Theory of Justice, Rawls invites us to consider a purely hypothetical situation in which we are in the “ original positionan imaginary pre-life where nobody knows anything about what their actual lives will be like. ”: an imaginary pre-life where we don’t yet know what our actual lives will be like. From this original position, in fact, no one knows “his place in society, his class position or social status, nor does any one know his fortune in the distribution of natural assets and abilities, his intelligence, strength, and the like.”John Rawls, A Theory of Justice (Harvard University Press, 2005), 12. In other words, imagine that you don’t know anything at all about what your life will be like. Imagine that everyone else is in the same position—no one knows whether they’ll be born into money or poor, smart or middling, strong or weak. Rawls calls our lack of knowledge a “veil of ignorance.”

With the veil of ignorance around us, then, Rawls asks the key question: given that we don’t know anything about our actual situation, what principles would we want to govern our society? If we didn’t know our advantages and disadvantages in advance, how would we want society to work in areas like economic opportunity, social support systems, education, and others?

figure.title:
The Veil of Ignorance
Photo by Diana via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A curtain showing a shadow of a plant

section.para: Rawls’s argument is that, from the original position, the only rational conclusion is to prefer egalitarianPrinciples of justice that would assure that individuals are treated equally, not only in terms of protection by the law but in terms of what resources are available to them as well. principles of justice, or “justice as fairness.” Egalitarian principles of justice would assure that individuals are treated equally not only in terms of protection by the law but in terms of what resources are available to them as well. If, therefore, you would choose egalitarian principles while in the original position, Rawls thinks you should also choose them now—even if you’re the one who has to give up some advantages. That conclusion is a strong one, and maybe more practical than some people would want!

Rawls thought that justice as fairness amounted to two principles: the principle of equal basic liberties, and the difference principle. My discussion of these principles follows the treatments given in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “John Rawls,” by Leif Wenar, 2021, and The Cambridge Dictionary of Philosophy, “Rawls, John,” edited by Robert Audi, 2015, 905–906. The first of Rawls’s egalitarian principles, the principle of equal basic libertiesThe principle that all individuals are equal in their possession of certain fundamental liberties, such as freedom of conscience and freedom of political affiliation. , is that all individuals are equal in their possession of certain fundamental liberties, such as freedom of conscience and freedom of political affiliation. By means of laws, society has a duty to protect these freedoms for each individual. Note that, for Rawls, these liberties are more basic than economic liberties, such as the right to private property; if that right or others do exist, they must come later, and be subject to constraints dictated by the basic liberties. A founding document, such as a state’s constitution, enshrines these liberties in law.

While the first principle has to do with the government, the second has to do with a society’s economic system. The difference principleThe principle that social and economic inequalities can only exist if the inequalities accompany positions that everyone could occupy, so that there is fair equality of opportunity, and if the inequalities offer the greatest benefit to the least-advantaged members of a society. says that social and economic inequalities can only exist according to the following conditions: the inequalities must accompany positions that everyone could occupy, so that there is fair equality of opportunity; and the inequalities must offer the greatest benefit to the least-advantaged members of a society.

An example will help. In 2022 Mark Zuckerberg, the founder and CEO of Meta, made around $27 million. Paul Kunert, “Meta's Zuckerberg Paid $27M in ‘Other’ Compensation for 2022,” Offbeat, April 18, 2023, . In 2022, the average annual salary in America was about $54,000.Frank Russo, “How Much Does the Average American Make in 2022?” First Republic, December 7, 2022, . If we set Zuckerberg’s earnings at $27 million, then he makes 500 times the amount of money an average worker makes. That’s an astonishing difference; the inequality is unfathomable. And it’s the kind of inequality that Rawls’s difference principle would disallow, since the principle would concentrate the inequalities for the benefit of those less advantaged than Zuckerberg. One way to bring about that benefit would be to simply take much of Zuckerberg’s money and give it to other people.

figure.title:
Logo of Meta
Photo by Julio Lopez via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: Holding a Smartphone with the Threads App with the Meta Platforms Logo in the Background.

section.para: In addition, although taking Zuckerberg’s money and just handing it out to others does seem unfair on the surface, Rawls is trying to make a deeper point: if Zuckerberg didn’t know what his life would be like—if he didn’t know he would create Facebook and become a billionaire—then he too would have agreed to the difference principle in the original position, because agreeing to it would be the only rational thing to do when you have no knowledge of your actual life. So while in this instance the difference principle may seem to be unfair, the fairness in “justice as fairness” is more basic than that. It’s a fundamental fairness that Rawls thinks would be fair to everyone, and that everyone would agree on, from a perspective in which we knew nothing about how things would turn out in reality. It’s not just about fairly distributing goods. It’s about a system in which everyone agrees that distributing them that way is the right thing to do, because they recognize that everyone’s agreement is the foundation for the fairness.

Finally, the difference principle doesn’t say that there can’t be inequalities. In a society regulated by Rawls’s ideas, there would still be people who were wealthier than others. The principle only regulates how much wealthier they could be.

You may still disagree with Rawls, and that’s fine. The important thing here is to see that business ethics sometimes demands that we question even our most basic assumptions about the way a society works. One of the greatest victories we can achieve with our method of reflect and test is the knowledge that everything, no matter what, can be reflected upon and tested.

What would you choose from the original position, and why? What arguments could you make against Rawls’s difference principle? What justifications are there for income inequality as extreme as that between Zuckerberg and an average American worker?

section.title: Communism
section.para: This section and the next will discuss communism and socialism. Our focus will be on understanding these economic systems and on dispelling common myths about them. We will raise a few ethical issues involving them, but will concentrate our efforts on the ethical issues of capitalism, which is the economic system that has the greatest influence over most businesses.

Although the term has roots in France in the 1830s and 1840s, communismA system marked by the total abolition of private property, in favor of community- or public-owned property. is associated with the work of political theorist Karl Marx (1818–1883). The most crucial feature of a truly communist society would be the total abolition of private property, in favor of community- or public-owned property. It is important to see that the “community” or “public” spoken of here is not the government. In the years following some of Marx’s work, the term “communism” developed to refer to a certain kind of society, as we read in the following description:

blockquote.para: Communism, from then on, would designate both a classless society without property, without ownership—either private or nationalized—of the means of production, without commodity production, money or a state apparatus separate and apart from the members of the community, and the social-political movement to arrive at that society.Earnest Mandel, “Communism,” in Marxian Economics, ed. John Eatwell, Murray Milgate, Peter Newman, (Palgrave Macmillan UK, 1990), 87.

section.para: In a communist society built on the original ideals of Marx and others, there would be no government over and above the people, no money, and no private property. Communities would own the tools, machines, and other goods which produce the things they need, and each would take what they needed from what the community produced.

Thus communism is a way of organizing an economy and determining ownership of property. Nowadays, though, many people use the term “communism” to refer to specific kinds of authoritarian governments, such as those of Soviet Russia or China.China, for example, declared on 22 December, 1978 that they would replace their planned economy with a market economy; fifteen years later, they announced that they would move to a socialist market economy. See Yuqiao Xiang, “Business Ethics in China,” in The Routledge Companion to Business Ethics, ed. Eugene Heath, Byron Kaldis, and Alexei Marcoux, (Taylor & Francis, 2018), 593-605. Inasmuch as these countries are not moving their societies toward communism’s founding ideals, we cannot consider them truly communist; however, this derivative meaning of the term is common.

One of Marx’s primary concerns was the relationship that laborers had to their work, or to the products of their labor. These people belong to the “proletariat,” or the class which does not own the means of production. The proletariat contrast with the “bourgeoisie,” or class of capitalists who do own the means of producing goods. According to Marx, within a capitalist system,

blockquote.para: human beings experience a loss of control over their lives and over the creations that constitute the basic institutions and processes of society, such as the state and work. This alienation or estrangement means that human beings have a sense of living in a world that is alien and hostile, and they experience their lives as meaningless, unsatisfying, and worthless. Ultimately human beings live their lives in a way that is less than fully human; they are dehumanized.Elliott Johnson, David Walker, and Daniel Gray, Historical Dictionary of Marxism, (Rowman & Littlefield Publishers, 2014), 24.

section.para: Over time, as they gather and expand their resources, the bourgeoisie are able to dominate the lives of the proletariat. The proletariat are asked to do more in exchange for a shrinking share of what they produce; their lives become a battle to secure the basics necessary for subsistence.

Motivated by alienation and their precarious lives, Marx thought that the proletariat would carry out a revolution against the bourgeoisie. The revolution would bring about a socialist system as a step toward a true communist society.

These hopeful pronouncements from Marx about the course of history in a capitalist society stand opposite the unfortunate reality of communism’s fruits in the twentieth century. Its iterations in Russia and China, and especially the latter under Mao Zedong, are responsible for the deaths of tens of millions of people. These facts in themselves, independent of any other considerations, constitute an argument against communism as an economic system, despite the response that Mao and others “just didn’t implement it correctly.”

Western culture in general, and American business culture in particular, trains its practitioners to reject anything that carries the slightest whiff of communism. This isn’t a surprise, since Marx represents a threat to the established institutions and relationships that make capitalist business culture possible.

However, the atrocities of communism and the innate revulsion Americans feel toward it do not undermine the truth of many of Marx’s fundamental insights. Many laborers do experience alienation from their work; even knowledge workers, many of whom would belong to Marx’s bourgeoisie, feel this alienation. In some cases, large corporations do dominate the lives of their employees, and the internet allows them to set cultural and political agendas. Many Americans do struggle to meet their basic needs, at times forced by circumstance to live on vanishing wages even as economic growth balloons in other areas. We will discuss alienation and work in greater detail in .

As ethical thinkers, we must be able to recognize the faults of Marx’s analysis while also appreciating its virtues. Business ethics is not an all-or-nothing thing; if we don’t grow beyond a simplistic black-and-white view of ethics in the world, we will never be able to recognize the ethical nuances of most situations, and we’ll never be able to appreciate the good we could do by breaking away from familiar patterns and ways of thinking.For a fuller discussion of communism in the context of business ethics, see Karl Marx and Frederick Engels, Manifesto of the Communist Party, (Chicago: Charles H. Kerr & Company, 1906), and Toby Scharding, This Is Business Ethics: An Introduction, (Hoboken: John Wiley & Sons, Inc., 2018), chap. 6.

sidebar.title: Case Study: Activision Blizzard
sidebar.para: Activision Blizzard is one of America’s largest gaming companies. They produce titles such as Call of Duty, World of Warcraft, Diablo, Overwatch, and Candy Crush Saga, among many others. In the fiscal year from 2021 to 2022, they had over $7.6 billion in revenue, which was a decrease from over $8 billion the year previous.

One of the company’s most successful games is Hearthstone, a computer-based collectible card game with an adventure theme. In 2018, Hearthstone had over 100 million registered users all over the world, with many local and regional tournaments in addition to the Hearthstone Grandmasters, the worldwide championship.

Chung Ng Wai, a gamer better known by his moniker “Blitzchung,” was an elite Hearthstone player from Hong Kong, who had advanced to the Grandmasters tournament in October 2019. Zack Beauchamp, “One of America’s Biggest Gaming Companies Is Acting as China’s Censor,” Vox, October 8, 2019, . At the time, many pro-democracy protests were happening in Hong Kong, a country whose government operates under the supervision of China’s. After winning a Grandmasters match, Blitzchung gave an interview in which he said, “Liberate Hong Kong, revolution of our time,” repeating a slogan popular among the protesters.

Activision Blizzard wasted no time in laying down punishments. They determined that Blitzchung’s comment amounted to “engaging in any act that, in Blizzard’s sole discretion, brings you into public disrepute, offends a portion or group of the public, or otherwise damages Blizzard image.”Blizzard Entertainment, “Hearthstone Grandmasters Asia-Pacific Ruling,” October 8, 2019, . The company banned Blitzchung from competing for a year, stripped him of the prize money he had earned, and fired the commentators who had run the interview. The end of the company’s official statement read, “While we stand by one’s right to express individual thoughts and opinions, players and other participants that elect to participate in our esports competitions must abide by the official competition rules.”

Although China accounted for only a small percentage of Hearthstone’s userbase and revenue, J. Clement, “Net Revenue Generated by Activision Blizzard from 2007 to 2022, by Region,” Statista, February 9, 2023, . many in the gaming community felt that Activision Blizzard was capitulating to Chinese interests in order to protect its expansion into that country. Rather than stand against the oppression and injustice over which Hong Kong citizens were protesting, many gamers felt as though the company was acting as a bully mouthpiece for the Chinese government in its crackdown on the unrest.

listitem.para: Do you believe that the company’s punishment for Blitzchung was appropriate to his violation of the Hearthstone tournament rules? Why or why not?
In punishing Blitzchung, was Activision Blizzard acting as a proxy for the Chinese government?
In operating internationally, do American or other western companies have any obligation to advocate for values that may be in tension with values held in other regions?
What right to free speech do athletes and esports competitors have in their competitions, and in their roles as public figures more broadly?

section.title: Socialism
section.para: The next economic system we will consider is socialismAn economy where the means of production are owned by a government or some other social entity, such as a community organization. .
