An economy is socialist when the means of production are socially owned, which means that they may be owned by a government or some other social entity, such as a community organization. Socialist economies don’t necessarily disallow private property or for-profit enterprises run by individuals, and we can’t draw an exact line dividing capitalist economies, featuring private property, from more planned economies that nevertheless allow for private ownership of some goods.

In America, many people who speak about “communism” are actually referring to socialism, since they’re usually thinking about government redistribution of wealth or heavy government regulation of business activities. As noted in the previous section, a true communist society has no government ownership of the means of production because there is no government. Governments are the groups which tend to own the property in socialist economies.

As used popularly, “socialism” also connotes a government-organized system for distributing wealth within a society. This distribution can take many forms: a universal basic income, industry subsidies, and welfare benefits are some common approaches.

There are already many socialist aspects to the economic system of the United States. The program of “food stamps,” now called SNAP, or the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, is a good example. SNAP provides help for low-income individuals and families to buy food, usually by giving them a special debit card which they can only use to purchase things to eat or drink. Depending on how long their nutrition benefits last, recipients of SNAP benefits receive a monthly deposit in their account.

Another such program is WIC, a specialized supplemental nutrition program for women, infants, and children (from which the program gets it name). Recipients of WIC benefits may also receive a debit card but more often get coupons which they exchange at the point of sale for supplies like baby formula, fruits, vegetables, cereal, and other basic foods. WIC focuses on new mothers and young children in low-income families that may not be able to meet nutrition needs.

We don’t need to worry about whether programs like SNAP and WIC are “truly” socialist. It’s enough to recognize that taxpayers—most of whom will not receive SNAP or WIC benefits at all, much less for an extended time—fund these programs through their taxes, and that local and state governments administer them. While these examples don’t necessarily involve the means of production, they represent the socialist spirit of government and community-based organizations running the institutions that provide basic necessities.

In thinking of socialism, many people associate the economic system with countries like Finland, which has a very high personal income tax rate and sales tax but also provides many government-subsidized or government-assisted social benefits. Once again, these features in themselves are socialist-leaning, but are not enough to determine whether a country has a truly socialist economic system. Inasmuch as Finland, Norway, Japan, Belgium, and other countries have a free and open market with legal ownership of private property and the means of production, then they can tax or redistribute wealth at whatever rates they’d like, but they still wouldn’t be socialist. They are capitalist economies with strong, institutionalized programs of government assistance.

figure.title:
A Hospital to Illustrate Social Medical Benefits
Photo by Tom Fisk via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A Hospital at Night.

sidebar.title: Case Study: Social Security
sidebar.para: Social Security is one of the primary government-administered financial benefits in the United States. Started in 1935 as part of a larger response to the Great Depression, Social Security now has an annual budget of more than one trillion dollars and paid out over one trillion dollars in benefits to an estimated 66 million Americans in 2022.

The vast majority of funds for Social Security come from the Social Security tax, a federal tax imposed on almost all employees in the United States, regardless of profession or income. This tax takes 6.2% of all income up to a certain taxable amount, and the resulting money then makes its way to Social Security beneficiaries around the country.
There are various ways to qualify for Social Security benefits, but each of them requires that an individual’s situation be different from that of most normal workers. Here are the ways to qualify:

listitem.para: You are age 62 or older.
You are blind and have accumulated enough work credits.
You are otherwise disabled.

sidebar.para: These requirements ensure that the vast majority of workers will not receive benefits until they either get older or get in an accident.

In 2023, the monthly maximum payment amounts are $914 for an eligible individual, $1,371 for an eligible individual with an eligible spouse, and $458 for an essential person (an “essential person” is someone who lives with a Social Security recipient and provides some sort of care).

Some of the most important questions about Social Security concern whether the program will be able to continue to fund itself into the future. As the number of beneficiaries increases, Social Security’s budget will need to increase as well, but whether it can do so will determine whether those paying taxes into the program now will actually receive benefits when they become eligible.

listitem.para: Is the Social Security program in the United States an example of communism? Why or why not? Is it an example of socialism? Why or why not?
What ethical justifications could be given for a program of Social Security, in which those who fund the program may not ever actually reach eligibility for its benefits?
Is the Social Security program an example of Rawls’s “justice as fairness”?
Should workers who currently pay Social Security tax be able to opt out of paying the tax, in exchange for agreeing not to receive any benefit in the future? Why or why not?
What obligations does a government owe its citizens who, for age, disability, or some other reason, are no longer able to work? Why?

section.title: Capitalism
section.para: The third and final economic system we’ll discuss in this chapter is capitalisman economic system characterized primarily by the private ownership of property and by the general absence of government regulation of business. . Capitalism happens to be the dominant system in most areas of the world, and since most business students and professionals spend all their time working in it, we’ll discuss it in greater detail than the other two systems, and will see more of its features in relation to ethical problems.

First, the system. Capitalism is an economic system characterized primarily by the private ownership of property. We understand the term “property” broadly here to include not only dwelling-places and land but also material goods, intellectual goods, and one’s own labor. As a consequence, an important feature distinguishing capitalism from socialism and communism is that it allows the near-total private ownership of the means of production. For the most part, individuals, groups, or corporations are the entities owning this property, rather than the government or other state-sponsored organizations.

Another characteristic of capitalism is the general absence of government regulation of business. In other words, in a capitalist economy, governments tend to avoid making laws that restrict how people can or cannot run their businesses. In general, businesses are free to decide what goods or services they will offer and how they will offer them, without much interference from a state.

Rather than regulate business activities through laws, capitalist economies prefer to let market forcesThe pressures of supply and demand which members of a market community exert on each other, on goods, and on other markets. regulate the system by themselves. A marketA community of individuals and organizations who buy and sell goods and services. is a community of individuals and organizations who buy and sell goods and services. In some places, a “market” might be an actual place, like a village center where community members gather to trade. We use the term “market” more abstractly here, though, since market activities can take place virtually anywhere; each person and each asset is part of one or more different markets.

Market forces are the pressures of supply and demand which members of a market community exert on each other, on goods, and on other markets. If the demand increases for ice cream during a hot summer, then ice cream producers and suppliers face pressure to meet that demand and satisfy that market force. They may therefore increase their supply of raw materials, increase output, hire more workers, or take other actions in response to that force.

figure.title:
Summer Ice Cream
Photo by Kamaji Ogino via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A child holding ice cream

section.para: As we said, capitalist economies prefer to regulate business activities through market forces, rather than through legal means or government oversight. Here’s a simple example of how this could happen. Suppose a member of a market intends to advertise and sell hand-made cakes, but in reality their cakes are made by a cake-making robot. Those who buy the cakes do so on the assumption that they’re buying one product but they actually receive another. One way to solve this problem would be by making laws about how cake-making businesses are to be regulated, perhaps involving site visits by regulatory officials at all locations which claim to make “hand-made” cakes. On the other hand, in certain conditions market forces may regulate this sort of business on their own. If it was discovered or suspected that the cakes were not in fact hand-made, then demand for them might decrease; if it fell enough, the business would cease to exist. In that way, market forces might be able to produce the outcome we desire by means other than government regulation.

Generally speaking, market forces determine how events unfold in a capitalist economy. Economist and political theorist Adam Smith dubbed this phenomenon the “invisible hand.” According to Smith, markets will tend to regulate themselves across time by the operation of different market forces. Smith assumes that most of these regulations will produce beneficial outcomes, and so from the outside, the market will look as though an “invisible hand” is guiding it in desirable directions. The hand is invisible, though, since there is no central regulatory body which determines how things happen; there are just markets and market forces operating in them.

A fundamental assumption in most capitalist economies is that the members of markets are acting in their own self-interest: they buy, sell, work, and otherwise act within markets to satisfy their own needs. Another assumption of Adam Smith’s invisible hand is that these self-interested actions will, in general, produce outcomes that are not just beneficial for the self-interested individuals who perform them; rather, they’ll benefit the market or a society as a whole. Thus, by self-interested individuals acting and market forces operating, a capitalist economy runs itself in many areas of business, in keeping with the idea of minimal government intervention.

We’ll discuss some of the ethical issues involved in capitalism in the next section. There’s no denying, however, that capitalism has been a spectacular engine of creation and wealth-generation in the world’s history. It is responsible for massive shifts in the lifestyle and ways of working of billions of people; it is at least partly responsible for improved standards of living in many areas and for the wide availability of quality goods and services in many industries.

If that was all capitalism did, though, we wouldn’t be talking about it in a textbook on business ethics. In the next few sections we’ll be looking at some of the ideas behind capitalist economies and some ethical problems we tend to find in capitalist environments.

Before we get there, let’s wrap up our discussion of capitalism as an economic system distinct from the others we’ve discussed. Table 1 gives some of the key characteristics of these systems and compares them against each other.

When the balance of elements tips toward socialism or capitalism, then it’s reasonable to call an entire system by that name. But we cannot forget that each system is a mixture of elements, and each industry or even sub-industry may greatly differ in its features from other industries or sub-industries.

table.caption: A comparison of communist, socialist, and capitalist economic systems.

section.title: Capitalism and Private Property
section.para: As we said in the previous section, an important feature of capitalist economies is the existence, backed by laws, of privately-owned property. In this section, we’ll discuss two approaches to justifying private property, and we’ll have a case study on CEO earnings.

We find one of the earliest serious attempts at justifying the existence of private property in the work of English political philosopher John Locke (1632–1704), who wrote a book called Two Treatises on Government. You might wonder, though—why would anyone need to justify the existence of private property? Why would anyone need to gives reasons, for example, for why the shirt I’m wearing is mine, and not anybody else’s? Wouldn’t it be weird if private property didn’t exist? Isn’t it a default expectation of much of our social behavior?

It’s difficult, but if we can wrench our minds away from what we’re used to, we might imagine the non-existence of private property—suppose, let’s say, that I make myself a sandwich, and I go outside for a walk. I’m enjoying the sandwich, but someone walks by and takes it out of my hands and finishes it in a single bite. I’m mad—the sandwich was good, and I’m still hungry. I say, “That was mine!” This claim of the sandwich being “mine” is built on the idea not just that I made the sandwich, or that I am currently the one possessing it, but that I have some claim on the sandwich—legally or otherwise, I am entitled to that sandwich. But I have this claim and entitlement only if private property really does exist—only if my claim to the sandwich is legitimate, or can be backed by reasons and arguments.

figure.title:
Whose Sandwich?
Photo by Roberto Hund via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A woman holds a sandwich on a park bench

section.para: One reason that could legitimize my claim to the sandwich, and to private property in general, is that a society full of sandwich-takers could not long function; everyone would be taking each other’s sandwiches, as well as all their other stuff too, and nobody could expect that what they possessed at one moment would be theirs at the next. It might not be possible to live very well or even very long in such a society, and so for that reason, we require the idea of private property in order to bring some stability to life in a community.

This justification for private property is in the spirit of the core idea behind Locke’s state of nature. A “state of nature” is an imagined situation in which all people live without cities, technology, or other modern developments, in simple dwellings with their families. In that situation, Locke imagines, there is no need for a government; that need only arises when the individuals and families begin to wonder about how to use the resources they all seem to have in common. That is, there’s an abundance of trees, water, food, and other resources, which are freely available to everyone; in the state of nature, there’s no need for anyone to “own” anything, since there’s more than enough for all.

But we don’t live in a state of nature, and it’s not clear that humans ever did; in entering the real world, those coming from a state of nature face a situation like I did when I was walking with my sandwich. I feel that the sandwich is mine; it isn’t just a common resource, and there isn’t enough for everyone. So what justifies my claim to the sandwich being my private property?

Locke says that my claims rest on my ownership of my own body and mind.Tobey Scharding, This Is Business Ethics: An Introduction, (Wiley-Blackwell, 2018) 96–100. In our sandwich thought experiment, we imagined that private property didn’t exist—but we didn’t consider whether my own body parts, or my own thoughts, could legitimately belong to me or even to someone else. According to Locke, my own body and mind are my property, because God made me, and as such my parts and thoughts belong to me. They are my private property, and so therefore some amount of private property already exists.

If you’re unsure about Locke’s appeal to God, we might put the argument this way: the existence of private property in general seems to depend on there being at least one specific example of private property. The most uncontroversial example of private property would be our own minds and bodies; if they aren’t legitimate private property, then nothing is. We must therefore begin by assuming that our minds and bodies are our private property, or we’ll never get anywhere.

Locke then says that our labor, or the actions we perform with our bodies and minds, can cause part of the common resources to become mine, and thereby become private property. So when I chop some of that wood, and shape it into logs and then build a cabin, I have used my labor to reshape part of the resources everyone shared. Because of my labor, that part is now mine—the cabin has become my private property. My labor gives me a legitimate claim to it; it belongs to me.

Locke’s basic reasoning, then, starts with the state of nature, in which everyone shares the world’s goods. But our bodies and minds always count as private property; they are uncontroversial cases of it, and without them, we’d have little claim on anything as private property. The use of our bodies and minds can then extend our claim of private property to other things that were formerly held in common—that portion on which we labor becomes our own. Thus Locke can justify the private property of not only our bodies, but of many other things as well.

Locke’s attempt to justify private properties gives shape to the conviction many people have, at least in the western world, that we really do own certain things. We won’t cover more details of Locke’s view here. The point to remember is that the existence of private property is something that must be justified. The fact that it seems obvious and even necessary for private property to be justifiable does not mean that it is in fact justifiable, nor does it mean that it will strike everyone as obvious and necessary in the same way.

American political philosopher Robert Nozick (1938–2002), for example, pointed out a significant issue in Locke’s view of private property. According to Nozick, it isn’t enough to justify the existence of private property; there must also be rules for what we can do with that private property. As he puts it, “one’s property right in a knife does not include the right to replace it between someone else’s ribs against their will.” In other words, there must be some moral principles that limit the use of private property, for our use of it cannot “cross another’s moral boundary.”Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia, (Basic Books, 1999), 282.

Another issue is the existence of public goods, such as water. A water purification company may clean a region’s water, and a distributor or utility company may deliver it to customers; these entities have thus added their labor. But does that mean they “own” the water? Is it possible to “own,” as private property, the water in pipes or in the ground?

To finish this section, note the similarities and differences between Locke and John Rawls, whom we discussed earlier. Locke’s “state of nature” and Rawls’ “original position” are both imaginary scenarios designed to make us think about how we relate to goods and to other people. In this they are similar. They differ, though, in the lessons they draw. Locke argues that private property may be unequally distributed from the very beginning, because different individuals may exercise their labor to different extents and thus make more goods their own. Rawls would have us distribute this property equitably before the question of labor even arises.

sidebar.title: Case Study: Private Property
sidebar.para: This case study will be about private property and money, or the idea that each person is “entitled” to what they earn.

The CEO of Meta, Mark Zuckerberg, earns between one and three billion dollars per year in equity-based compensation. In 2021, Elon Musk, founder of Tesla and SpaceX, earned approximately ten billion dollars; Robert Scaringe, CEO of Rivian, around two billion. Apple CEO Tim Cook makes several hundred million dollars yearly, and so do many CEOs of other companies.

At the same time, the average American worker earns less than $60,000 per year. That means that the average worker earns roughly 166,000 times less than Musk did in 2021. That worker’s salary would have to double more than twenty-five times to reach Musk’s.

The wealth of these individuals would seem to be their “private property”—it’s the result of their labor, and so they “own” the product of that labor. But for many wealthy people, their wealth continues to accumulate regardless of whether they do anything; they don’t need to labor, because their private property is arranged in a such a way as to labor for them. Do they still own the products of that labor, then, in Locke’s sense? Or perhaps in some other sense?

Another example is hedge fund managers. Some earn hundreds of millions of dollars per year, but in what sense is it true that they have “earned” this money? It cannot be that they’ve earned it in the same sense that a childcare provider earns her paycheck, for taking care of children requires much more effortful physical labor than does managing numbers. A person who earns more than a billion dollars per year earns more than $30 per second, for every single day in that year. In addition, the pay of many hedge fund managers is not at all proportional to their performance, for their rising pay is not linked to actual increases in the value of the funds they manage. From 2011 to 2020, for instance, the average S&P 500 index fund outperformed the average hedge fund in each year.Mark J. Perry, “The SP 500 Index Out-Performed Hedge Funds over the Last 10 Years. And It Wasn’t Even Close,” American Enterprise Institute (blog), January 7, 2021, . In other words, if they used the labor of hedge funds, most investors would do worse than they would by putting their money in index funds and then doing nothing.

Are people whose wealth so astronomically outstrips that of their employees or average workers “entitled” to their wealth as private property? They may be, but the conditions of the American economy, as well as the sheer numbers involved, make their situations very different from any that Locke could have imagined.

listitem.para: In what sense does someone who makes one billion dollars per year “earn” that amount of money?
What gives labor value? What, for example, makes Elon Musk’s “labor” so much more economically valuable than that of a childcare provider?

Should money be considered private property in the same sense as material goods, such as food or shelter? Do the rules which govern the distribution and protection of private property apply to money as well? Why or why not?
Can the wage gap between an average worker and a CEO be justified on Locke’s theory of private property?
Can the wage gap between an average worker and a CEO be justified on Rawls’ theory of the original position?

Capitalist economies are characterized by a relative absence of government regulation on business. Under what circumstances could governments have a justification to (forcibly, if necessary) redistribute the money of extremely wealthy corporations or individuals?

section.title: Capitalism and Government Regulation
section.para: As we’ve noted, one of the features of capitalism is that it tends to discourage government regulation of businesses. The government is considered to be slow and cumbersome; at times, government interference in business seems like the experience of going to the DMV for a new driver’s license. Everyone knows the normal way of doing things doesn’t work, but how can we change it? It’s the government, you know, and those are the laws.

The reputation of government regulation as being slow to act is well earned. A good recent example is the cryptocurrency industry, which came about in its recognizable form in 2009. In less than two decades since then, almost 10,000 cryptocurrencies have hit the market, and there are certainly more to come. The industry is accelerating despite massive losses in some sectors and outright scandals in others, such as the collapse of FTX, a leading cryptocurrency exchange. Amid this rapid movement, industry standards are being made up and revised as things change. Both the technology that makes the industry possible and its normal industry practices are developing so fast that no one, not even those most closely involved with its development, can say for sure where it will end up next.

Thus we end up with the circumstances that cryptocurrency faces now: although the industry handles billions of dollars and its fluctuations affect billions more, it’s a financial domain that’s almost totally unregulated. It’s even difficult to call it an “industry,” as there is no central organization or group responsible for the development of crypto, and this decentralized, authority-less state is intentional.

This lack of regulation has both a positive and a negative side. On the positive side, crypto is open to anyone who wants to be involved on either the creation or investment sides. Billy Markus and Jackson Palmer created Dogecoin in a few hours in 2013, as a way to make fun of Bitcoin and other early digital currencies. Nevertheless, Dogecoin grew, and it’s now one of the largest and most valuable cryptocurrencies in the world. At one point in 2020, the price of Dogecoin rose 800% in less than a day.Arjun Kharpal, “Reddit Frenzy Pumps Up Dogecoin, a Cryptocurrency Started as a Joke,” CNBC, January 28, 2021, .

On the other (negative) side we have a company like FTX, mentioned above. FTX, short for “Futures Exchange,” was a cryptocurrency exchange and hedge fund that managed billions in assets, but also relied on fraudulent relationships between itself and subsidiary companies as well as misuse of customer funds. In late 2022, FTX cofounder Sam Bankman-Fried was charged for his role in plans to influence elections using those funds. In addition, he had been arrested prior to that charge on suspicion of fraud.Phil McCausland, “Samuel Bankman-Fried Accused of Making Illegal Campaign Contributions,” NBC, December 13, 2022, . Customers small and large lost billions of dollars with the fall of FTX, and it wasn’t clear whether much of that money would ever be recoverable.

FTX operated in an unregulated industry, and thus its customers were not able to rely on the same sort of regulatory protections that exist in other financial markets. Yet it’s worth asking whether it’s even possible for the SEC or other groups to effectively regulate a decentralized industry that changes as quickly as technology does. How should governments try to protect consumers in such a market, if at all?

From here we can appreciate the most fundamental ethical question about government regulation in business. Assuming that some minimal level of regulation is necessary—how do we decide what to regulate, and when and how to regulate it exactly? This question manifests in different ways for different industries. In the case of local businesses, less regulation is probably best; in the case of the food production and foodservice industries, we need enough to reach a reasonable level of safe consumption; for internet-based vendors, less might be best too. But each industry requires its own approach, and in the case of cryptocurrency, it simply may not be possible to regulate it in the way we would like.

More generally, government regulation of business is not a failsafe; it is not possible to perfectly protect consumers. Those who invested in FTX knew, or at least reasonably should have known, that they were entering a volatile, unprotected market characterized by frequent, wild changes in value. Are they to blame for their losses? Does the government have an obligation to offer them reasonable protections by enforcing laws about how cryptocurrency platforms can function? If it does, how far does the obligation extend? If it doesn’t, does it have an obligation to regulate any financial industry, or offer any level of protection to any investor?

A related issue concerns the regulation of monopolies. The three primary antitrust laws in the United States—the Sherman Act (1890), the Federal Trade Commission Act (1914), and the Clayton Act (1914)—prohibit “every contract, combination, or conspiracy in restraint of trade”15 U.S.C. § 1. and all “unfair methods of competition . . . and unfair or deceptive acts or practices.”15 U.S.C § 45(a)(1). These laws do not normally restrict the size of businesses, focusing instead on whether they restrict competition among businesses. But whether there is competition among businesses is a determination we make relative to a given region or geographical area.

For example, consider the question of internet access. There are many internet service providers in the United States: AT&T, Verizon, Xfinity, Cox, and Spectrum are just some of the largest. In some areas of the country, these companies do compete against each other, and customers can choose from among several options. But a quarter of the country—over 80 million people—has no such choice. Those people are able to access the internet through only a single provider, or they must choose between high-speed internet and a much slower alternative, which for many people is not a real option.Christopher Mitchell and Katie Kienbaum, “Report: Most Americans Have No Real Choice in Internet Providers,” Institute for Local Self-Reliance, August 12, 2020, .

Thus monopolies both do and don’t exist in internet access, depending on the scale at which we look. If we look at the scale of the entire country, we see competition between many companies, large and small. But if we look at a smaller scale and examine specific places, there are many effective monopolies.

From an ethical perspective we can therefore ask, at what scale should antitrust laws apply to companies? Can they apply in more limited areas? Or do they only apply to the market as a whole? The answers to these questions aren’t trivial. Companies with an effective monopoly over internet access, or over other industries within certain areas, are free to charge what they wish or treat customers however they want, without the normal mechanisms of a free market being able to correct the problem. Customers could drop their internet access, of course, but for many people this would not be possible. We might even consider internet access to be a public good, like air and water.

As you consider the role of government regulation in business, keep in mind that it may not be possible to find ethical principles that give perfect guidance in all cases. Most of the time, and especially for unsettled or volatile markets, we can’t know what the right thing to do is. We must choose our ethical values, such as protecting individual consumers, and then make the best possible decisions with limited information.

sidebar.title: Case Study: Texas Utilities
sidebar.para: Texas is the second-largest state in the United States and the second-most populous, with more than 30 million inhabitants. Supplying such a huge number of people with utilities is a major policy, engineering, and operational project. In 2021, Texas had almost nine hundred thousand energy workers, representing more than 10% of all energy jobs in the United States.

Utilities in Texas are notable not only for the size and population they must supply but also for the way the infrastructure is set up in relation to other states. The most important of these here is the power grid. In the United States, the electric “grid” or infrastructure system for electricity is divided into three parts: one for western states, one for eastern states, and one for Texas. It may seem unusual that a state, even one as large as Texas, has its own power grid, but in the early twentieth century the state decided to go it alone for electricity. As other states and the federal government were deciding who could sell electricity where, for how much, and across which state lines, Texas decided to remove themselves from the national power grid and create their own system. The state would generate its own power and not send any of it to other states in an effort to make sure it could supply the needs of its own citizens.

Texas does in fact face an unusual problem in supplying electricity, making it different from other states. The state is so large east-to-west that there can be massive differences in power demands made by people on the eastern side compared to those on the western side. In other words, because sunset times can be so different from each other among cities in Texas, there may be significantly different power demands depending on where you live. The demands aren’t uniform across the region that Texas power companies supply.

In addition to this difference from other states, though, Texas’s choice about its own power grid was also about being free from federal electricity regulations. Texas power companies could operate more how they wanted and less how they were told to, and in some cases this freedom led to lower prices and better power service for Texas residents. But the lack of regulation also meant that power companies in Texas could maintain the infrastructure in the way they chose as well, and weren’t subject to requirements that might otherwise have made their power grid more reliable.

This problem emerged very quickly and very seriously in February of 2021. Over Valentine’s Day, snow and sleet pounded many areas of the state. Since Texas normally has mild winter temperatures, roads and other services quickly became unusable, and most people stayed home. And since the temperature was freezing, they required much more power than normal to heat those homes: demand for electricity skyrocketed. The power grid could not meet this demand, however, and millions were left without power in some of the coldest temperatures ever recorded in the state.

As pipes burst in unheated homes and people burned furniture and other possessions to stay warm, there was nothing the electricity grid could do to help. It simply was not equipped to handle such a weather event; many places were without electricity for days in temperatures that stayed below freezing for dozens of hours at a time. In all, around 250 people lost their lives. The majority froze to death. The storm also caused billions of dollars in damages.

listitem.para: What right, if any, do states have to make their own regulatory rules in response to federal-level business and infrastructure regulation?

What responsibilities do utility companies, such as those in Texas, have to prepare their infrastructure systems for extreme weather events? Remember, the ice storm of 2021 was a rare occurrence, but not so rare that it we wouldn’t expect it to happen again in the next few decades.

Under what circumstances should governments regulate utilities such as electricity and water distribution? Does control of these services belong in a special regulatory category that differs from, say, control over sales tax across states?
Who, if anyone, should be held accountable for the deaths of those Texans who froze in the ice storm?
What other ethical questions does this case study raise?

section.title: Capitalism and Ethics
section.para: Let’s bring to a close our discussion of economic and political systems by broadening the scope of the ethical problems involved in capitalism. We’ll be looking specifically at how capitalism’s actual implementation, along with the assumptions built into it, raise questions about how ethical the economic system can really be.

We’ll begin by imagining a system of pure capitalism—one completely free of government interference of any kind. Note that we aren’t imagining Locke’s state of nature, though, or Rawls’s original position; those are idealizations meant to illustrate certain principles about setting up governments and economies. Here we’re imagining that we live in the place we live now, but our economic and market interactions with each other and with businesses are completely free of laws or rules set by regulatory agencies.

So imagine that we head to the store to buy some fruits and vegetables in order to prepare a meal. We go to the produce section and notice that there are three different brands of a certain kind of apple, and we can choose from any of them. They’re all the same price. How do we know which to choose? How do we make such a decision?

Before we start to answer, we want to remember what’s different about the world we’re imagining: we’re pretending that there is no government regulation of any kind on the way businesses perform their functions. When we’re in the produce section in the real world, it may never occur to us, but for any given item we can be reasonably sure that it is safe—that the products used to grow it were safe, that the processes used to pick and store it were safe, and that the distribution chain and store’s handling of it were safe. We can have this confidence because, in the real world, there are regulatory agencies that make and enforce rules about these practices. But in our imaginary world, there are no such regulatory agencies; the growers, pickers, distributors, and stores that handle apples (and every other product) are free to run things the way they please.

Staring at the three kinds of apples, then, we might first search for information online about the three different brands, to see which is safer or which has a better reputation. This would be a reasonable thing to do, but it’s also an action that’s only recently been possible, since before the internet it would have been very difficult or even impossible to find detailed information about companies and their production processes.

Focusing on the information available on the internet, though, obscures an important fact about our situation in this government interference-free imaginary world: the only thing constraining the way a company does business is its mandate to seek profit. That is, the only thing stopping a company from cutting corners in its production processes is that doing so might be harmful to its bottom line; if it gained a reputation for producing applies that made people sick or didn’t taste good, it would lose revenue and might cease to exist.

Thus, in the absence of government regulation, the profit motiveThe mandate to make as much money as possible. , or the mandate to make as much money as possible, would regulate business practices. The profit motive appeals to the self-interest of those whom it motivates: earning more money seems to be in the self-interest of business owners, and earning less money would go against that interest, and so it would seem that the profit motive would produce a sort of self-regulation whereby businesses would ensure that they are keeping employees and customers safe. To do otherwise would appear to contradict the profit motive and its appeal to an individual’s self-interest.

The history of business practice teaches us otherwise, however. It teaches us instead that, rather than self-regulate with the interests of customers in mind, many businesses allow the profit motive to override ethical considerations. In fact, it would be more precise to say that the seeking of profit becomes the primary “ethical” imperative by which many businesses act; seeking profit becomes an ethical activity in itself. And when this happens, the only “unethical” thing would be something that harmed a business’s profits. From Ford’s Pinto to Enron to countless other cases, capitalist motives are transformed into a system where anything that a business can get away with in the long run is ethical, because ethics is about seeking profit.

You may disagree here, on the basis that we’re taking an unduly negative attitude toward businesses and their motives. There would be good reasons to disagree, because some businesses care deeply about their employees and customers; for some companies, “ethics” is a real thing, separate from seeking profit, and those companies are willing to put their money where their mouth is in order to take an ethical position regardless of the financial consequences. Some companies really do care.

While that is true, it is equally true that the vast majority of economic interactions—certainly in reality, as well as in our hypothetical regulation-free economy—are governed by the profit motive, rather than any ethical considerations. And this raises the question of whether, on a large scale and in the long run, ethical behavior is really possible in an economic system based on self-interest. By “large-scale” we mean an economic system the size of an interconnected world; by “in the long run,” we mean not just in the near future but in the more distant future as well. Is ethical behavior possible in an economic system based on self-interest, at that scale and for that time?

At least right now, perhaps the correct answer to that question is, “Not always, and only with great difficulty.” But we cannot yet say what the answer to this question will be in the future. As it stands in the United States, the actual result of capitalism, regardless of its noble intentions, is to create a reasonable standard of living for many people, but also to concentrate an enormous amount of wealth in the hands of a very small number of individuals. Due to their wealth, these individuals then get a drastically disproportionate say in the ongoing creation of that system, and tend to guide it in a way that best suits their own self-interest. In a sense, the features of the American economic system reflect not just what would be good for people in general, but what would be good for the small number of people who get to make the rules.

Is ethical behavior possible in that system? Is it possible for companies to be ethical in a system that encourages their untrammeled growth and that perpetuates significant and sometimes crushing income equality? Is a capitalist economy compatible with principles that stem not from economic expediency or profit, but from considered reflection on how to treat others and on what makes human lives good?

Perhaps. Business professionals answer these questions by their actions every day; but it may be the system itself, rather than individual decisions, that must change before we can achieve a vision of ethical behavior in a system built on seeking profit in the service of self-interest.

This isn’t a call for a proletariat revolution, nor is it a naïve denunciation of corporate behavior made from a privileged background that is itself only possible because of that same corporate behavior. It’s merely an injunction to remember that the system in which we live, and the imperatives by which it operates, are not the unchangeable given; we decide whether we will guide our behavior by those imperatives, through our action or inaction. And the only ethical thing to do to a system that is failing many of its members would be to make a change.

In that way, then, ethical behavior is possible in a system based on self-interest—but only by recognizing that ethics does not perfectly overlap with self-interest, and that the “self-interest” involved in a system must at least sometimes reach beyond our own if it is to have any ethical value at all.

listitem.para: Understand the idea of corporate responsibility and what difference the idea makes to business operations.
Identify and apply the most important theories of corporate responsibility.
Consider the effect of corporate codes of ethics on how businesses see themselves and on how they operate.
Apply the lessons of corporate responsibility to your own work as a business professional.

section.title: Corporate Responsibility: What Could It Be?
section.para: In our first three chapters we focused on broad ethical ideas that apply to many different situations. We also examined how the background systems in which economies and markets operate shape the ethical landscape for both individuals and companies.

The remaining chapters will use those broad ideas to look at ethical issues in many narrower contexts. We’ll start by discussing corporate responsibility: does it exist? If it does, what does it amount to, and why?

Before we begin, let’s take a look at the idea of responsibilityThe principle of being accountable for something; generally, someone is reponsible for something when they played a role in creating it or allowing it to exist. itself. Someone who is responsible for something can be held accountable for that thing; they have played a role in creating it or allowing it to exist. But there are different senses in which a person can be responsible for something, and not all of them are equally relevant for business ethics.

For example, I can be “causally” (not “casually,” note the difference) responsible for something when I am the cause of it. If I’m hammering a nail into a wall in order to hang a picture, but the hammer accidentally slips out of my hand and breaks the TV, then I am the cause of the TV breaking. It was my action involving the hammer that broke the TV; if I hadn’t done what I did, the TV wouldn’t have broken. Since I’m causally responsible, if someone sees the TV and asks, “Who did that?” it would make sense for everyone to point their finger at me.

figure.title:
Hammering a Broken Television
Photo by Cottonbro Studios via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A person swinging a mallet at a broken Television

section.para: I can also be morally responsible for something. This means that I can be held accountable for an outcome—not only as a cause, but as an agent capable of making moral decisions (an “agent” is just someone who can act on their own will). When we are morally responsible for something, it makes sense to talk about reward and punishment, or whether I’ve done the right or wrong thing. If no one cares about the TV, for example, then even if I break it, I’m not morally responsible for the action, because there’s no issue of right and wrong. But if I walk into someone’s house unannounced and smash their TV with a hammer, then I’ve done a wrong thing. I’m responsible for the broken TV not only as a cause, but also as a moral agent.

Moral responsibility is the kind of responsibility we mean when we say things like, “She’s a good person” or “He has a lot of good qualities.” We mean that these people are good in a moral sense—not at soccer or at singing, but at being a person. Moral goodness is goodness of character, and moral responsibility involves evaluating actions from the perspective of how people ought to act and how they do act to develop or change their character.

When we talk about “corporate responsibility,” we mean responsibility in this moral sense. Corporations are causally responsible for lots of things: they cause many things to happen in the world. But are they morally responsible for their actions? If they are, why? If not, why not?

Two quick notes before we move on. First, moral responsibility is the same as being responsible for something in an ethical sense. We could talk about “ethical responsibility,” but the term “moral responsibility” is much more common. We’ll stick with “moral responsibility,” but by those words we mean an ethical obligation to do what is right or act in a certain way.

Second, in our brief discussion of responsibility, we haven’t necessarily covered every possible sense of responsibility. We also haven’t tried to separate different kinds of moral responsibility from each other. We’ll do this in some places, but only to the extent that it helps us understand what moral responsibility in a corporate environment means for us. Remember, we’re taking a practical approach to business ethics here, not trying to solve puzzles about how different senses of responsibility might relate to each other.

section.title: Corporations and the Theory of the Firm

figure.title:
Offices Representing Corporations
Photo by Lucas Pezeta via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A street view of an office building.

section.para: We begin by thinking about the idea of a “corporation.” Most of our thinking about moral responsibility has to do with individual people: I’m responsible for hurting someone’s feelings with a thoughtless remark, or a thief is responsible for stealing someone’s last bit of cash. Both of these things are wrong, and the agents, or the entities that produced the actions, are clear in this case: they are individual people. This problem gets harder, though, when we talk about corporate responsibility. Who or what is a “corporation”? And is it the kind of thing that can actually have moral responsibilities?

Thus we must first consider whether a corporation—or company, or small business, or some other kind of unit—could even have moral responsibilities to begin with. People have them, we’re sure about that. But corporations are not people—at least, not in the sense that you and I are people. People are biological creatures that sleep and eat and interact one-on-one with each other. Corporations don’t do those things. They might be “sleeping” on the job, if they let competitors catch them, or they might “eat” money by wasting it on needless projects. But these are only figurative expressions. Corporations are in fact groups of people, any one of whom could bear moral responsibilities as an individual. But when those people combine together for the purpose of business activities, is the resulting entity as a whole capable of bearing responsibilities as well? Does the ability of individuals to be morally responsible somehow transfer to the group?

These moral questions go with others about the identity and nature of business-related groups, and one attempt to answer at least some of them is the so-called “theory of the firm.” I say “so-called” because there is no general agreement about exactly what the “theory” is. “It is doubtful if there is yet general agreement among economists on the subject matter designated by the title ‘theory of the firm’, on, that is, the scope and purpose of the part of economics so titled. There is, probably, general agreement on the subject matter of economics itself: the allocation and distribution of scarce resources. (Some economists would have us add explicitly ‘and growth’ to ‘allocation and distribution’, but traditionally growth is subsumed under ‘allocation’.) Then we may take it that the purpose of the theory of the firm is to investigate the behaviour of firms as it affects allocation and distribution.” G. C. Archibald, “Firm, Theory of the” in The New Palgrave Dictionary of Economics, ed. Matias Vernengo, Esteban Perez Caldentey, and Barkley J. Rosser Jr., (London: Palgrave Macmillan, 2018), . Economists and others have simply recognized that, when a person or persons act in a business capacity, it is useful to consider the resulting group—even if it’s just a single individual—as a new kind of entity: the firm. “Firm,” then, is a broad term referring to any organization that acts in a business capacity. The firm is not identical with the people that make it up, or even with the people and equipment and infrastructure—the firm is a separate thing. According to A Dictionary of Economics, “the theory of the firm models how a firm would behave given assumptions about its objectives, which may include profit maximization, avoidance of risk, and long-run growth.”John Black, Nigar Hashimzade, and Gareth Myles, A Dictionary of Economics, (Oxford: Oxford University Press, March 15, 2012), s.v. “firm.” In other words, the theory is about how organizations act in economic and market environments.

That there exists a theory of the firm, though, is a clue to our question about corporations and moral responsibility. In economics and other fields, it makes sense to treat groups of people and their activities as a single unit, because the unit resulting from their organized behavior acts as though it were an individual: it seems to have goals and pursue ends and move quickly or slowly and take lots of other actions. We can model these behaviors as a unity—we don’t need to worry, for example, about what individual employees of IBM had for lunch today or what their weekend plans are in order to model the economic behavior of IBM itself. As we consider the corporation to be an independent entity, we see that beliefs and actions of individual members become less important or even irrelevant to our thinking. What we care about is the corporation as a whole, and what actions it takes, rather than the actions of any one person.

It isn’t difficult to extend this line of thinking to ethics. If economists find it useful to use a theory of the firm and analyze corporate behavior from that perspective, why shouldn’t we do the same thing for the purposes of ethics? We can consider a corporation or any other “firm” to be a unit that not only acts in certain ways but that can also bear moral responsibility for those actions. If it makes sense to think of firms as considering alternatives, making decisions, and taking actions, it seems like it also makes sense to hold those firms responsible for the good or bad they do with those alternatives, decisions, and actions. On this view, corporations aren’t people, but they’re capable of having moral responsibilities just as people do, in the same way that they can take unified actions for economic or business purposes.

This might make sense to you, and it may be natural for you to think of corporations as capable of being morally responsible, but we shouldn’t be too hasty. The parallel isn’t perfect: while corporations and people are similar in some ways, they might not be similar enough for something like real corporate responsibility to exist. It might be instead that “corporate responsibility” is really just holding particular individuals responsible for what they do as members of the corporation. So though we have an entity—a corporation—and though it looks like it’s at least possible for that entity to be morally responsible, we still face important questions about how that moral responsibility is able to exist, what it’s like, and how it relates to the moral responsibilities of decision-makers within the corporation.

These questions will be with us throughout this chapter. While we’ll be treating business organizations as morally responsible units, we shouldn’t forget that the kind of moral responsibility they bear may not be the same as ours.

sidebar.title: Case Study: Luckin Coffee

figure.title:
A Cup of Coffee
Photo by Jason Villanueva via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A Cup of Coffee

sidebar.para: Luckin Coffee is a China-based coffee company founded in Beijing in 2017. Luckin saw itself as a competitor to coffee providers such as Starbucks and Seattle Coffee Company, but it took a different approach to the industry. Starbucks, for example, is well known for having storefronts in some of the busiest metropolitan areas in the world, along with inside seating and many baristas working at once. Luckin Coffee’s business model was different. While they do manage a small number of staffed physical locations, they focus most of their business on employee-less coffee kiosks.

A Luckin kiosk looks somewhat like a vending machine and works in a similar way. Customers use an app to find a kiosk and then make an order. When they arrive at the kiosk, they’ve already made the purchase, and so machines mix their order and make their coffee. Because they have few employees and traditional locations, this model allows Luckin to operate with far less overhead than competitors. Many Starbucks locations are leased from property owners, and their rent and staffing costs are major expenses. Luckin can do without most of those expenses, preferring to sell individual orders taken and fulfilled by machines. In their own words, Luckin said that “Our pick-up stores have limited seating and are typically located in areas with high demand for coffee, such as office buildings, commercial areas and university campuses. This enables us to stay close to our target customers and expand rapidly with low rental and decoration costs.” They also claimed, “Our mission is to be part of everyone’s everyday life, starting with coffee.”Luckin Coffee Inc., Form F-1, as filed with the SEC on April 22, 2019, .

In the lead-up to Luckin Coffee’s IPO in May 2019, Muddy Waters LLC, an investment research firm, received an anonymous tip about problems in Luckin’s financial reporting. The tip claimed that Luckin was claiming false revenue and lying about total sales. Though external auditors from a division of Ernst & Young had been reviewing quarterly statements from the company, they had not seen records from 2019 before they sent a letter to investment banks expressing their confidence in the company’s stability. The IPO generated around $600 million from investors, and the company’s valuation reached as high as $5 billion.Emma Chung, “Case Study: Luckin Coffee Accounting Fraud,” Seven Pillars Institute, (August 27, 2021), .

But the hints that Muddy Waters had received turned out to be true. Sometime in early 2019, Luckin had begun making fraudulent reports about coupon use: employees and other individuals would purchase coupons on Luckin’s app and then redeem the coupons to make it seem as though they had purchased coffee when they had not. Other coupon-related schemes followed in the same year, including a plan to sell coupons to shell companies that would then resell the coupons themselves, all while none of the purchasers ever intended to get a cup of coffee. Partly due to these made-up sales, Luckin overreported its revenue throughout 2019.

In early 2020, the SEC had enough information to charge Luckin with fabricating financial statements and lying about revenue. In a settlement and penalty announced in December 2020, Luckin agree to receive permanent injunctions and pay a fine of $180 million.Emma Chung, “Case Study: Luckin Coffee Accounting Fraud,” Seven Pillars Institute, (August 27, 2021), .

listitem.para: Luckin Coffee was a China-based company which made an entrance into the US market. To what extent can a global company be taken as a single unit, for the purpose of considering moral responsibility?

Luckin agreed to pay a large fine and change some of its business practices. Is it true, however, that the company is morally responsible for what happened? Or is it that the individual people who made the unethical or unlawful choices are morally responsible for what happened?

Twelve employees who worked with Luckin’s CEO were fired, as well as various members of the company’s governing board. Are these individuals morally responsible for Luckin’s actions as a group? If a board member objected to the company’s practices but did not act to stop them, could she still be morally responsible for the company’s wrong?

Should it be lawful for a government or for private individuals to pursue litigation against CEOs and others for the actions they take as executives and managers of the company? Or should they be shielded from being held personally responsible for those actions because the company itself can receive a punishment?
What punishments are appropriate for individuals who deceive investors? What level of involvement in schemes like those at Luckin Coffee would merit a punishment, and why?

section.title: Friedman on Corporate Responsibility and Shareholder Theory
section.para: In our previous section we explored the “theory of the firm”—a way of thinking about business organizations and their behavior. While we noted some potential problems with the idea that firms can be morally responsible, we concluded that, at least in some circumstances, they can bear moral responsibility for their actions, even if how they do it differs from how a person would.

Let’s next take a look at the two major theories of corporate responsibility; other theories are, in one way or another, offshoots of these two. The first comes from the twentieth-century American economist Milton Friedman, and we’ll call it shareholder theoryThe concept that shareholders choose executives to serve their interests, and that executives can take legitimate action on behalf of shareholders only when they act within their agreement to serve those interests. In other words, maximizing profits is the only legitimate action for executives because any other action would be outside of the agreement on which executives can act for a corporation’s owners..

The title of a famous article by Friedman expresses his view: “The social responsibility of business is to increase its profits.”Milton Fiedman, “A Friedman Doctrine—The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits,” New York Times Magazine, (13 September 1970), . He begins by discussing the idea of a “social responsibility” for a business as something beyond the business’s stated purpose of earning a profit. If businesses had such a responsibility, then they would have moral obligations to society—to individuals, perhaps, or to groups—that were independent of their fiduciary obligations to the owners. Examples of social or community obligations like these could be a duty to take care of the environment, provide jobs for local workers, or give to worthwhile charitable causes.

For Friedman, however, this entire way of thinking does not make sense, for “a corporation is an artificial person and in this sense may have artificial responsibilities, but ‘business’ as a whole cannot be said to have responsibilities, even in this vague sense.” In other words, Friedman asserts that businesses are not the kind of things that can have moral responsibilities. Only people can have them, Friedman thinks, and so any responsibilities that appear to rest upon a business could in reality only rest upon the executives of that business. Businesses themselves cannot have ethical obligations.

The problem is that “the manager is the agent of the individuals who own the corporation,” and so if a manager does have a social responsibility going beyond their duty to maximize profit, this “must mean that he is to act in some way that is not in the interest of his employers.” According to Friedman, the only real responsibility that a manager has is to increase profit; acting on any “responsibility” outside of that would mean a manager was doing something other than increasing profit, which would violate the manager’s only real responsibility.Milton Fiedman, “A Friedman Doctrine—The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits,” New York Times Magazine, (13 September 1970), .
Here are some examples Friedman gives to support his argument.
section.blockquote: To refrain from increasing the price of the product in order to contribute to the social objective of preventing inflation, even though a price increase would be in the best interests of the corporation. Or that he is to make expenditures on reducing pollution beyond the amount that is in the best interests of the corporation or that is required by law in order to contribute to the social objective of improving the environment. Or that, at the expense of corporate profits, he is to hire “hard core” unemployed instead of better qualified available workmen to contribute to the social objective of reducing poverty.

In each of these cases, the corporate executive would be spending someone else’s money for a general social interest. Insofar as his actions in accord with his “social responsibility” reduce returns to stockholders, he is spending their money. Insofar as his actions raise the price to customers, he is spending the customers’ money. Insofar as his actions lower the wages of some employees, he is spending their money.Milton Fiedman, “A Friedman Doctrine—The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits,” New York Times Magazine, (13 September 1970), .
section.para: Any of these actions taken to fulfill some “socially responsible” purpose would violate the principles on which a business is based. The owners—in the case of corporations, the shareholders—choose executives to serve their interests. Executives can take legitimate action on behalf of shareholders only when they act within their agreement to serve those interests—and they do so by maximizing profit. Anything else would be an illegitimate action, because it would be outside of the agreement on which executives can act for a corporation’s owners.

Thus Friedman denies that businesses have any “social” responsibilities, whether these responsibilities would involve individuals, communities, the environment, or anything else. The only responsibility businesses have is to maximize profit.

Friedman is also a strong advocate for free markets. In his words, “In an ideal free market resting on private property, no individual can coerce any other, all cooperation is voluntary, all parties to such cooperation benefit or they need not participate. There are no ‘social’ values, no ‘social’ responsibilities in any sense other than the shared values and responsibilities of individuals.” Given this position and Friedman’s view on responsibility, we see that the responsibility to maximize profit is in fact a social responsibility, because it is maximizing profit that will, in a legitimate way, produce the greatest benefit for society.

Let’s consider some of the advantages in Friedman’s view. It gives a clear answer to the question of whether businesses can have moral responsibilities: no. It also gives reasons for this answer: only people can have moral responsibilities, because only people take actions as part of a business. Friedman’s view also makes clear the relationship between the shareholders of a business and the executives who act on behalf of those owners. That relationship is based on a commitment to do nothing other than serve the owners’ interests, and a “social” responsibility wouldn’t do that. You may be able to think of other advantages to Friedman’s position as well.

Now let’s consider some possible problems. In pursuing the interests of their principals, to what extent should business executives be able to act freely? For example, it may be that a company could increase profits by cutting down trees at a faster pace or by upping the pollution created by a factory. Are executives licensed to do things like this, if taking those actions would maximize profit? Friedman does say that businesses ought to follow “the basic rules of the society, both those embodied in law and those embodied in ethical custom.” But what are those rules, and why must businesses follow them? Is it really true that businesses bear no moral responsibilities to the people who may be harmed, even incidentally, by their actions? Is it true that large, wealthy American corporations have no responsibilities to the societies or cultures in which they operate, outside of using them to make money?

Following the arguments of Jeffrey Moriarty,Jeffry Moriarty, Business Ethics: A Contemporary Introduction (New York: Routledge, 2022). we can also challenge Friedman’s view by criticizing his notion of ownership. Friedman’s argument is built on the assumption that shareholders do, in fact, own the business, and this gives them the right to demand that executives maximize profit in how they run the business. But what does it mean to “own” a business? A shareholder owns a share of stock, which is a commodity that can be bought and sold without having any impact on how the business runs. Does owning stock mean that one owns a company’s infrastructure? Does it mean they own a portion of the labor provided by employees? Or does it mean that they merely have a share in the company’s assets? Depending on what it means to “own” a business, the agreement that executives have with shareholders to maximize profit may be difficult to clarify.

From questions about ownership we can move to two challenges for Friedman. First, it is not clear whether accepting a management position at a company involves the agreement to only act in a way that will maximize profit for that company. In fact, it may even be that one accepts employment with an explicit agreement, detailed by shareholders, to promote some social responsibility! For Friedman, actions taken in such a role would violate the agreement to maximize profit, but what is the nature of that agreement—who in particular has made it, and when?

The second challenge calls on shareholders. It is not necessarily the case that shareholders want profit to be maximized—they may have other purposes and may wish for executives to carry them out as part of their employment. As Moriarty puts it, “What do you and I want the corporations in which we are stockholders to do? Do we really want them to maximize our wealth? Or do we want them to pursue social objectives as well? I do not recall being asked, and I bet you weren’t either.” Given that we weren’t asked, could we not choose a social responsibility that a business could fulfill, in addition to its profit-generating activities?

section.title: Stakeholder Theory
section.para: The second major theory of corporate responsibility arose partly as a response to Friedman’s view, and partly as a way of reconciling many apparently conflicting interests. The theory’s creator is R. Edward Freeman, and he called it “ stakeholder theoryThe theory that businesses can and do have responsibilities other than maximizing profits, based on the good of those who have a stake in the company—many of whom will not be shareholders. ” in order to call attention to those who have some kind of stake in a business’s activities beyond its shareholders.R. Edward Freeman, “Managing for Stakeholders,” Darden Business Publishing (Charlottesville: University of Virginia, January 2007), .

Freeman begins by noting the dominance of Friedman’s shareholder theory. “It has become common wisdom,” he says, “to ‘increase shareholder value,’ and many companies have instituted complex incentive compensation plans aimed at aligning the interests of executives with the interests of shareholders.” That is, when executives increase shareholder value, companies will pay them more, because they’re fulfilling the responsibility that Friedman thought was their only real responsibility as executives. “Meeting Wall Street targets and forming a stable and predictable base of quarter over quarter increases in earnings per share has become the standard for measuring company performance.”R. Edward Freeman, “Managing for Stakeholders,” Darden Business Publishing (Charlottesville: University of Virginia, January 2007), .

figure.title:
The Stock Exchange
Photo by Pixaby via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: Numbers illustrating stock data

section.para: There is a problem with this idea, though, one different from those we saw in the previous section. Shareholder theory “puts shareholders’ interests over and above the interests of customers, suppliers, employees, and others, as if these interests must conflict with each other.” The “as if” part is where Freeman focuses his attention: shareholder theory appears to set customers, employees, and other interested parties in opposition to each other as part of a zero-sum game, where a gain for one party is a loss for another. When we view business this way, “the only interesting questions are whether and how these forces for change affect shareholder value, measured by the price of the stock every day.”

To resolve this problem of conflicting interests, Freeman suggests that shareholder theory rests on the “separation fallacy.” The separation fallacyThe mistake of believing that a business’s “business” decisions can be cleanly separated from its “ethical” decisions. is the mistake of believing that a business’s “business” decisions can be cleanly separated from its “ethical” decisions. There are business decisions and activities, and there are ethical decisions and activities, and more importantly, the business ones don’t overlap with the ethical ones. Doing business is just doing business, with the implication that ethics is a constraint on business which may hold it back from maximizing profit.

Against the separation fallacy, Freeman claims that “almost any business decision has some ethical content”—in other words, it isn’t possible to perfectly separate business decisions from ethical ones. There won’t always be overlap between them, of course, but they’ll overlap some of the time. When they do, it won’t be possible to say that the only responsibility of businesses is to maximize profit, because their profit-maximizing activities will be interfering with the interests of stakeholders.

Unlike Friedman’s “shareholders,” Freeman’s “stakeholders” need not be owners of a business. In fact, they frequently won’t be: stakeholders in a company include people like suppliers, distributors, customers, and even the communities in which the company operates. In general, anyone who has a “stake” in a business is a “stakeholder”—and to have a “stake” in a business is just to be someone affected by a business’s actions, in one way or another.

To respect these stakeholders and try to show that their interests don’t actually conflict with each other, Freeman proposes an ethical principle called the responsibility principle The principle that most people, most of the time, want to, actually do, and should accept responsibility for the effects of their actions on others. . The responsibility principle says that “most people, most of the time, want to, actually do, and should accept responsibility for the effects of their actions on others.”R. Edward Freeman, “Managing for Stakeholders,” Darden Business Publishing (Charlottesville: University of Virginia, January 2007): 9, . This principle is incompatible with the separation fallacy, and it also suggests that businesses must take responsibility—morally and socially—for their actions in a way that goes beyond concerns for profit. They must think instead about the stake each person has in those actions, and how to fairly balance their interests.

Freeman writes, “Seeing stakeholder interests as ‘joint’ rather than ‘opposed’ is difficult. It is not always easy to find a way to accommodate all stakeholder interests. It is easier to trade off one versus another. . . . Managing for stakeholders is about creating as much value as possible for stakeholders, without resorting to trade-offs.” Stakeholder theory concludes, therefore, that businesses can and do have responsibilities other than maximizing profits. Corporate responsibility does exist, and while individual people are the ones who carry out decisions, businesses themselves can bear moral responsibilities.

Stakeholder theory has several strengths. It makes room for executives to do things other than maximize profit, but doesn’t deny that generating profit is an important part of what they do. It also respects the conviction that businesses must take into account the interests of customers, communities, and others affected by their actions. Companies don’t exist in a vacuum, and people unconnected from a company often face consequences for its actions. Stakeholder theory allows us to reject the separation fallacy and evaluate a company’s moral responsibility as it goes beyond basic compliance with existing law and custom.

Stakeholder theory has several important weaknesses, however, and we will draw on the thoughts of Eric Orts and Alan Strudler to examine three of them.Eric W. Orts and Alan Strudler, “Putting a Stake in Stakeholder Theory,” supplement, Journal of Business Ethics 88, no. S4 (2009): 605–615, . The basic idea behind their criticisms is that, while identifying the various “interests” of stakeholders is useful, what we need is not just a way of identifying them but of understanding how, in reality, to balance them.

The first problem is that stakeholder theory does not give us a well-defined way of identifying who or what is actually a stakeholder. If the theory is to go beyond Friedman’s view of shareholders, then the idea of a “stakeholder” cannot just include people who, like executives and employees, have an obvious connection to the business. But once we extend the umbrella to more than just shareholders, it isn’t clear who we shouldn’t let in. Everyone, no matter their relation to the business, has some stake in its activities, even if that stake is very distant and poorly defined. Who counts a stakeholder, and why? If we can’t answer this question, then we can’t specify whose interests we are attempting to balance.

The second problem is that stakeholder theory is too broad and too vague. It is too broad because it seems to apply to anyone and everyone, as mentioned above. And it’s too vague because the idea of an “interest” is not specific enough.

For example, suppose we live in a community where a company operates a large factory. As members of the community, we have a stake in this company, since they produce a lot of waste and we’re worried about what they’ll do with it. But why stop there? Why not say also that we have a financial stake in the company? We have financial interests, after all, and some of those interests may be related to the company, so what stops us from using stakeholder theory to argue that the balancing of our interests includes the company just gifting us money?

Finally, the third problem is that stakeholder theory does not give any real guidance for what to do when interests of stakeholders do actually conflict. While it’s true that we don’t need to see the interests of stakeholders as necessarily conflicting, it’s also true that sometimes they do in fact conflict, and when that happens, we need more than just the mandate to “balance” them. How do we do so? Does everyone’s interest get the same weight? If not, which carry more weight, and why? How do we put stakeholder theory into practice, if we can’t answer these questions?

Some aspects of stakeholder theory look like promising alternatives to shareholder theory. But unless we can specify exactly how to put stakeholder theory into practice, then it may not amount to more than some useful-sounding ideas.

sidebar.title: Case Study: Baby Formula in Developing Countries

figure.title:
A Baby Drinks Formula From a Bottle
Photo by Han Nguyen via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A Baby Drinks Formula From a Bottle

sidebar.para: The choice of whether to breastfeed or formula feed can be a difficult decision for new mothers. While many feel that breastfeeding is best and wish to breastfeed exclusively, that is not always possible—some women cannot produce enough milk to feed their babies and a few cannot produce milk at all.
