When it comes to work, the basic features we’ve mentioned—understanding allegations of wrongdoing, permitting a rebuttal, and allowing appeals or grievances—may be sufficient.

sidebar.title: Case Study: Respectful Workplace Behavior
sidebar.para: In a recent meeting with her HR director, Valeria was told that some of her coworkers have recently been offended by comments she’s made in casual conversations. The director didn’t share specifics, but she did ask Valeria to be careful with how she spoke.

Over the next week Valeria paid close attention to her words and tried to avoid saying anything that might hurt someone. At the end of the week, though, the HR director called her in again and said that she had received more complaints, this time from an additional employee. She said that the complaints didn’t detail the remarks, but noted that Valeria’s attitude had seemed hateful and callous.
After another week of extreme care taken by Valeria, HR spoke to her a third time, saying that if they received any other complaints, they would have grounds to fire her.

listitem.para: In facing allegations of workplace misconduct, should Valeria be entitled to have a representative acting in her defense, analogous to a defense attorney?
Should Valeria be able to find out the details about which of her comments caused offense? What if those details were never reported—should she be allowed to investigate them?
What obligation does the company have to investigate the truth of the accusations made against Valeria? On the basis of what evidence can they make a determination about her actions?
Should it be possible for employees of a company to make anonymous allegations against other employees regarding matters that might affect their employment? Why or why not?
In a situation like Valeria’s, what constitutes “fair treatment” in the workplace?

section.title: Hiring, Discrimination, and Affirmative Action
section.para: So far we’ve seen many examples of unethical or at least ethically dubious conduct at work. Anyone who has worked in business or professional settings knows that those settings can be fraught with ethical issues, and some of those issues may even reach backward in time.

A good example of this phenomenon is the case of someone lying on their résumé. A résumé is supposed to be just a document listing someone’s education and position-relevant experience. However, since hiring managers normally don’t have the time to follow up on each item in a job candidate’s résumé, they mostly take the truth of the information for granted: if it’s written on the résumé, they assume it’s true. But since an appealing résumé can be so important for getting a job interview, there may be great temptation to exaggerate or even lie on a résumé—especially since it’s possible to do both with reasonable confidence that you won’t be caught.

Exaggerations can include inflated descriptions of responsibilities at previous positions or just overly generous descriptions of one’s education and professional training. Outright lies are things like making up a degree from a college you never attended, inventing a previous professional role, or misconstruing your contributions to successful projects in the past.

A famous case of both was discovered near the beginning of 2023. George Santos was elected to the House of Representatives in the United States in 2022 and took office near the beginning of 2023. Just prior to that, some people began to question claims he had made about his family history and background. It was later revealed that Santos had lied about where he went to high school (he didn’t attend Horace Mann, an elite prep school), where he went to college (he didn’t graduate from Baruch College or take coursework from New York University, and later admitted he didn’t have a college degree), his work history (he didn’t work for either Goldman Sachs or Citigroup), his contributions to other organizations (he wasn’t a vice-president of an investment group), where his money came from (it didn’t come from working, though no one knows where it came from), and founding an animal charity (he didn’t run the Friends of Pets United). Santos also lied about many other things.Matt Stieb and Margaret Hartmann, “Here’s Every Single Lie Told by George Santos,” Intelligencer, updated June 26, 2023, .

The Santos case, of course, is so egregious as to be laughable; we hardly need discuss the question of why lying on your résumé to that extent is an unethical thing to do. Perhaps the more interesting ethical question is, what should be done after such lies get discovered, either in the hiring process or later on?

For example, should Santos be forced to resign? Is telling the truth a qualification for his job, in a political world where exaggerations or open lies are common? Should the Republican party take action to remove him from his seat, when the voters of his New York district chose him as their representative? Moreover, what if Santos starts doing a good job, and the voters are happy? What impact do his lies about his life have on his actual ability to get the job done?

We may also compare the action of exaggerating or lying on a résumé to marketing a product. It’s common for companies to exaggerate the capabilities or benefits of their products, or to lie about them in the form of half-truths which get qualified in long, fine-print disclosures on the back of the box or in the instruction manual. Are these actions unethical? Why or why not? If these actions just amount to marketing in a competitive environment, can we not see what Santos did as marketing himself in a particular way? Sure, he lied, but many people lie about many things. Has he done something more serious than others? Do we expect him to meet a higher standard, because of his position? After you’ve been hired, does job performance matter more than what is or was on your résumé?
We’ll consider other marketing-related questions in . For now, let’s look at a case study.

sidebar.title: Case Study: Truth in Résumés
sidebar.para: Ginnifer Trejo is a staff administrator at a regional university. She works with campus committees and student organizations to plan student activities, like game nights and dances. She’s often on campus late and students call her “Miss Ginny.”

To get her job, Ginnifer survived a hiring process that included three rounds of interviews and many interactions with students. She stood out to the hiring committee because of previous experience with event planning, including weddings, and because she’d worked in similar student-facing positions at smaller universities.

However, Ginnifer’s résumé isn’t entirely truthful. Her experience in “event planning” is just the time she threw together a baby shower before her sister-in-law’s shotgun wedding, and she was never actually employed by those smaller universities—she was just a student there, and attended activities.

The problems with Ginnifer’s résumé were discovered by accident one day, when a former college roommate of hers started dating another administrator at Ginnifer’s college. When confronted, Ginnifer admitted she’d fabricated the information, but said that she’d done so because she was a single mom with two young children and was desperate for a stable job with benefits. Since she started at her current position, she’s been an exemplary employee, and the students and other staff love her.

listitem.para: Do Ginnifer’s exaggerations amount to lying? Does it matter?
Does Ginnifer deserve to be fired? Why or why not?
Are there any circumstances that could justify lying on one’s résumé? If they exist, what might they be?
If you were Ginnifer’s boss, what would you do, and why?

section.para: Another ethically-charged part of the hiring process concerns discrimination and efforts toward affirmative action. We’ll look at these issues for the remainder of this section.

In its simplest form, discriminationTreating people unequally in a situation that would otherwise call for equal treatment. is treating people unequally in a situation that would otherwise call for equal treatment. The unequal treatment may be a conscious choice on the part of the person acting, but it doesn’t have to be so; near the end of this section, we’ll discuss the possibility of “implicit” discrimination, usually called implicit bias, which refers to subconscious differences in how we react to or treat people of different groups.

The simplest cases of discrimination involve treating two people unequally simply because you prefer or like one of them more than the other. For example, if two people have the same qualifications and do the same job, and they’ve both been with your company for the same amount of time—but only one of them is your friend—then your choice to pay your friend more than the other employee may be a case of discrimination. Remember that discrimination is unequal treatment in a situation that would otherwise call for equal treatment, as this one would appear to.

The ethical principle violated at the root of discrimination is that of justice, or fairness. Those performing the same action in the same circumstance should receive the same reward; those committing the same crime in the same circumstance should receive the same punishment. The ethical principle of justice demands that we treat others fairly and that differences in how we treat them reflect differences in them or in the situation, and not just differences in our preferences.

We’ll be discussing discrimination in the context of hiring below, but we could also investigate it more broadly. For example, suppose that you work at a hospital campus, and you notice that many janitorial employees smoke outside the buildings in the mornings when they’re almost done cleaning after the overnight shift. Then suppose that the hospital administration announces that smoking is now prohibited not only inside buildings but also outside them or anywhere on the campus. Such a policy might make sense for a hospital—but what if the only employees who smoked were the janitors, and what if most of them were Black? The administration’s policy would be grounded in good reasons, but because of staff demographics, it produces a differential effect on a certain minority population. Is the no-smoking policy ethical? Is it discriminatory? Why or why not?

In the context of hiring, discrimination refers to a preference, unstated or otherwise, for job candidates who belong to a certain group, even though there is no legitimate basis for such a preference. While discrimination can occur on the basis of membership in any group, it’s most commonly associated with the following groups, as discussed by the EEOC, or Equal Opportunity Employment Commission, in the United States: “Under the laws enforced by EEOC, it is illegal to discriminate against someone (applicant or employee) because of that person’s race, color, religion, sex (including gender identity, sexual orientation, and pregnancy), national origin, age (40 or older), disability or genetic information.”“Prohibited Employment Policies/Practices,” U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, accessed September 11, 2023, . Thus, broadly speaking, there are six protected groups or “classes” in hiring, which means that it is illegal for an employer to show preference for a job candidate on the basis of their membership or non-membership in any of the following groups:

listitem.para: A certain race or color
A religion
A sex or gender identity
A nation of origin
An age
A medical class, including having a disability or genetic marker

section.para: Because it’s illegal, job candidates who believe they have been discriminated against can take legal action against a company that refuses to hire them or that fired them.

The success of a legal case about discrimination will depend on many specifics of the hiring process. Since many of those specifics involve legal technicalities, we will keep our attention on the ethical principles and values underlying discrimination in hiring.

It’s not difficult to see why discriminating against someone on the basis of their age or gender identity is unfair. Most of the time, age and gender, along with the other classes in the list above, do not have anything to do with an applicant’s ability to perform a job; it would therefore be unjust and thus unethical to make a hiring decision on those bases. In addition, the Americans with Disabilities Act offers additional protections to individuals with disabilities, including requiring that hiring companies offer reasonable accommodations.14 CFR § 1251.201. The fact that a job is on the third floor of a building is not a legitimate reason to disqualify job candidates who use wheelchairs. Reasonable accommodations could be offered such that those candidates could still fulfill their responsibilities.

In addition to justice and fairness, however, there may also be other reasons that discrimination is unethical. One reason is the harm it does to the individuals who are discriminated against. Although related to justice, this principle can stand by itself, since the expectation of equal treatment is a separate issue from the damage done to those who experience discrimination. If discrimination does harm those discriminated against, as seems likely, then we’d have another reason to consider it unethical.

Another possible reason, perhaps less often considered in the context of business ethics, is the harm that discrimination can do to the individuals and organizations responsible for the discrimination. If discrimination harms those individuals and organizations as well, then we might have a third reason it is unethical.

We must take care in discussing this third possibility for the ethics of discrimination. In many cases, it is not immediately obvious that a company that discriminates against women is itself harmed by not hiring women. In addition, we must be careful to make sure that the harms such a company experiences, if there are any, are truly ethical or moral harms, rather than economic or business-related ones.

For example, suppose it became widely known that a certain company’s hiring processes discriminated against women and so made it very difficult for female employees to be hired. Depending on the public’s reaction, that company may face significant financial consequences if customers or clients drop them. They may also face legal consequences that have financial implications. But neither of these consequences, financial or legal, are in themselves ethical harms; ethical harms would have to involve the violation of ethical principles and the resulting damage done to individuals because of their actions.
Do those who discriminate incur ethical harms on themselves, then? We’ll return to this issue after discussing affirmative action.

Affirmative actionPolicies designed to include members of certain groups, usually “underrepresented” groups, in contexts in which they have not traditionally been included. is a catchall term referring to policies designed to include members of certain groups, usually “underrepresented” groups, in contexts in which they have not traditionally been included. A university whose student population has traditionally been white and upper middle-class may adopt affirmative action policies in order to prefer candidates of racial minorities or poorer backgrounds in the admissions process. Such candidates would be students who are “underrepresented” at the university, meaning that the number of students from a particular group doesn’t reach a certain acceptable threshold.

Affirmative action is sometimes called “positive” discrimination, in recognition of the fact that it is discrimination: to prefer a Latino student over a White student for a spot at a university, when both are equally qualified and the preference is made because of the student’s ethnicity, is discrimination. The term “positive” suggests not necessarily that the discrimination in itself is a good thing, but that it is intended to produce an outcome considered to be fairer or more just on the whole, with all factors taken into account.

Since affirmative action is a form of discrimination, the major ethical question surrounding it is, does the value of the outcomes produced by affirmative action justify the means taken to reach them?

When put that way, the question seeks a utilitarian argument. A utilitarian argument in favor of affirmative action could recognize discrimination as wrong, and even accept that individual acts of discrimination in the affirmative-action process are also wrong. But that wrongness would be justified on the basis that the overall good produced by affirmative action in the long run outweighs the harm.

On the other hand, we could speak of affirmative action in another way and offer a different kind of justification. We could say that affirmative action policies, along with positive discrimination, are owed as one group’s ethical duties to members of other groups that have been discriminated against in the past. On this view, the purpose of admissions and hiring policies favoring Blacks in America, for example, would not primarily be to increase the number of Blacks in universities or workplaces. Instead, the purpose would be to offer those opportunities as a payment owed for past mistreatment; affirmative action would be a way of redressing past wrongs, or compensating for lost opportunities.

One of the appeals of a duty-based argument in favor of affirmative action is its fit with the idea that past injustices can lead to present injustices. In the United States, for example, there is a widely held idea about equality of opportunity: that every person plays on a roughly equal playing field, and that all that’s needed to be successful in life is hard work and a little gumption. Now, while it is true that opportunities for economic advancement in the United States are better than those in many other countries, it is difficult to argue seriously that the playing field is equal or even roughly equal. A person whose family has more money and who therefore lives in a safer area of a city with better schools has clear advantages over someone who doesn’t have those things. Hence, while the world is open to both of those people, it is much more open to the first, and to say that the second did not succeed simply because she didn’t try hard enough is to misunderstand the reality of her situation. Winning a race is admirable and takes effort, but if half the participants start thirty yards behind you, then their failure to match or overtake you may not be due to a lack of effort. It may be due instead to the conditions in which they are forced to race.

According to this view, affirmative action could therefore be a way of redressing past injustices that have caused members of certain groups to be more likely to live in disadvantageous circumstances. The justification for affirmative hiring policies could be that they exist to fulfill an ethical duty that is owed to members of a certain group.

Many people will not find the duty-based argument for affirmative action to be convincing, and it is not without its problems. It remains true, however, that the idea of a level playing field or equality of opportunity is itself much more doubtful, in many cases, than the policies intended to fix that problem.

Now let us consider a job candidate passed over for a position in favor of someone that they consider to be an “affirmative action” hire. Such a person might complain that they deserved the position more, because they are more qualified. Perhaps their education is superior, or they have more relevant experience in a particular field. Isn’t it true that opportunities ought to be based on merit? Would it be unethical to hire a candidate who is less deserving than another, or who has less “merit”?

The answer to this question depends on what we mean by “merit,” and may also depend on what “merit” is supposed to accomplish. Normally when we think of merit, we think of things like education, on-the-job experience, or prior work in a related field. We’re thinking of abilities and knowledge that allow someone to fulfill the responsibilities of a position. There’s no question that these are elements of merit, but on the other hand, there’s no reason to think that other aspects of a person’s character couldn’t be a part of their “merit” or set of qualifications for a job.

For example, imagine a Black administrator at a small college who has a role working with students. If the student population is primarily but not exclusively white, then it’s not difficult to see that this administrator’s race could be a qualification for his job: being Black himself, he may be able to connect with and help students that other administrators could not, or that others could not help as effectively. This ability, stemming from his race, is as much a qualification for a position as the ability to code in Python or to paint with a steady hand. There is a direct relationship between the characteristic and effective performance of the job requirements.

None of this is to say that race is a qualification for a position independent of everything else. It may be one qualification among others, and could be overridden by the qualifications of other people or by a candidate’s own deficiencies in other areas, just as competence in Python is not itself sufficient to get a job as a software developer. So while race may not be identifiable as a qualification in a vacuum, there may be positions or circumstances where it is one of the qualifications that weighs in favor of or against a person’s candidacy.

Here we may offer some comment about DEI initiatives, or efforts toward “diversity, equity, and inclusion” in the workplace. DEI programs trace some of their roots to affirmative action but are more properly considered to be products of more contemporary movements toward social justice in the United States. These programs may include affirmative action hiring, but in most cases go beyond hiring to make people of all backgrounds feel welcome and supported at work. For example, a company may design career tracks for employees from underrepresented groups who are interested in management or executive positions. DEI efforts often pay close attention to words, ideas, or practices that may marginalize or offend individuals or groups. These are just a few projects often taken up under the umbrella of DEI; there are many more. There is no reason to think that at least some of these projects aren’t doing good.

On the other hand, it also seems clear that terms such as “diversity,” “equity,” and “inclusion” are so poorly defined that it’s impossible for anyone to say exactly what activities would further those ends, nor to say when the goals associated with the terms have been reached. They are business buzzwords, currently both fashionable and controversial, and such buzzwords don’t have a history of sticking around in the business world for long. However, if more sense can be made of the terms, and the goals of these initiatives can be more clearly spelled out, DEI may well become the long-term force for good which its proponents imagine it to be.

Other notions surrounding affirmative action face problems similar to these. The idea of “underrepresentation” is one example—on what basis exactly do we measure it? In other words, which numbers do we choose to fix the meaning of “underrepresented”—the general population, an industry population, a company population, or something else?

Once again, though, we shouldn’t suggest that in making these criticisms, these ideas or initiatives are automatically worthless. As ethically-minded business professionals, we must evaluate the arguments on their own merits to determine their value in our ethical life. If we enter a situation having already decided that DEI is a fad and a sham, we won’t be in a position to see how underlying principles and reasons could make a positive ethical difference to our organizations.

To finish up this section, then, let’s return to the third possibility discussed above—that discrimination is unethical because it harms those who discriminate. We’re now in a better position to see how we could make this argument. When we discriminate or otherwise fail to see how the backgrounds and experiences of someone else affect who they are and what they can do, we are failing to respect basic values of autonomy and dignity. We violate the autonomy and dignity of others, because we refuse to acknowledge those values in them as full human beings. And we fail ourselves in a double respect. We restrict the exercise of our own autonomy and dignity, in that we don’t allow ourselves to learn and benefit from others in ways we could have. We also take steps toward becoming people who aren’t as sensitive as we could be to the ethically-relevant dimensions of our environment.

sidebar.title: Case Study: Discrimination in Hiring
sidebar.para: Placido is a human relations director for a regional distributor of in-ground pools. As part of his work, he oversees the company’s hiring decisions, although he doesn’t usually participate in job interviews or make decisions about particular candidates.

Over the last few months, Placido has received a few emails about the possibility that his company is discriminating against people of a particular race. At first he discounted the information, but more emails came in, seemingly independent of each other, suggesting the same thing. Placido began to worry more when he had conversations at a regional conference with his human relations counterparts at other companies. They told him stories they’d heard from job candidates whom Placido’s company passed over, but who were able to secure employment elsewhere.

Placido decides to run an experiment. He chooses ten positions throughout the region for which his company is currently hiring, in specialized areas that are not likely to receive many applicants. He then prepares two résumés to send to each position. The résumés are identical in every respect, including the contact information and all the qualifications and prior experience, except that they have different names: one set of résumés are under the name “LaShondra Jonson-Rimes,” and the other is under the name “Brian Smith.” He submits the résumés from mock email addresses.
A week later he receives the results. Of the 10 LaShondra Jonson-Rimes applications, 2 received requests for interviews; 9 of the 10 Brian Smith applications received requests for interviews.
Placido wonders what to do next.

listitem.para: Do the results of Placido’s résumé experiment give evidence in favor of discrimination in the hiring processes of his company? Why or why not?
What could Placido do in order to get more information about this issue in the hiring process?
Is discrimination on the basis of a person’s name unethical? How could someone’s name have such a strong effect on job interviews?
If you were Placido, what would you do, and why?

section.title: Whistleblowing
section.para: A whistleblowerSomeone who reports on illegal activity. is someone who reports on illegal activity. That definition by itself makes it seem as though whistleblowers are tattle-tales; in reality, a whistleblower is usually someone who reports on illegal activity that they themselves are involved in, or that they happen to have first-hand knowledge of, usually because they are an employee of the organization responsible. These illegal activities include financial fraud, government corruption, abuse of the environment, and others.

Many government agencies have dedicated reporting channels for whistleblowers. For example, part of the website for the Director of National Intelligence (DNI) in the US defines the activity in this way: “lawful whistleblowing is the process through which an individual provides the right information to the right people while protecting national security equities and avoiding unauthorized disclosure” (emphasis in original).“Introducing IC Whistleblowing,” Office of the Director of National Intelligence, accessed September 11, 2023, . The Office of the Inspector General, together with the Department of Homeland Security, has a hotline for reporting border corruption, cybercrime, contract fraud, conflicts of interest, and other possibly unethical actions.“Hotline,” Office of Inspector General, U.S. Department of Homeland Security, .

A crucial feature of most whistleblowing, and one that gives rise to an ethical issue we’ll discuss in a moment, is that whistleblowers usually receive special legal protections in return for their reporting. The DNI website mentioned earlier states that, because of various federal laws related to whistleblowing, those who report “have protections against personnel actions taken in reprisal for a Protected Disclosure,” where these personnel actions include “an appointment, promotion, detail, transfer, reassignment, demotion, suspension, termination, reinstatement, restoration, reemployment, or performance evaluation,” as well as other possibly retaliatory actions.“Personnel Actions” in Whistleblower Protections, Office of the Director of National Intelligence,; Presidential Policy Directive 19, “Protecting Whistleblowers with Access to Classified Information,” F(4).

The purpose of offering legal protections to whistleblowers is to encourage them to report what they know. Someone with knowledge of illegal or unethical actions may wish to tell someone about it, but their beliefs about the personal consequences of reporting may stop them. In some circumstances, a job transfer, termination, or suspension may be such a significant harm to someone that the mere threat of such an action would be enough to stop them from sharing what they know. Although legal protections cannot perhaps eliminate this threat, they can mitigate it.

There are three primary ethical questions involving whistleblowing, all of which concern the ethical duties possessed by whistleblowers. These questions are, does an employee’s ethical duty to their organization prohibit whistleblowing? Is there ever an ethical duty which would require someone to report something? And do the groups which receive the information have an ethical duty to protect the whistleblower? We’ll consider each question and finish the section with a case study.

First, does an employee’s ethical duty to their organization prohibit whistleblowing? In a previous chapter’s discussion of corporate responsibility, we noted that, because a corporation interacts with individual people, it can have legitimate ethical responsibilities. Fulfilling these ethical responsibilities requires actions taken by employees. In our discussion, these responsibilities could have involved people within the corporation itself, but more often included those outside, like customers.

Whistleblowing, however, forces us to consider the possibility that individual employees bear ethical responsibilities not to customers or even fellow employees but to a company itself. In many cases, it is the company as a whole that receives legal punishment for its actions, especially fines, and so someone who reports a company’s illegal activities puts the company at risk. In the case of fraud, environmental abuse, and other actions, we can see how a whistleblower could have a reason to report. But could they also have a reason not to?

One such reason may come from an employee’s contract, which could contain language obligating that person not to report what they learn on the job, perhaps under the cover of industrial secrets. Another possible source for an ethical obligation to a company is simply loyalty: the sense that an employee owes the company their loyalty in virtue of the fact that they work there. In the same way that we feel loyalty to our families and may therefore not share even bad secrets, perhaps employees have the same loyalty to their companies, which could then give them an ethical obligation not to report.

From where could this loyalty come? It cannot come from the fact that an employer pays a wage or salary, or offers benefits; these are compensation for performing the requirements of a position, and it usually is neither explicitly or implicitly understood that an employee’s salary is also based on keeping her mouth shut. If this loyalty exists, and could be a ground for an ethical obligation not to report, it must have another source—but it’s difficult to see what other sources there could be.

In addition, it is worth considering whether an employee’s loyalty implies any reciprocal loyalty on the part of the company. The jobs of most American workers can be terminated with very little notice for almost any reason; while loyalty from a company to employees is an inspiring ideal, it’s often the first thing to go when executives feel pressure to cut costs or boost earnings. If there is no serious loyalty on the part of the employer, could there be any on the part of the employee?

The second ethical question about whistleblowing is whether there could be an ethical duty that would require someone to act as a whistleblower and report something. Another way to put this question is, are there activities that are so unethical, so dangerous or objectionable, or so illegal, that a person with knowledge of them would have an ethical responsibility to share what they know?

Right away we can imagine scenarios in which such a responsibility may exist, as when a company’s business practices involve harming children, egregious mistreatment of animals, or other serious wrongs. In these situations, the company’s activities would be so harmful or objectionable that anyone with knowledge of them would have an ethical duty to tell the authorities. This duty could exist even if reporting required the whistleblower to assume financial, professional, or other risks. Some wrongs are so wrong that they lay an obligation on those in the know to do something.

In general, however, outside of such egregious cases, it may appear that an ethical obligation to report does not exist. Ethical obligations or moral duties usually arise from the sorts of treatment that human beings owe other human beings. Some illegal activities, such as insider trading or other forms of market manipulation, have no real, specific victims; reporting those activities might be a good thing to do, but may not be a duty required by an ethical argument. Perhaps the ethical principle here, then, is that the existence of a duty to report illegal activity as a whistleblower depends on what the illegal activity is, what harm it causes, and who receives the harm. Many cases have few or no victims and cause only minor harm in the form of moderate financial losses. Other cases involve physical harm, death, or financial losses so significant, and with so many victims, that a reasonable person would be obligated to report.

As you consider the argument in the last paragraph, think about which activities you feel you’d be obligated to report if you knew about them, and which you would not be obligated to report. What makes the difference between them? Can you offer a sharper ethical principle to identify cases where whistleblowing is an ethical duty?

Our final ethical question is about whether the groups receiving a whistleblower’s information have an ethical duty to protect the whistleblower. In asking this question—as with all our questions about ethical duties—we are not just asking whether it would be a good idea to offer protections for whistleblowers. It probably would be a good idea, since protections make it much more likely that people will report illegal activity. But is there an ethical principle which requires such protections?

We could look for the source of a principle in the transactional nature of a whistleblower’s report. By offering valuable information about illegal activity, in other words, a whistleblower entitles herself to legal protections as an implicit “reward” for the good that she has done. The source of the duty to give protections would be similar to the source of the duty that binds us to keep other contractual agreements.

Another possible source for this duty might simply be in a principle like, “Those who report illegal activity, especially at risk of harm to themselves, have not committed any wrong themselves.” This principle would suggest that people who whistleblow, even if they had willingly participated in the illegal activity before reporting, should not be subject to ethical or legal reproach. The reporter would then enjoy all protections and benefits they would otherwise enjoy as an employee who hadn’t done anything wrong, and thus might be protected from termination or reassignment by their company.

A more difficult question is whether a whistleblower is owed more than protection against prosecution or reprisal by their company. For example, are they entitled to another job, perhaps even in the same industry? The United States Congress passed the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 as a response to the Enron accounting scandal and other problems. Part of the act beefed up whistleblower protections for publicly-traded companies: “No company with a class of securities registered under section 12 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 or any officer, employee, contractor, subcontractor, or agent of such company, may discharge, demote, suspend, threaten, harass, or in any other manner discriminate against an employee in the terms and conditions of employment because of any lawful act done by the employee [in order to report illegal conduct].” But neither this act nor other pieces of legislation make any guarantees to whistleblowers outside of immediate legal trouble and reactions by their own companies.

Suppose that someone reported instances of illegal activity at General Motors, for example. A former president of that company, James Roche, once had this to say about whistleblowing: “Some critics are now busy eroding another support of free enterprise—the loyalty of a management team, with its unifying values and cooperative work. Some of the enemies of business now encourage an employee to be disloyal to the enterprise. They want to create suspicion and disharmony, and pry into the proprietary interests of the business. However this is labeled—industrial espionage, whistleblowing, or professional responsibility—it is another tactic for spreading disunity and creating conflict.”James M. Roche, “The Competitive System, to Work, to Preserve, and to Protect,” Vital Speeches of the Day (May 1971), 445. Apart from the fact that industrial espionage, whistleblowing, and professional responbility are all very different from each other, if this attitude were shared by other industry professionals, it’s easy to see how a whistleblower at one company could be informally blacklisted and therefore never hired again for a position in their area of expertise. Could a whistleblower have a right to a new position, even circumstances like those?

While it would be nice for us to fix a problem like that one by providing a new job, it’s probably too idealistic, at least right now, for whistleblower protections to extend beyond legal prosecution and company reprisal. A deeper principle remains, however, in considering the purpose and protections behind whistleblowing in the context of hiring and firing. Whistleblowing reports illegal activities—this is a valuable thing to do, and we can protect reporters in at least some ways. But wouldn’t it be better for whistleblowers not to be necessary in the first place? What if there weren’t any activities for anyone to blow the whistle on?

This is the thinking behind the following remark from George Brenkert. He summarizes the hope not only of whistleblowing, but of business ethics in general, to improve human conduct in the business world, even when financial incentives lean in another direction: “More generally, however, we should work to create organizations and a social and political system that renders whistle-blowing and such sacrifices unnecessary. We need to transform organizations that shape and form our lives so that the wrong, the harms, and the abuses that occur through them can be identified and corrected. We may not be able to ensure that this is always the case, but we can do a better job than we have.”George Brenkert, “Whistle-blowing, Moral Integrity, and Organizational Ethics,” in The Oxford Handbook of Business Ethics, eds. George Brenkert and Tom Beauchamp (Oxford University Press, 2009), 594.

sidebar.title: Case Study: Whistleblowing
sidebar.para: Cheryl Eckard was a quality control manager at a GlaxoSmithKline manufacturing facility in Puerto Rico. The facility made medicine for children and others, and Eckard noticed many problems with the manufacturing processes over the course of many years. Some of these problems involved violations of industry and government standards, including pills that contained either more or less than the proper amount of medicine in each dose as well as bacteria-contaminated baby cream. Eckard reported her observations to her company on a number of occasions, but they ignored her warnings. GlaxoSmithKline’s own internal compliance department found that her complaints were “unsubstantiated” by their own findings. The company fired her in 2003.

Eckard then filed reports with multiple government agencies, which led to FDA-backed search warrants for the Puerto Rico facility. The violations were discovered across several months and, at the time, the FDA’s seizing of the medicine was the largest it had ever carried out for drug products.

A court case followed in which many groups were involved, both government and non-government. GlaxoSmithKline was found liable for its violations and ordered to pay hundreds of millions of dollars in fines and accrued interest. In addition, because of a part in the False Claims Act known as the qui tam provision, Eckard was able to be a plaintiff in the government’s case against GlaxoSmithKline. The terms of the settlement required that 22% of the payout, or just short of 100 million dollars, go to Eckard herself.

listitem.para: Eckard’s complaints against GlaxoSmithKline noted that medications, including some for children, were being incorrectly manufactured. Are these activities serious enough that any reasonable person with knowledge of them would have an ethical duty to report? Why or why not?
Did Cheryl Eckard have an ethical duty to report what she’d observed?
What factors might have caused GlaxoSmithKline’s own internal compliance department to repeatedly reach conclusions that contradicted Eckard’s in their own investigations?

How should an internal auditing or compliance department relate to the rest of a company in order to assure that they can reach independent judgments? Or are independent judgments even possible in such cases?
If GlaxoSmithKline’s medications were being manufactured outside the United States but sold within it, what country determines the regulations that apply to the manufacturing process?

In her case against GlaxoSmithKline, Eckard received a financial settlement so large that it wouldn’t matter if other companies refused to hire her. Should other whistleblowers be entitled to proportional financial compensation? Why or why not?

section.title: The Ethics of Employment-at-Will
section.para: So far in this chapter we’ve discussed the ethics of many issues involved in hiring, firing, and behavior at work. While we haven’t made this explicit, our discussion has assumed that we’re speaking of the hiring, firing, and behavior of employees with a close relationship to the company they work for. In the United States, this usually means full-time salaried employees with benefits.

But there are other classes of employees whose relationships to their employers are very different. Workers receiving hourly wages, for example, don’t often get health insurance or other benefits, and so while they may work hard and love their jobs, they stand in a different relation to their company than salaried employees with benefits.

The class of employees we’ll be discussing here are those whose positions fall within the category of employment-at-will or EAWA legal stance that employers take to their employees, which allows them to fire those employees at any time and for any reason. . EAW is a legal stance that employers take to their employees, which allows them to fire those employees at any time and for any reason. In every state except Montana, employees—salaried, paid hourly, or otherwise—are generally hired and kept on under the assumption that their employment happens on an at-will basis. The only regular exceptions are employees with contracts stating that their employment is not at will; the default assumption is therefore that most positions are EAW.

In order to fire someone with a contract stating that they are not employed at will, an employer must usually have “cause,” or a legitimate and documented reason to terminate their employment (the possible “causes” often appear in the contract). It’s common, for example, for tenured professors at universities or for partners in certain types of firms to take up their positions without an at-will basis; as a result, it is much more difficult to dismiss those kinds of employees from their positions. Everyone else works under the assumption of EAW.

EAW is a business policy that many people in the United States will not have thought to question or even consider at all. Given the free market assumptions on which the US economy is based, the most natural thing for people to believe is that employers have a right to hire and fire as they wish; likewise, employees themselves have a right to continue in a position or quit, depending on what they want. EAW applies to employees as well, giving them the right to leave a job when and how they choose, regardless of the expectations their employer may have. In a business world where free decisions such as these are taken as essential to the health of a market, EAW seems natural and even desirable.

Thus we see here another sense of the term “right to work,” discussed previously in Chapter 5. There we examined employee rights at work—what rights do employees have, and why those? One of our important conclusions was that any right not protected by a law and enforceable in court is only a nice-sounding idea.

The same is true when we think of a person’s “right to work” in the context of EAW. If an employee enjoys their work and doesn’t want to leave their position, but is employed under a condition of EAW, they have nothing like a right to work. They may have rights at work, in the sense that there are grievance processes for complaints, and so on. But they have no right to work in the form of a legally-protected claim to their current position. Even if they love their job, and their employer loves them, EAW allows a company to fire them for any reason.

Employees who wish to challenge their firing in court often do so with a wrongful terminationA legal challenge that alleges that, even though someone’s employment might have been on the assumption of EAW, their employer was still wrong to fire them. suit. A legal challenge based on “wrongful termination” alleges that, even though someone’s employment might have been on the assumption of EAW, their employer was still wrong to fire them.

Given the doctrine of EAW, it may seem that employees without contracts stating otherwise could never have a legitimate complaint of wrongful termination. That isn’t the case, however, and we’ve already seen examples: an employee in a wheelchair could claim wrongful termination if she believes that she was fired because of her requests for accommodations to her disability; an employee who believes he was fired because of his race could claim wrongful termination as well. In both these cases and others, the legal backing for wrongful termination would come from a specific law, such as the Americans with Disabilities Act or an amendment to the Constitution.

Note, then, that challenges to EAW usually come on the basis of other laws. The going assumption is that all employment is EAW, unless either (1) an employee has a contract stating otherwise, or (2) an employee can prove that their firing violated some specific law. In situations of the latter kind, the burden of proof is always on the employee.

sidebar.title: Case Study: Wrongful Termination
sidebar.para: Consider the case of John Guz, an employee of Bechtel Corporation who was fired after 22 years of satisfactory work and good performance reviews. When the company began to transition its workflow to require more computers, Guz was notified that he would need to become more familiar with how to use them in order to complete his work successfully. Not long after, in the midst of major restructuring at Bechtel, the company put Guz on a “holding status” in which he was not paid but continued to receive medical benefits. Six months after that status took effect, in June 1993, Bechtel terminated Guz’s employment.Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc., 54 Cal.App.4th 1303 (Cal. Ct. App. 1997).

Guz then brought a wrongful termination suit against Bechtel. He didn’t claim that the company had violated his civil rights, nor that it had violated some other law; his basis for the claim was that his long-term employment, entered into in good faith by both himself and the company, was enough by itself to constitute an unspoken agreement of continued employment which could only be ended with cause. In other words, Guz’s longevity at Bechtel gave him an “implied contract,” which the company had breached in firing him.

The lower-level court hearing Guz’s case issued a summary judgment, or a decision without a trial, in favor of Bechtel. The court reasoned that Guz “was an at-will employee and has not introduced any evidence that he was ever told at any time that he had permanent employment or that he would be retained as long as he was doing a good job.”Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc., 54 Cal.App.4th 1303 (Cal. Ct. App. 1997). Guz did not deny this characterization; he admitted he’d never been told he could keep his job, but appealed the decision anyway, again on the basis of a breach of contract.

After the appeals court found that there was evidence suggesting Guz had a legitimate case, the disagreement reached the California Supreme Court. While agreeing that there might have been an implied contract between Bechtel and Guz, that Court ruled that such an implied contract could not override the actual contract or firing policies under which Guz had agreed to work. The case was found in favor of Bechtel, thus strengthening the position of EAW for other employers as well.

listitem.para: How would you respond to Guz’s case?
Do long-term employees with good work histories have an implied contract guaranteeing them future employment?
Does an employee’s “loyalty” to a company create an obligation to show loyalty in return?
Could there ever be circumstances in which a good-faith implied contract could supersede the employment terms that were actually agreed on?
Why or why not?

section.para: Questions surrounding implied contracts are legal questions, but they have ethical implications as well. Stepping back from the merits of individual cases, we can ask a broader question: is a widespread, default assumption of EAW ethical in itself?

We can motivate this question by considering the sometimes-catastrophic consequences that a firing can have in an employee’s life. In some cases, an employee’s entire livelihood, including their ability to provide for dependents and children, requires that they remain employed; losing employment can mean upending whole lives or, in the worst cases, things like hunger or eviction. In addition, because access to health insurance is usually so closely tied to someone’s employment, a termination can mean an end to critical medical care.

The ethical questions thus become, is it ethical to open an employee to such risks by firing them without cause? Might an employer have obligations to its employees that would make firing them unethical, at least in some circumstances?

By and large, both the market and the legal system in the United States have answered those two questions with a “yes” and a “no,” respectively. And, as we’ve discussed before, employee rights only go as far as they are enforced by meaningful laws; if there are no laws, there are no rights, however great the rights may seem on paper.

However, the ethical implications surrounding EAW make it a topic worth considering carefully. Just as hirings and firings have financial costs for businesses, they also carry human costs for actual people. To ignore those costs is to deny some of the basic values that characterize human life. This isn’t to say that someone whose position is EAW can’t be fired without cause; perhaps it is ethical to do it. But recognizing that EAW is an ethical issue in itself is a form of ethical progress for many people.

section.title: Workers Outside of Work
section.para: The last issue that we’ll discuss in detail in this chapter is that of workers outside of work. Until now our discussion of hiring, firing, and worker behavior has confined itself to these activities as they take place in the workplace. Of course someone can be fired over the phone or while they’re on vacation, but the conduct we’ve considered, along with the ethical implications of that conduct, has concerned only things done at work.

In contrast, this section will consider worker behavior outside of work. Does it matter for one’s employment? If it does, should it? Are there ethical principles that govern the way employers deal with employee conduct outside of work, or is that conduct something that ought to be independent of employers?

To begin, it’s worth noting that, at least in the United States and other countries, the current assumption is that an employee’s conduct outside of work is relevant for an employer in determining whether to retain the employee. Companies make most retention decisions on the basis of performance on the job: in general, if an employee does good work and isn’t hard to get along with, companies want to keep them. But some recent events show that employers are monitoring employees outside of the workplace, and sometimes using what they learn as a basis for termination.

At the end of , for example, we discussed the case of Justine Sacco, who was fired for remarks she made online while on a trip to South Africa. Several companies parted ways with employees over their participation in the Capitol riots in early 2023, including a marketing organization in Maryland, a real estate management group in Chicago, and an insurance firm in Texas.

It’s not difficult to find other examples of companies which, upon discovering an employee’s actions outside of work, have chosen to fire them. Sacco’s case in particular was one of the first in an ongoing string of high-profile firings based on social media. She made her remarks on Twitter, and most of the negative reaction to what she said happened there as well; pictures and videos on Facebook and Instagram were crucial in the Capitol riots, even when companies fired employees who didn’t actually invade the building or trespass into offices.

Thus an important part of considering workers and their actions outside of work is social media, as well as the internet more broadly. While it’s no longer common, people can still choose to keep their lives off the internet; when they don’t make that choice, harmful information often becomes public, even when the original posters didn’t intend it to.
Given all this, the most pressing ethical question involving behavior outside of work is this: is it ethical for companies to monitor and act on information about employees’ behavior outside of work?

In one sense this question is easy to answer—if someone is convicted of a serious crime, then it doesn’t seem ethically problematic for their employer to dismiss them. But here we aren’t considering such easy cases. Justine Sacco didn’t commit a felony or any crime at all; many of those rioting at the Capitol did, but there may have been some who legitimately meant to join a peaceful protest, and thus were acting within their constitutional rights. In cases like these—when an employee’s actions outside of work are not illegal and may actually be protected by law—is it ethical for companies to fire that employee, if the company disagrees with the actions?

In observing some reactionary cases on social media, it is difficult to avoid the impression that companies’ decisions are driven by fear, rather than by any ethical principle. In other words, it often seems as though companies do not actually object to the employee’s behavior as much as they fear backlash from customers or negative media attention. By cutting ties with an employee, they can end what could be a negative connection in the eyes of the public.

That choice, however, doesn’t seem ethically problematic either. For reasons we’ve discussed previously in this chapter, the employer-employee relationship differs greatly from company to company and even from individual to individual. Choosing to fire someone because they’re bringing negative attention to the company, at least from a business perspective, may not be that different from pulling an under-performing radio ad. Although firing someone has more significant human consequences, the underlying principle is the same.

In its current form, the problem of workers’ actions outside of work seems to lie with the very public ways in which people live. Prior to the internet, only celebrities could lead such public lives, and then only because photographers and reporters wished to follow them. Now it is possible for anyone to live as public a life as they wish. That development in itself is ethically neutral: it isn’t good or bad, it just is. But it is a new way of living life in a human society, and both employers and employees must decide how they will react to it. The operative ethical principle here may be caveat agens: “let the agent beware.” This principle was true before social media, but it’s even more important now, as one’s formerly “private” life becomes public, just as one’s work life has usually been.

sidebar.title: Case Study: Termination in the NFL
sidebar.para: In the 2013 NFL season, the San Francisco 49ers reached the Super Bowl and lost by only three points to the Baltimore Ravens. In the following season they came one game short of returning to the Super Bowl. Their quarterback in both of those games was Colin Kaepernick, who had entered the league in 2011 before becoming the team’s starter in 2012.

A quarterback leading his team to the Super Bowl in only his third season, and just the second as starter, is a remarkable accomplishment. During his best years, Kaepernick was one of the league’s best players and still holds the single-game playoff record for rushing yards by a quarterback. However, despite his skill and winning history, Kaepernick never played another game after 2016, just a few years removed from almost winning a championship.

The reason is that Kaepernick, who is Black, chose to kneel during the national anthem, which is traditionally played before NFL games. Kaepernick first did it before a preseason game in 2016, but continued to do so in each game following. He explained his choice by saying that it was his way of protesting against police brutality and other racial and social justice issues. Kaepernick was almost universally criticized for his choice by those connected to the NFL, though he received support for his actions from many others.

After he became a free agent following the 2016 season, no NFL team wished to sign him, even as a backup. That alone was unusual—although he did play poorly in 2016, most quarterbacks with his record of success receive chances again and again, because the position is so difficult to play. Not Kaepernick. He refused to apologize for kneeling during the national anthem, and in interviews and tryouts with other teams, he would not commit to ending his protests. While some said that his poor performance in his final season doomed his future chances, it’s difficult to believe that his kneeling had nothing to do with it. As the statistical analysis website FiveThirtyEight put it, “No above-average quarterback has been unemployed nearly as long as Kaepernick this offseason [in 2017].”Kyle Wagner, “Colin Kaepernick Is Not Supposed to Be Unemployed,” FiveThirtyEight, August 9, 2017, . He never played again.

A few years later, following widespread protests surrounding the death of George Floyd and others, the NFL began social justice initiatives of its own. Before the 2021 and 2022 seasons, players could choose from various slogans to add as decorations to their helmets, including “End Racism,” “Black Lives Matter,” “Say Their Stories,” and “Stop Hate.” The league also began to inscribe “End Racism” at the ends of NFL fields, just past the touchdown area; it committed millions of dollars to social justice-related employees and initiatives.

“I wish we had listened earlier, Kaep, to what you were kneeling about and what you were trying to bring attention to,” said Roger Goodell in 2020, after another offseason in which no team signed Kaepernick.Alex Didon, “Goodell Apologizes to Kap, Wishes NFL Had Listened Earlier,” NBC Sports, August 23, 2020, .

listitem.para: To what extent should employers be allowed to consider off-the-clock behavior by employees in deciding whether to retain them?
Were NFL teams discriminating against Kaepernick for his stance on social justice? How would it be possible to show it?
Should a company be allowed to ban protests by employees during work hours? Why or why not?
Do organizations that have a disproportionate number of minority employees, like the NFL, have more significant obligations for social justice and other social issues?
Given its about-face on issues of social justice, does the NFL owe Colin Kaepernick anything? Why or why not?

section.title: The Ethics of Hiring and Firing
section.para: This chapter has focused on issues involving hiring and firing, including discrimination, whistleblowing, and employment-at-will. While we’ve seen many case studies and examples, the truth is that there are many topics we didn’t cover. These areas of business are rich with ethical challenges.

As we’ve noted in previous chapters, individual executives, managers, and employees are the keepers of ethical values. Those people may wish to ignore ethical values in their actions, and in doing so may not face any legal problems. But the foundation of business ethics is not what is legal. Ethical considerations apply to many decisions and actions that the law is indifferent toward. Unless we take those considerations and our ethical values seriously, we cannot expect anyone else to do so.

We’re now ready to close the sixth chapter of our book. In the remaining chapters, we’ll be zeroing in on more targeted areas of business, including marketing, accounting, and globalization. As always, our goal will be to understand principles we can use to turn mere good ideas into ethical action.

section.title: Introduction to the Ethics of Exchange

listitem.para: Understand some of the main ethical problems involved in buying and selling.
Be able to explain the ethical implications of certain kinds of pricing strategies.
Identify the ethics of piracy, informed consent, and internet commerce in particular.

section.title: What Can Be Sold
section.para: Our topic for this chapter will be the “ethics of exchange,” or the ethics of buying and selling. As with almost all the material we discuss in this book, there’s much more to say about this topic than we can cover in a single chapter—we have to pick and choose the most important and interesting issues. With that in mind, we’ll begin by looking at the issue of what can be sold and bought; then we’ll talk about pricing, and after that, piracy. Our final two sections will be about problems of informed consent in buying and the internet as a medium of exchange.

You might notice that none of these issues have to do with marketing, or the ways in which companies present their products to customers and try to convince customers to buy them. We’ll save the ethics of marketing for our next chapter.
Let’s begin, then, with what can be sold.

The very title of this chapter suggests that ethical issues with exchange begin before any exchange can even occur. Think about all the people and processes involved in bringing a product to market and placing it on a shelf at a particular store, so that you can enter to purchase it. It’s possible to find ethical issues in the decisions each of those people make and at each step of those processes. So many of the problems we’ve discussed so far in this course circle around the interaction between organizations and individuals, or between companies and customers; as we think back to stakeholder theory in , customers themselves are an important part of any business. And, in most cases, the most personal interactions that customers have with a company is at the point of sale.
But what can ethically be sold? And why those things, and not others?

In asking these questions, it’s common to approach them from the perspective of a seller. When we are the ones doing the selling, we’re also usually the ones who can decide what we want to sell in the first place. We’re thus faced with the question of what is ethical for us to sell. But we can also approach those questions from the perspective of a buyer. Although it perhaps isn’t as natural an idea, buyers too can make choices about what is ethical for them to buy.

We’ll take up both perspectives at different times in this chapter with examples and case studies. As we’ll see, there may be ethical responsibilities for both buyers and sellers in determining what can ethically be sold.

We’ll start with a no-controversy example: a stuffed toy animal. Let’s assume that the people who assembled the toy received a fair wage for their labor and did it in acceptable working conditions. The toy is an elephant with a friendly smile and a trunk that honks when you squeeze it; children love to hug it when they walk by it in the store. It’s made of sustainable materials and could even be recycled.

If we’re considering the question of what can ethically be sold, this toy elephant appears to be an example of something whose sale would be very difficult to object to on ethical grounds. Given the circumstances of its creation and its purpose, it would take a bit of ingenuity to devise an ethical reason for why no one should sell it.

But suppose that we take this exact product and change those circumstances, so that the people who assembled it received very little pay for their labor, even relative to the third-world country in which they live. When these people went to work they were forced by oppressive supervisors to stay long hours and exceed their production quotas so the supervisors could look good.

Now, the product itself is identical—nothing has changed about the friendly elephant, but something is different about its creation. Since the creation process involves significant ethical issues, the very sale of the elephant may be an ethical issue as well; this product may be something that, for ethical reasons, ought not to be sold.

Note, then, that whether something can ethically be sold is not just a matter of what the product is, but involves other factors as well. Knowing about these circumstances, could a distributor have an ethical duty not to sell the elephant or other toys from the same factory? Why? To what extent do those circumstances affect distant points in the supply and consumption chains?

Consider next a product known to produce significant harms to health: cigarettes. Even if we suppose that the process of creating the cigarettes involves no ethical issues, the product itself is so bad for most people that this one factor might be enough to make it unethical. What if we slap health warnings on the box, and plaster pictures of diseased lungs on the packing cases? Can the producers and sellers of a product exonerate themselves from responsibility for its health harms by giving enough warnings? Or could they still be responsible for what it does to buyers? Speaking of the latter, given that they’re mostly doing harm to themselves, do buyers have an ethical duty not to purchase cigarettes? Or does this duty lie only on the side of the sellers?
We’ve now seen another reason a product could be unethical to sell: the harm it does to health.

There are other kinds of harms, though. Let’s say that a stand-up comedian records a comedy album filled with misogynistic and racist jokes. It’s unlikely that any physical harm will come out of people buying a CD or downloading the album, but what about mental and emotional harm? Can those count as ethical reasons why something shouldn’t be sold? Would we fix the problem if we put a bunch of warning labels on the CD case, as we do for cigarettes?

Going beyond questions of creation and product harm, there are also things that just seem like they ought not to be sold at all. For example, in 2017, an American woman known as Giselle reportedly sold her virginity to a German businessman for almost four million dollars.Frank Chung, “ ‘Dream Come True’: 19-Year-Old Auctions Virginity for $3.9 Million on Controversial Website,” The Chronicle, November 17, 2017, . Giselle herself saw this “product” as something that belonged to her and could therefore be treated as a commodity, and understood the whole process to be a “form of emancipation” which would allow her to “study wherever I want, buy a new house and travel around the world.” Is the right to an individual’s first intimate encounter something that can be bought? To what extent can such a thing be made into a commodity and given a price? Of course, since she already did sell her virginity, the question is not whether it is possible. The question is whether such a thing is ethical, and even if it is ethical for Giselle to do, would it automatically be ethical for an online marketplace to allow such a sale?

In view of these examples, we can see many reasons why it might be unethical to sell a certain product, and even unethical to treat something as a product in the first place. Ethical duties regarding the prohibition of such sales would, in some cases, correspond to ethical duties of buyers, as (perhaps) in the case of Giselle.

On the other hand, it’s difficult to distill these observations into a general principle about what can and cannot be ethically sold. A great deal depends on the circumstances and on other applicable rights. In the case of cigarettes, the health harms of tobacco have been widely accepted public knowledge for years, but people still retain the right to decide how to treat their bodies. In addition, ethical opposition to Giselle’s choice may seem disingenuous in light of the prostitution and sex-work industries more generally. Because of poverty or other reasons, some people have no choice but to sell themselves, and for a lot less than Giselle was to receive. Is one situation more ethically problematic than the other? Is there a principle that could capture many of our judgments about the ethics of what is sold?

Another factor making it difficult to derive general principles about what can be sold is cultural variation. Norms about what is appropriate to sell differ from culture to culture; in the Philippines, for example, dogs are routinely raised and slaughtered for human consumption. From our cultural background we can ask about the ethics of eating dogs—many people would find it abhorrent. But we could also ask whether it’s ethical for us to impose conventional western thinking about morality onto a different culture, in order to make them act in ways we believe are right.

In sum, most questions about what is ethical to sell will depend on culture, context, and other factors. More universal values, such as autonomy and human dignity, may be able to help us resolve some of the ethical puzzles we’ve raised so far, but they probably can’t fix everything.

We’ve been examining these puzzles from the perspectives of both seller and buyer; now let’s shift to the buyer’s perspective alone. Suppose you’re in a coffee shop and you have a choice between two coffees: one is just coffee, while the other is “fair trade” coffee. “Fair trade” coffee can mean various things, but is often associated with bean growers receiving a generous, fixed price for their beans in addition to other benefits. If you don’t know anything about the first coffee, but you’re sure that this “fair trade” variety really is fair trade, do you have an ethical obligation to purchase the latter, assuming you’re able to afford both? In general, do buyers have an ethical responsibility to prefer products that are “sustainable” for either the producers, the environment, or both? What do you think?

In evaluating buying behavior we may have better luck formulating a general ethical principle. Let’s take a look at one: when possible and feasible, buyers should prefer products that do less harm to others and to the environment, including in both their effects and in how they were created. The first part of this principle allows it to apply only in cases when a person is actually able to buy less-harmful products—no one would violate the principle, for example, if such products weren’t available in their area, or they couldn’t afford them. The principle next focuses on the possible harm caused by products, mentioning both other people and the environment, which could include animals. Finally, the principle notes that a product can cause harm in ways beyond its actual effects.

Is this principle true? It does seem to help us understand the examples we’ve seen so far in this chapter. It’s a practical principle and so could easily guide our action, which is what we’re looking for.

Perhaps a better question is, is our principle governing buying behavior specific enough? Could it guide our behavior in enough situations to be useful? Why or why not? What do you think about it, as you reflect and test?

sidebar.title: Case Study: Ethics of Selling Food
sidebar.para: Jimmy Dean flips burgers at a fast-food restaurant. Jimmy is good at his job, but not that good; sometimes he drops the burgers on the floor when he’s flipping them. When a burger hits the floor, he picks it up and slaps it back on the grill for a moment, thinking that the additional heat will kill any bacteria the floor may have had. Then he finishes cooking the meat and uses it to assemble hamburgers.

listitem.para: In reusing the meat that’s fallen on the floor, has Jimmy done something wrong?

How far does Jimmy’s responsibility to customers extend in terms of how clean the food is that he serves? If food falls on the counter, for example, should he serve it? Try to think about this question from the perspective of a harried fast-food employee, rather than from the perspective of a buyer. What is Jimmy’s ethical responsibility here?
Would Jimmy’s ethical responsibilities change if he were paid more? What about less?

sidebar.para: Consider the following examples of products discussed in this section from the perspective of both the seller and the buyer. What other ethical issues might be involved? Would you sell them? Would you buy them?

listitem.para: A stuffed toy animal, produced fairly
A stuffed toy animal, produced by exploiting workers
A pack of cigarettes
A comedy album with racist and sexist jokes
Coffee that you know isn’t fair trade
Coffee that you know is fair trade

section.title: Pricing
section.para: For most consumers, a product’s price is one of the most important parts of an exchange. In fact, it may be a product’s price that initially prompts an exchange in the first place; all things considered, we’re more likely to buy something when the price is low, and when the price is really low, we might think about buying something that we never intended to buy at all. On the other hand, when a price is high, the decision is more difficult; a price that’s too high locks some people out entirely.

The question we wish to consider here, though, is what factors should determine a price. Note that this question differs from asking what factors do determine a price—we can take classes in economics and business to answer that one. The “should” question is an ethical question, inviting us to consider any ethical reasons that bear on the question.

We can begin by thinking about what makes a price “fair.” Various things might go into it, but first we should ask, fair to whom? There is a sense of the term “fair” in which it means that a seller and a buyer have agreed on that price; if both agree, and both are aware of what they’re doing, then it seems as though the price they choose would be fair regardless of how it compares to the market. On the other hand, there’s a sense of the term “fair” in which a seller sets a price because she believes it is the price she is rightfully owed for the product; it is “fair” to her. The same goes for a buyer. Lower prices might be more “fair” to buyers, regardless of how they impact sellers, simply because they make it easier for buyers to enter an exchange.

In most cases these different senses of the term “fair” balance themselves out through the normal forces of supply, demand, and market conditions. A high-end clothing store in a poorer area of a small town probably won’t sell many products because its prices are too high; the issue in such a case, though, isn’t about fairness and has only to do with a correct choice of market. In different market conditions, the same store could sell the same products at the same price, and the question of fairness wouldn’t arise.

We can also put questions about fair prices in terms of whether sellers, buyers, or both have a “right” to certain prices. For many products the answer to this question appears to be an obvious “no.” Cars are products that take many people and many supply chains to create; do I, as the buyer, have a “right” to demand a price that I can afford? It doesn’t seem so. If prices are too high, it is likely that another seller will fill the market niche opened by the too-high prices, and I will soon be able to buy lower-priced cars—but perhaps still not at the price I consider “fair.”

sidebar.title: Case Study: Fast Fashion
sidebar.para: Sarah runs an upscale boutique in downtown San Antonio. She sells clothes made locally as well as pieces made overseas. The overseas products sell best, because Sarah has found an empty space in the San Antonio clothes market: she’s the only one selling fast fashion garments.

Sarah pays close attention to fashion trends on Instagram and TikTok. When she notices pieces she likes, Sarah sends pictures or videos to a contact in Los Angeles, who then works with clothing producers in Bangladesh and other South Asian countries to create the garments. The resulting products are shipped quickly and, if the conditions are right, Sarah can go from noticing a cute dress in a video to having it stocked in her store in less than three weeks.

Sarah’s use of social media and fast fashion trends has made her store very successful. She’s able to charge low prices and intentionally undercuts other retailers in her area by charting their pricing for similar goods.
