When asked whether her clothes are the result of fast fashion production processes, Sarah usually gestures to the sales floor and says, “All our producers are paid fair wages for what they do.”

listitem.para: Given the market share of Sarah’s boutique, is she doing something unethical in undercutting the prices of other retailers? Why or why not?

Sarah is able to charge such low prices because the garment producers in Asia are paid very low wages. As a business owner in the United States, does Sarah have any ethical duties to those garment producers? If so, what are they, and what should do they obligate her to do?

section.para: The previous fast-fashion case study raises an important point about pricing: like the issue of what can ethically be sold, the price of a product carries ethical implications that go beyond the people involved in a particular exchange.

In fast fashion, for example, garment producers in South Asia and elsewhere do follow trends on social media or on the catwalk among major designers. Once they spot a product they think others will like, they use cheaper materials and cheap labor to produce an enormous product volume that they then sell for cheap, with thin but manageable margins. Retailers in the United States and elsewhere can then sell the goods for cheap as well, since they buy them from distributors for so little.

This price, however, relies on a production process that by its very nature seems to exploit garment workers. It isn’t just an issue of wages and hours; the working conditions are also very dangerous, because the garment facilities are themselves very low quality. In April 2013, for example, the Rana Plaza building in Dhaka, Bangladesh, collapsed into pieces, killing 1,134 people and injuring almost twice that number. Besides housing a bank and other stores, Rana Plaza also held five garment factories which made clothing for less-expensive retailers like Walmart but also higher-end retailers like Benneton and JCPenny.“Rana Plaza,” Clean Clothes Campaign, accessed September 12, 2023, ; “Who Paid Up and Who Failed to Take Responsibility?” Clean Clothes Campaign, accessed September 12, 2023, .

Low prices, then, or prices that are “fair” in the sense of being able to compete in a global market, come with their own ethical price tag. In order for western companies to be able to sell some of their wares at prices that western consumers consider “fair,” they must often treat others unfairly—or, at least, they must treat them in a way that they could not treat American workers.

Thus at least one factor in an ethically “fair” or just price for a product must be, once again, the circumstances of the product’s creation. Note, again, that we are not discussing how products are priced; we are discussing how they ought to be priced. This latter question is the ethical one, and the one that demands we pay attention to the details of the production process that normally lie outside our view of the product.

So far, however, we’ve only been discussing luxury items, such as high-end clothing; the ethical issues with pricing for those items have much to do with the circumstances of production. But things change when we look at other kinds of products. Let’s think about basic goods next, such as food and groceries.

Because many people are not able to grow their own food at all, much less grow enough to meet all their needs, they must buy it from markets or grocery stores. The prices of food and other staple goods fluctuates from market to market, but in general these regional differences track income levels: groceries are more expensive in places where it’s more expensive to live.

But unlike a pair of Gucci loafers, groceries are a necessity. Should their status as a necessity affect the way they are priced? For example, is it ethical for stores to mark up the prices of milk, bread, and eggs, when such items are staples of many families’ diets?

You could respond to this question by saying that the question of ethics never arises here, because a store that marked up basic food items would soon not be selling them, as customers would choose not to buy them. This response ignores the reality that many consumers face, however, in their needs and what they are able to purchase. As we discussed in the case of internet companies and monthly charges in , as long as consumers have few or no real options for buying groceries, they find themselves in a position where they have no choice but to pay higher prices. In some market conditions, then, a store could continue to raise food prices, and consumers would continue to pay the higher prices. But this wouldn’t be because the selling and buying behavior were reaching a stable equilibrium between supply and demand; it would be because the consumers would starve if they stopped buying. They would simply devote more and more of their income to buying food, which means they must take the money from whatever other things they might use it for.

Here we see another factor in determining a fair price: the buyer’s ability to pay. This factor may not apply in all cases; it doesn’t seem to matter at all, or matters very little, for luxury fashion brands. But for other kinds of products it matters a great deal and is an important ethical consideration in pricing.

sidebar.title: Case Study: Raising Prices
sidebar.para: Bill is a butcher who sources meat from local farms. Bill tries to keep his prices stable, setting them high enough to receive a comfortable margin for himself, without making his goods too expensive for his clientele.

Last year the national economy went through a rapid rise in inflation and prices skyrocketed for many products, such as gasoline and food. For whatever reason, though, Bill’s costs didn’t increase. The ranchers he worked with didn’t seem to notice the price difference in animal feed and never demanded more money for their meat. As a result, for the first few weeks of the inflationary period, Bill’s prices stayed the same. People began to notice, and he was soon selling more meat than usual.

Then Bill decided to raise his prices. He reasoned that, because prices were rising across the board for many goods, he ought to be able to raise his prices as well. Although the price increases weren’t required by his financial situation, Bill started charging more for cuts of beef, pork, and other meat. The higher prices led to a significant rise in profits, since Bill wasn’t paying his distributors more.

listitem.para: Bill chose to raise his meat prices even though his products weren’t affected by inflation. Was his action ethical? Does he have a duty to his customers to only charge them a certain amount above what he himself pays for his goods?

Would your answer to the first question be different if Bill sold fishing gear, video games, or floor mats for cars? How much does a product’s use or status as a necessity impact the ethics of its pricing?
In what ways do inflation and other uncontrolled changes in regional or national prices affect the ethics of pricing?

section.para: In the previous case study, Bill chose to raise his prices simply because he could. In most circumstances this doesn’t seem like an unethical thing to do, because customers can always choose not to buy. In situations where that choice is hard or even impossible, though, raising prices for higher margins may be ethically problematic.

Consider again the case of Bill—do his actions constitute profiteering? ProfiteeringThe practice of marking prices up to make greater profits by unethical means. is usually defined as the practice of marking prices up to make greater profits by unethical means. This definition is somewhat unhelpful for us, though, because it assumes that we must already know what ethical means are in order to judge whether profiteering has happened. Is Bill guilty of it, in our case study? What about Matt Colvin? Colvin is a Tennessee man who bought thousands of bottles of hand sanitizer in the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic. In March 2020 Colvin was able to sell the bottles online at heavy markups and was “in a situation where what [he had] coming and going could potentially put [his] family in a really good place financially.” But after online retailers such as Amazon and eBay made it impossible for him to sell his goods, Colvin was stuck with over 17,000 bottles that he could not sell.Jack Nicas, “He Has 17,700 Bottles of Hand Sanitizer and Nowhere to Sell Them,” New York Times, updated March 15, 2020, . Did Colvin profiteer? Is there is a difference between what he did, and what Bill did? Why or why not?

Another form of unethical pricing is price fixingThe practice of multiple sellers agreeing to keep prices at artificially high levels. , the practice of multiple sellers agreeing to keep prices at artificially high levels. In normal circumstances, sellers in the same market compete against each other, but things don’t have to be that way. Imagine three gas stations in a small town, located a hundred miles from any other town. The gas stations could compete against each other to lower prices, but they could just as easily agree to raise prices and keep them up—what choice do consumers have in the matter, anyway? If people need gasoline in this small town, they’ll have to pay whatever the stations charge, because they can’t go anywhere else.

Price fixing is illegal and is normally thought to be wrong, but on what grounds is it actually unethical? In cases like the gas stations, it isn’t clear that collusion on price actually harms anyone; it just forces certain people to pay small amounts more for things that they would need to buy anyway. In other words, there isn’t anything in the economics of the situation or even in the harm that makes price fixing wrong; if it’s wrong, it must be wrong for some other reason.
Is price fixing wrong? Can you think of an ethical principle that would describe why it’s wrong?

Our discussions of profiteering and price fixing lead us to an important point, with which we’ll finish this section. At first glance, pricing doesn’t seem to be an ethical issue at all, for economic mechanisms like supply and demand normally take care of gross inequities. But the view that “fair” prices will eventually be reached by economic mechanisms alone requires many assumptions. Some of these assumptions are about other economic factors, but others are about people and their behavior, such as what they will do when grocery prices increase.
The nature of a product, its necessity for human life, its circumstances of creation, and the action of other agents are all important issues, then, in the ethics of pricing.
Think of an industry you know well, either as a buyer or a seller. Can you think of an ethical principle that could govern how fair prices are created in that industry?

section.title: Piracy
section.para: The third issue we’ll discuss in the ethics of exchange is piracyThe unlawful use of another’s property for profit or other benefits. . In general, piracy is the unlawful use of another’s property for profit or other benefits. This definition is intentionally vague, as the concept of “piracy” can extend to cover many actions, from an academic plagiarizing someone else’s research to a child unintentionally buying counterfeit Pokémon cards from an online retailer.

For now we’ll just consider clear examples of piracy, where the “pirate” has knowledge of both the theft and the benefit. Near the beginning of , we discussed the case of Napster, a company whose file-sharing software allowed users to download music for free. For the most part, the music they downloaded was “pirated”—that is, neither Napster nor individual users owned the music legally and therefore had no legal right to download it or offer it for download. Other clear cases of piracy include ripping the movie from a DVD to a computer hard drive and then burning other DVD copies, or putting digital copies of books on servers outside the United States and European Union in order to let users download them. While the term “piracy” can mean many things, actions like these are what we’re normally referring to by that word.
Our discussion of piracy here will address two questions. First, if we assume that piracy is ethically wrong, what makes it so? And second, what are ethical means for trying to stop it?

Let’s first consider the question of what, if anything, is ethically wrong with piracy. If piracy is unethical, we ought to be able to identify a reason why; so what is it? One plausible answer to this question is that piracy is wrong because of the harm it does to the true owners of the property. While the “harm” here can be of various types, in most cases it will be financial. Thus the reason Napster-style music download piracy is wrong is that the practice harms the artists and their record labels—they don’t receive pay for the downloaded music, and thus they suffer a financial harm. The ethical wrongness of piracy could stem from that harm.

One possible objection to this explanation of piracy is that the financial “harm” referred to is tiny—only a few dollars at most in the case of a music album. Taylor Swift’s net worth hovers between $500–$600 million, and so a loss of a few dollars isn’t very much. This objection isn’t very convincing, however, because the financial harm need not be large in order for it to exist and ground the wrongness of piracy. If the harm is real, the action may be unethical according to the harm explanation.

A more significant weakness for the harm explanation of piracy’s wrongness is that, in many cases, the harm may not in fact exist. When someone downloads a pirated copy of Taylor Swift’s new album, it isn’t as though four dollars are deducted from her bank account. Instead, it must be true that the pirate downloaded the album instead of buying it, and that, if they hadn’t pirated the songs, they would have bought them legally. Most cases of piracy only amount to financial harm if this assumption is true, but it’s often false—many people who download music illegally only do so because it’s free and available, and wouldn’t ever consider buying the album otherwise. In other words, the pirate’s choice is often not between pirating the product or buying it legally, but is instead between pirating the product or not obtaining it at all, either legally or illegally. However, even in cases like these where financial harm is ruled out, piracy still seems to be wrong. Since the harm explanation of piracy’s wrongness relies on an assumption that is false in many cases, there must be some other explanation.

Here is another suggestion: piracy is wrong because it’s a form of theft. Stealing something is a dishonest thing to do and constitutes breaking an agreement, implied or otherwise, about property rights. Breaking this agreement can be ethically wrong independent of whether there’s any financial harm—in fact, the question of financial harm doesn’t really arise in thinking about why theft is wrong. Theft can cause financial harm, but that harm isn’t the reason that theft is wrong.

It may be, then, that the explanation for piracy’s wrongness is that it’s an instance of stealing. The owners of a piece of property, such as a book or a song, have rights to that property; they can sell it or give it away, but the choice to do either of those things, or something else, is their choice as the property owners. Piracy is a violation of property rights and is therefore wrong for the same reason that other cases of theft are wrong—you’re taking something that isn’t yours.

This explanation is superior to the previous one, because the truth is that small-scale piracy of property owned by large companies does little to no real financial harm. We therefore don’t want to explain the wrongness by reference to financial harm or some other kind of harm, because the act would still be wrong if the harm didn’t exist.

Does the theft-based explanation for the wrongness of piracy get it right, though? Is that really the reason piracy is wrong? Can you think of any counterexamples, or cases where this understanding doesn’t apply?

sidebar.title: Case Study: Pirated Video Games
sidebar.para: Wilson, who lives in Nebraska, is taking a vacation to visit some countries in South America. One day he notices that someone in a street market is selling video games. Wilson looks more closely and realizes that the games are illegal pirated copies of big-name games made by game designers in American and Europe, sold for the equivalent of one or two US dollars. Wilson asks the man selling the games how he justifies such an illegal practice. The man tells him that no one in his country can afford video games, much less the consoles to play them on; it would take most families months to save up enough disposable income to buy a used console, and then months more for controllers and games. The man selling the pirated copies says that he’s making the games available for cheap as a service to the poor in his country.

listitem.para: Does selling video games in a street market, like this man is doing, constitute piracy? Why or why not?
Has the man performed an unethical action in making copies of the video games? Has he performed an unethical action in selling them to others?
Would it be unethical for Wilson to buy a game or two while he’s visiting? Why or why not?

As discussed in this case study, there are people so poor that they would never be able to see a movie without watching a bootleg copy or play a video game unless using a pirated version. Do ethical principles about piracy apply to those people as well? Why or why not?

section.para: Given the connection to theft, we can assume at least for now that piracy is ethically wrong—we’ve identified an ethical principle, involving property rights, which many acts of piracy violate. The second question we’ll address here is, what are ethical means for companies to stop piracy? (Remember, in discussing this question, we don’t need to connect the wrongness of piracy to any financial harms. Piracy can be wrong for other reasons, and if it is wrong, then companies are justified in attempting to stop it.)

The question of ethical means to stop piracy might seem like a strange one—why would we need to ask it? Consider a parallel case, in which a city decides that it’s had enough of people driving faster than the speed limit, and is going to take action. Rather than educating citizens about the dangers of high speeds or installing more speed bumps or traffic lights, though, this city is going big: they’re going to fly unmanned drones over the major thoroughfares, and the drones will automatically track the speeds of hundreds of cars below them. When a car exceeds the speed limit by a certain amount, the drone will descend and airlift the car directly to traffic court, where the offender will receive a harsh sentence.

Of course this proposal would be silly and impractical, but things that are silly and impractical aren’t necessarily objectionable. The real problem with this traffic proposal is that it’s unethical—it kidnaps people without warning and transports them somewhere they don’t want to be. In this case, the means this city will use to stop traffic violations aren’t ethical, even if the city chose them as a way to combat something that is itself unethical.

In the same way, some ways of trying to stop piracy may themselves be unethical. For example, in late 2003 and early 2004, the RIAA, or Recording Industry Association of America, began suing people who the RIAA claimed were sharing songs on sites such as Napster and Kazaa. One person who became a defendant in an RIAA lawsuit was twelve-year-old Brianna LaHara of Los Angeles. According to the suit, Brianna had shared more than one thousand songs on Kazaa. In order to avoid a court case, she settled with the RIAA by agreeing to pay $2,000, or about two dollars per song she had shared. In response to the settlement, Mitch Bainwol, RIAA chairman, said that “We’re trying to send a strong message that you are not anonymous when you participate in peer-to-peer file-sharing and that the illegal distribution of copyrighted music has consequences.”CNN, “12-Year-Old Settles Music Swap Lawsuit,” February 18, 2004, . For preteens, apparently, one of these consequences is being taken to court by a powerful organization that spends millions of dollars per year in lobbying efforts alone.“Client Profile: Recording Industry Assn of America,” Open Secrets, accessed September 13, 2023, .

Illegal music downloads and other forms of piracy are unethical, but what about the RIAA’s approach to the issue in 2003 and 2004? Was that an ethical response? Brianna LaHara was one of millions of people sharing and downloading music illegally during that time; the RIAA’s lawsuits focused on “major offenders” who shared many hundreds or thousands of songs. But with so many other people doing it, LaHara likely wasn’t chosen by anything other than random chance; in addition, given the ubiquity of the practice and the emergence of the internet, it isn’t clear whether some offenders even understood that what they were doing was wrong, much less than a company might take such action against them.

In other words, think about it this way—which is more unethical: a random teenager illegally downloading an MP3 file of her favorite song, or a large, wealthy company suing her when she has no ability or means to defend herself? The former action is illegal, the latter is legal. But what about their ethics?

The point of this discussion is not to suggest that piracy may not have serious consequences, or that it isn’t wrong. The point is to observe that the response to something unethical can also be unethical. A lawsuit against someone like Brianna LaHara may be unethical for various reasons: it’s bullying by a powerful group against someone powerless; a lawsuit is totally out of proportion to the action LaHara actually performed. In addition, the RIAA’s tactics of bringing lawsuits against defenseless individuals may be unethical from a broader perspective as well.
What do you think? Were the RIAA’s actions ethically justified? Why or why not?

So what would be an ethical response to unethical piracy, then? There ought to be one, since companies whose property is pirated have suffered a wrong done against them and ought to be able to respond. Perhaps the most ethical response is to target raids and legal action not against regular users but against those who own servers or run sites that allow digital or other forms of piracy. Those people provide the means for digital piracy to occur; without their technology or websites, pirated materials would not be available on the internet in such large quantities. Beyond that, targeting the facilitators of piracy is much more likely to yield good results in the long run.

There are many more recent examples of this approach to piracy. One is the prosecution of the founders of Pirate Bay,Mikael Riknäs and IDG News Service, “Pirate Bay Appeals Looks Set to Start in September,” PCWorld, March 11, 2012, . and another is the legal action brought against Kim Dotcom and Megaupload.Cyrus Farivar, “Why Kim Dotcom Hasn’t Been Extradited 3 Years after The US Smashed Megaupload,” Ars Technica, January 18, 2015, . Even more recently, the FBI seized websites and assets of Napolsky and Valeriia Ermakova, two people who ran an online library of books and other academic resources. They were charged in a Brooklyn court.Emanuel Maiberg, “Feds Arrest Two Russians Behind ‘World’s Largest Library’ of Pirated Books,” Motherboard, Vice, .

In this section we’ve focused on common forms of piracy surrounding mainly digital media. We’ve argued that piracy is wrong because it’s a form of theft and therefore violates the property rights of the owners. But the response by those owners is also subject to our ethical analysis.

But what do you think? What is the proper response to the kind of piracy we’ve been discussing here? What about other forms of piracy? Can our method of reflect and test give us any principles we could apply to many cases?

sidebar.title: Case Study: Downloading Textbooks Online
sidebar.para: Heidi is a biology major at Big Important State University. She worked hard in high school and is on a scholarship that pays her tuition, room, and board. She’s expected to pay for her textbooks, but part of her scholarship agreement is that she cannot work, so that she can focus on her studies.

For this upcoming semester, Heidi is taking several upper-division courses in her major, and her books will cost more than $1000. For two of them she’s able to buy new copies, but for two others she had to buy used versions of older editions that aren’t exactly the same as the newer versions.
Many of Heidi’s classmates use a website based in Eastern Europe to download their textbooks for free. They have the latest editions as well as all the digital materials.

listitem.para: Many of Heidi’s classmates are in a position similar to Heidi, where they aren’t able to afford certain textbooks. Have they done something unethical in downloading free copies of textbooks?
Given the unequal access to new textbooks, do Heidi’s upper-division biology classes represent ethical competitions for students? Why or why not?
Is it ethical for publishers to charge such prices for their books?
What other ethical issues might be involved in this situation?

sidebar.title: Case Study: Open Access to Journal Articles
sidebar.para: Sci-Hub is a website that hosts non-paywalled articles from scientific and other academic journals. The founder is Alexandra Elbakyan, who was studying in college in her home country of Russia when she became convinced that human knowledge ought to be “open,” and therefore available for free, to anyone who wishes to read it.

Most academic articles are behind paywalls, or account logins that require either a fee or membership in a certain institution in order to access. Without university- or organization-subsidized access, many researchers would not be able to afford the large number of accounts they would need in order to access the research necessary for their work.

Sci-Hub works by using actual academic credentials to legally download papers, then offers those papers to download to anyone for free. In most cases, researchers can access papers through Sci-Hub more quickly and more easily than they can through legal means.

There are two primary arguments in favor of Sci-Hub as an ethical means to access research. The first is an argument about “open knowledge,” or the idea that scientific knowledge is a public good in the same way that air or water are. Everyone should therefore have unfettered access to scientific knowledge; it makes as much sense to put that knowledge behind a paywall as it does to horde air and sell it. The second argument is that most scientific research is publicly funded anyway, and cannot therefore be legitimately put behind a paywall managed by private companies.

listitem.para: Does the argument from knowledge as a public good succeed? Could it give us a reason to think that Sci-Hub’s activities are ethical?
Does the argument from publicly funded research succeed? Could it give us a reason to think that Sci-Hub’s activities are ethical?
Is downloading individual scientific articles from Sci-Hub unethical? Why or why not?

section.title: Informed Consent in Buying
section.para: Many people are familiar with the Latin phrase caveat emptor, which means “let the buyer beware.” The phrase sums up a certain attitude about exchanges between buyers and sellers: the buyer is the one who ultimately makes the choice about whether they’ll purchase something, and so the responsibility for vetting what they’re buying falls to them. If the decision to buy something goes badly, then it’s the buyer’s fault, since they’re the ones that should have “bewared.”Bewore? Been aware?

Let’s begin our section on informed consent in buying by asking some questions about caveat emptor. How far does the motto extend, for example? In other words, does it apply to all aspects of an exchange—is the buyer responsible for doing all the research, and does the buyer hold all the responsibility? We could also ask about the status of the motto itself—is “let the buyer beware” an ethical principle, or just shorthand for a certain attitude people have?

These questions and others concern the concept of informed consent in exchanges. We find concepts of “informed consent” in various fields, including in medical research involving human participants. The Declaration of Helsinki, a document developed by the World Medical Association, “WMA Declaration of Helsinki – Ethical Principles for Medical Research Involving Human Subjects,” World Health Organization, accessed September 13, 2023, . outlines some of the points involved in informed consent:
section.blockquote: In medical research involving human subjects capable of giving informed consent, each potential subject must be adequately informed of the aims, methods, sources of funding, any possible conflicts of interest, institutional affiliations of the researcher, the anticipated benefits and potential risks of the study and the discomfort it may entail, post-study provisions and any other relevant aspects of the study. The potential subject must be informed of the right to refuse to participate in the study or to withdraw consent to participate at any time without reprisal. Special attention should be given to the specific information needs of individual potential subjects as well as to the methods used to deliver the information.
section.para: According to this declaration, people who participate in medical research, such as drug trials or new surgeries, must be “adequately informed” of many different things, including the anticipated benefits and potential risks as well as their own right to refuse to participate or to withdraw their participation at any time. Once the participant has learned about all these things, the declaration suggests that “the physician or another appropriately qualified individual must then seek the potential subject’s freely-given informed consent, preferably in writing.”

It’s clear why a concept of informed consent would be so important in medical research—participants in drug trials, for instance, are ingesting chemicals that, prior to the study, have only been tested on animals. The actual effects those chemicals will have on human bodies are hypothesized, but not known. An important part of carrying out such a research study in an ethical way would be to make sure that all the participants know, as much as possible, what they are getting themselves into.

Is there a parallel concept of informed consent in exchanges between buyers and sellers? Caveat emptor might be such an idea, but the phrase seems to suggest that the one responsible for informing the buyer is the buyer themselves, and that the seller bears no responsibility at all.

A buying-based concept of informed consent like that one would be unbalanced. While it may be true that the buyer bears the greater responsibility for informing themselves of what they are thinking about buying, it can’t be true that they have all the responsibility. Sellers, for example, are subject to both laws and ethical principles that govern how they can market their products; misleading pricing and other deceptive practices are both illegal and unethical. In one sense, these laws and principles place some of the responsibility for informed consent onto sellers, because buyers can enter into exchanges with the knowledge that they probably aren’t being deceived about basic aspects of the exchange, like the price. Sellers might try to upsell them or bait-and-switch, but the buyer can refuse or demand what was originally agreed on.

A more reasonable concept of informed consent in buying, then, would better distribute the responsibility to inform the buyer by spreading it between the buyer, the seller, and legal or regulatory bodies. Here we see a limit to caveat emptor—whatever the phrase means in practice, it can’t mean that buyers are fully responsible for all of the knowledge and risk in an exchange.

Another apparent limit to caveat emptor comes in the form of rules about product safety and product liability. It is a seller’s responsibility to ensure that what they sell is safe for consumers—this is true not only for ingestible products like medicine, but for anything else as well. Companies that sell unsafe products, either knowingly or unknowingly, can be held liable for damage their products cause. A common example is car manufacturers, who issue product recalls for different parts of the vehicles they produce. In the first half of 2020, manufacturers issued over thirteen million recalls for entire cars or parts of them, most due to safety issues.Justinas Baltrusaitis, “Over 13 Million Vehicles Recalled Year-to-Date Globally,” Finance, Finbold, July 14, 2020, . Safety recalls range in seriousness from “this is something you should probably get checked out” to “do not drive” recalls, such as the one issued for early-2000’s vehicles using Takata airbag inflators.“Critical Do Not Drive Warning for Certain Vehicles with Takata Air Bags,” National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, U.S. Department of Transportation, accessed September 14, 2023, In most cases, manufacturers perform the repairs in safety recalls for free.

Now, imagine an unrestricted version of caveat emptor applied to buying a car. In fact, we don’t even really need to imagine it, for we’ve already seen a real-life example of such an application in our earlier case study on the Ford Pinto in . Prospective buyers of the Pinto might have been able to learn about the problems with the Pinto’s gasoline tank, had they undertaken a sophisticated program of industrial espionage. They therefore might have been able to inform themselves of the problems; or they might have put together information from disparate reports to notice a pattern of accidents involving Pintos.

They might have been able to do these things, but they might also have been able to do a lot of things, and shifting the burden of informed, consenting responsibility onto buyers for all aspects of an exchange is unreasonable. Companies have not only a legal responsibility but an ethical one to design and build products that, to the best of the company’s knowledge—not to the best of the customer’s knowledge—will function correctly and be safe.

Let’s think about the ethics of activities such as intentionally refusing to fix a defect, planning to pay out lawsuits instead. It is not that these activities are unethical because they are illegal; this gets thing backwards. These activities are illegal because they are unethical; the unethical-ness is prior to the illegality. Companies may choose to follow ethical principles in the hope of avoiding financial or legal retribution, but the motivation of a company in following a principle does not determine what kind of principle it is. An ethical principle is still an ethical principle, even if everyone follows it just to avoid practical consequences.

Informed consent in buying, then, as we mentioned above, must involve a fair distribution of responsibility between buyer, seller, and regulator. This distribution must use a realistic account of a buyer’s ability to find and understand information regarding a product. It cannot be the buyer’s job to know everything about a product, or about every possible harm; that is impossible. It is the ethical responsibility of producers, distributors, and sellers to inform buyers about what they buy. The informed consent we’re discussing here can be achieved in various ways—most of the time sellers can fulfill their responsibility by putting accurate information about a product on the back of a product’s packaging. But in other situations, such as with first-time homebuyers, informed consent probably requires much greater effort on the part of the seller and other entities, such as the lending bank.

From here we can see, then, that the proper distribution for informed consent in buying depends on the specific context of an exchange. This lesson won’t be new—many of the ethical principles and conclusions we’ve reached in this book are dependent on context. This is one reason why studying business ethics is valuable. Our study makes us sensitive to the features of a situation that help determine what is ethical and what isn’t. On the basis of those features, we can generate and apply ethical principles.

Now, to return to the example of buying a car—what would reasonable informed consent be for an exchange like that one? Because the auto industry is heavily regulated, buyers can know in advance that the vehicle they are buying is probably safe; in addition, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration assigns safety ratings to each make and model of car for crash tests. Since those tests and ratings are public knowledge, buyers are free to use that information in making their choice.

In buying cars, it seems, we find a reasonable distribution of the responsibility of informed consent: sellers must conform to safety standards and industry regulations in producing vehicles that are, for the most part, safe and reliable; buyers can depend on that conformity when entering into an exchange, which releases them from an unreasonable or unbalanced burden of informed consent. Beyond that, buyers are free to do their own research on a mountain of publicly-available information regarding which vehicles are the best or are the best values for a certain price point. Informed consent here is a responsibility shared among sellers, regulators, and buyers.

We should expect to find a similar shared balance with other products in other industries, although the balance shifts depending on the product. Homes and cars are major purchases that most buyers make only a handful of times in their life; for those reasons and for the money involved, the responsibility for informed consent is more balanced. But for regular consumer goods, like most things sold at a grocery or department store, the money and commitment involved are much less, and so it is reasonable for the burden of informed consent to shift more onto the buyer.

While the production and sale of many products is regulated by many industries and agencies, the actual interaction of exchange is not—in general, buyers and sellers are able to enter into or withdraw from an exchange at their will. This means that the whole system of unregulated exchange often relies on the good faith of its participants. This is one way we can know that there is an ethical component to the exchange of buying and selling. For the most part, laws can only punish bad actors by looking backward in time; they cannot prospectively punish a company for something it hasn’t done yet, even if the company intends to do it. Companies may conform to regulations or industry safety standards from fear of legal or financial punishment, but there is more to their action than what is legal or financially viable. There is also a component of ethics.

In the end, caveat emptor does not appear to be an ethical principle. It’s best understood as a piece of practical advice which may apply in some ways to some situations. The actual ethics of exchange, including informed consent in buying, are much more complicated.

sidebar.title: Case Study: Used Car Sales
sidebar.para: Sharica sells used cars. Her business contracts with a third-party loan provider to offer various financing options to buyers. When buyers are ready to complete a purchase, Sharica arranges a phone call or video chat with a representative from the loan provider, who then works with the buyer to agree on financing terms. Once the buyer has secured a loan, Sharica receives the details from the loan provider and completes the purchase.

Customers often ask Sharica about the details of the financing options. Though she suspects that the loan terms which her customers are receiving are not very favorable, she rationalizes her sales and use of the third-party financer by thinking about how people are able to buy cars from her when they might not be able to buy them from elsewhere. Many of her customers have poor credit or no credit and would not qualify for regular auto loans from dealerships, banks, and credit unions.

In fact, over the course of Sharica’s time at the dealership, she has learned that it is better for her not to know the details of the financing options—because if she doesn’t know the details, she can tell her customers honestly that she doesn’t know the options and cannot help them. Since she doesn’t know the answer to their questions, she can tell them that they’ll have to ask the representative from the loan provider.

Sharica wonders whether she has a responsibility to know more about the financing options. When she is closing sales, she sometimes gets the impression that the buyer doesn’t understand what they will be required to do in order to pay back the loan.

listitem.para: Sharica’s dealership contracts with a third-party loan provider to offer financing options for car buyers. What responsibilities does the dealership have to its customers when using a third-party service in this way?

What responsibility does Sharica herself have to understand the different financing options offered by the loan provider? Since she isn’t the one administering the loan, does she have an ethical duty to understand any of it? Why or why not?

For car buyers with little financial literacy, what duties does a loan provider have to educate them on the details and implications of a car loan? What would “informed consent” in such an exchange look like?

What responsibility do buyers have to educate themselves about their own loan agreements or other financing agreements? To what extent, if any, does the idea of caveat emptor apply in these situations?

Sharica sees that, while some of her customers have loan troubles, her dealership does make it possible for people to own vehicles who otherwise wouldn’t be able to afford them. To what extent, if any, should this service exempt Sharica from understanding how her loans are affecting her customers?

section.title: Exchange and the Internet
section.para: In the previous sections of this chapter, we’ve been considering buying and selling exchanges of all kinds without differentiating between how they take place. In our final section, we’ll discuss whether internet-based exchanges ought to be governed by ethical principles different from those that govern traditional exchanges.
In short: does the internet make a difference?

There are many ethical issues connected to business on the internet. For example, the growing market for internet-connected virtual reality carries with it many significant moral concerns, some of which might only have seemed like science fiction until recently. In fact, we could take any issue we’ve discussed so far in this chapter and explore it further from the perspective of the internet: should companies be allowed to use variable pricing for internet purchases based on a customer’s real-world location? What would price-fixing on the internet look like, if it exists at all? Does our concept of “informed consent” for exchanges change when we focus only on online exchanges?

Unfortunately we can’t treat all of these issues here, or even many of them. We’ll instead restrict ourselves to a single question, one having implications for many others: how should the data companies have about individual consumers affect the way they operate internet exchanges?

Let’s think about an example. You’re at home, making a meal and talking to a member of your family. You’re making stir fry and you use the last bit of soy sauce. “Need to get another bottle of soy sauce,” you say. Then, an hour later, you open your phone to check a message, and one of your social media accounts is displaying an advertisement for soy sauce.

Has something like this happened to you before? Probably. Your phone is listening to you, after all. Even if it isn’t recording conversations, it’s well aware of what you’re doing and what is going on around you. We laugh at how our phones “know,” but there’s nothing eerie about this—they’re monitoring our behavior, and using the internet to spread that information widely.

This kind of experience is becoming more commonplace, but consider how unusual it is when we separate it from computers and the internet. Imagine it’s 1980 and you’re at home making the same stir fry. You run out of soy sauce and comment about it, but this time, a woman shows up at your house an hour later and knocks on your door. She walks inside and opens a briefcase to show you bottles of soy sauce, and wouldn’t you like to buy one? There’s a sale? Oh, you’re pushing me out of your house? I’m sorry. Wouldn’t you at least like a coupon to a nearby grocery store?

It’s clear that no one would tolerate this sort of unsafe and unethical behavior outside of the internet, but it’s normal online. As most people realize, the internet is even more invasive than these examples suggest, because websites and other services make it difficult for people to refuse to be tracked.

All of this drives us toward the following fact: exchanges on the internet take place in an environment very different from the stores we’re used to entering in order to buy something. Many of the sites we use have an enormous amount of information about us, and target us with ads and special offers that are literally built for us.
In that sense, does the internet make a difference?

Despite how nosy it is, there are some good reasons to think that the internet doesn’t make a difference for buying and selling exchanges—at least, not an ethical difference. For one, the fact that our phones are listening to us may not actually be that different from other situations that don’t seem as problematic. In 2005 there were no smartphones but there were people typing searches into Google, and by then the company had been using searches and other collected information to target people with ads for almost five years. Are phones that different? If you think they are, a better example might be comparing your phone to a person—if you don’t want someone to know something, then you can simply choose not to tell them. Likewise, if you don’t want Google or Facebook or other companies to know things about you, then don’t use their services.

Thus one reason to think that the internet doesn’t make much of an ethical difference to exchanges is that a consumer can still opt out of them. It’s difficult, sure, and maybe uncomfortable, but anyone can just choose not to use the internet, and many of these “ethical” issues would just disappear.

On the other hand, as the internet and online activity slowly become an even more significant part of everyday life, it will be more difficult to explain away the ethical problems the internet creates for exchanges. If certain kinds of exchanges must take place online, then it isn’t possible to opt out of them, and the ethical problems become more pressing.

A second way to suggest that the internet doesn’t present any unique ethical problems is to see internet use as an exchange in itself. The software products of most major internet-based companies—Google, Facebook, Instagram, Amazon, Alibaba, and others are all free to use. But when we look at using them as an exchange, we see that they aren’t in fact free—our very use of them becomes the price we pay to use them. By using them, we necessarily reveal things about ourselves, and the price we pay to use them is to allow the companies to use what we’ve revealed. We get a service, and pay a price in return. What could be unethical about that?

As a counterpoint, we can observe that, in some cases, we aren’t required to let companies track us in order to use their services. It seems natural to let them do so, but phones must give us the option to deny them that privilege. In late 2021, Apple introduced a feature on iPhones that allowed users to refuse to let apps track their behavior across the entire phone. It was hailed as a major new development in tech, but it only looks so important if we start from the assumption that companies should be able to track us, perhaps as part of an exchange.

Perhaps the best way to appreciate the ethical problem of internet exchange is to reflect on the sheer amount of data that companies can bring to bear in targeted exchanges. For people who use Google’s services regularly, for example, the company frequently has many gigabytes of data about them, including detailed information, often dating back years, of every place they’ve taken their phone. It is difficult to get the correct mental picture: imagine a map of every place you’ve been in the last five years, and imagine being able to search for where you were at a particular time, getting answers that are accurate down to the city block and down to a couple of seconds. And that’s just a small portion of what they know.

Do we want companies to know those things about us? More importantly here, do we want them to be able to use that information as part of the way they try to get us to buy things? How has your exchange behavior been influenced by that massive pile of data? Is it even possible to know?

The fundamental ethical issue here is privacy, but it’s a unique kind of privacy problem. Just from our regular interactions with others, we come to know a great deal about them—if we work with someone, for example, and we know what days they’ve been at work, then we automatically know a lot about their locations on those days.

The difference that computers and the internet make is the scale and the reach. The scale is enormous—the amount of data companies use to target exchanges is beyond anything a person could ever collect about someone, and is only possible with computers. And the reach is unlimited—in the right circumstances, that data can be communicated to anyone, anywhere, without necessarily needing our consent.

Thus both the scale and the reach of the internet present a special ethical problem. Computers and the internet are capable of doing these things, but should they? The fact that these methods of data collection and sharing are legal is irrelevant—nowhere more than the internet do we sense how far behind legislation is in protecting consumers. We are asking the question from an ethical perspective: is it good for us to live in a world where the companies selling things to us know more about our habits than we know ourselves? What do you think? What are the ethical harms and benefits of these developments?
Do the scale and reach of information really change the ethical landscape for online exchanges? Why or why not?

listitem.para: Understand the idea of the "game" as applied to business and marketing.
Be able to identify cases of false advertising and unclear disclosures of information.
Develop an understanding of which approaches to marketing are likely to lead to ethical problems, and why.

section.title: The Rules of the Game and “Normal” Business Practices
section.para: Discussing the ethics of exchange leads us naturally into another topic—one of the most well-known in business ethics—marketing. MarketingThe practice of making known and promoting goods and services to potential consumers. is the practice of making known and promoting goods and services to potential consumers. In other words, marketing is what happens in order to create an exchange—it’s any attempt to get you to buy or agree to something.

The most visible form of marketing is advertising, but the field has many facets, including activities like market research and word-of-mouth campaigns. The primary goal of all such endeavors is to get people to think about a good or service in a particular way, either to purchase it now or to affect the way someone interacts with it in the future.

The reason marketing is one of the most well-known areas of business ethics is that it features one of the most common ethical problems: false advertising. We’ll cover this issue in the next section, but the basic issue will be familiar to everyone—is it ethical for a product creator or seller to lie about their product in order to get people to buy it? Most people believe that it isn’t, and that false advertising is unethical. But by its very nature advertising involves choices about how to portray something, with the goal of changing someone else’s behavior. In those situations, does ethics require that marketers speak as though they’re in court, where they say “the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth”? Or can they embellish or even make some things up?

After our discussion of false advertising and deception, we’ll have three other sections on related issues. The first is the ethics of sales negotiations. The second deals with disclosure of information, and what amount of information is ethical for product creators and sellers to share with potential buyers. The last section is a somewhat narrow topic, which has had significant consequences in the United States in the last twenty years: direct marketing of products to experts, such as doctors and other service providers.

As we proceed through these sections, you’ll notice close connections between the issues we discuss and previous chapters. For example, some of the issues surrounding sales negotiations could belong to the previous chapter on the ethics of exchange, but others belong to the ethics of marketing, such as the way sellers entice buyers to enter a store in the first place. Likewise, disclosure of information involves the concept of informed consent in exchanges as well as broader values like human autonomy.

The overlap between topics and chapters shouldn’t be surprising, however. Business ethics is a highly integrated field, and many situations have multiple ethical dimensions. One of the skills we want to learn as ethical investigators is how to discern all those ethical dimensions at once—including both how they relate to each other, and how we can separate them from each other. Certain ethical principles may apply only to certain dimensions of a situation, and we’ll best be able to use those principles when we understand exactly how the principles apply and why.

That’s a summary of what to expect for the other sections in this chapter. In the remainder of this section, though, we won’t be looking at specific issues but will instead be considering the entire landscape of marketing ethics as a whole.
And to do it, we’ll be thinking about the “rules of the game.”

In 1968, Albert Carr published a classic article called, “Is Business Bluffing Ethical?”Albert Z. Carr, “Is Business Bluffing Ethical?” Harvard Business Review, January 1968, . By “business bluffing,” Carr refers to any sort of less-than-fully-honest behavior in a business environment, from openly lying in an advertisement to an employee telling her boss that something is a good idea even though she thinks it isn’t, because she’s worried that telling the truth might harm her professional standing. While there might be degrees of dishonesty among instances of business bluffing, all cases involve some form of lying, whether innocuous or malicious.

Carr opens his article by recounting a conversation he had about business bluffing with a businessman he knew. “You mean to say you’re going to encourage men to bluff?” the man said. “Why, bluffing is nothing more than a form of lying! You’re advising them to lie!” Carr tried to convince him otherwise but the man persisted and responded, “Maybe that’s good enough for some businessmen, but I can tell you that we pride ourselves on our ethics…I regard my handshake on a deal as a contract.…If I do say so myself, our ethical standards are of the highest!”
Carr then made the following observation:
section.blockquote: But this same fine man, at that very time, was allowing one of his products to be advertised in a way that made it sound a great deal better than it actually was. Another item in his product line was notorious among dealers for its “built-in obsolescence.” He was holding back from the market a much-improved product because he did not want it to interfere with sales of the inferior item it would have replaced. He had joined with certain of his competitors in hiring a lobbyist to push a state legislature, by methods that he preferred not to know too much about, into amending a bill then being enacted.
section.para: Following this description, Carr noted that, for this man, “these things had nothing to do with ethics; they were merely normal business practice. He himself undoubtedly avoided outright false-hoods—never lied in so many words. But the entire organization that he ruled was deeply involved in numerous strategies of deception.”

Carr’s story invites us to draw a distinction between two things: what is ethical and unethical, on the one hand, and what is simply part of the “rules of the game,” or “normal business practice,” on the other. This book, and all of business ethics, is about what is ethical and unethical; but as you’ve noticed, the principles we’ve discussed sometimes push against “normal business practice,” or the set of rules by which business is typically conducted. Ethics is about principles and values; the rules of game are the guidelines you follow in a quest to win a business game.

As we’ve discussed several times in this text, many business professionals recognize no distinction between ethics and the rules of the game, nor would they accept the distinction if we pointed it out to them. Carr quotes a certain “Midwestern executive who well summarized an extremely common belief”:
section.blockquote: So long as a businessman complies with the laws of the land and avoids telling malicious lies, he’s ethical. If the law as written gives a man a wide-open chance to make a killing, he’d be a fool not to take advantage of it. If he doesn’t, somebody else will. There’s no obligation on him to stop and consider who is going to get hurt. If the law says he can do it, that’s all the justification he needs. There’s nothing unethical about that. It’s just plain business sense.
section.para: You probably know many people who believe something like that, and you may believe something like it too. In fact, it might be more accurate to say, you probably know many people who act according to that idea in their business activities, even if they claim to believe otherwise. Many people are like the businessman with whom Carr conversed about business bluffing: they believe, probably sincerely, that they adhere to the strictest codes of ethics; but they knowingly and willingly engage in commonly-accepted dishonest behaviors because those behaviors are part of “normal business practice”—they’re part of the rules of the game.

By now we’ve done enough ethical analysis to appreciate that ethical principles don’t just boil down to the rules of the game and the law. The Midwestern executive quoted above is wrong. The rules are guidelines within which one acts to make money; they are therefore the rules one follows in order to win at the game of business. That status, however, does not mean that the rules of the game aren’t subject to ethical evaluation. They are. We can identify them, reflect on them, test them, and refine them. Our evaluation can change them and change our behavior too. We can become aware of the rules guiding our conduct, and even when we choose to obey them, we can do so consciously.

After all, if the rules of the business game aren’t subject to ethical evaluation, then there cannot be any such thing as business ethics—business “ethics” would just be a list of actions legal under current law. When the law changed, ethics would change, because there would be no distinction between them. But the entire premise of this book is that there is a difference—our method, our identification and application of principles, our case studies, are all built on the assumption that business ethics can be and is something beyond the rules of the game. Far from just acceptable guidelines for conduct, business ethics is about how our deepest moral priorities and values ought to influence our behavior, even in an environment that pushes against us.

Carr, in his 1968 article at least, didn’t agree. He drew an analogy to poker, where bluffing—the intentional deception of other players about your cards and intentions—is not only legal but a fundamental part of the game. Powerful hands like a royal flush or a full house are rare in games of poker; most of the time, the winning hand is much weaker, like two pair or three of a kind. But poker players know that how they manage information and relate to the other players at the table is fundamental to their success. If they folded every bad hand and kept only the good ones, the other players would catch on immediately; such a player could never be successful.

In the same way, Carr argues, the successful businessperson is one who learns the rules of the game, including the particular view on ethics Carr claims is necessary to business success. This person cannot be someone with the moral courage to speak out against what is wrong—those who would seek in business to maintain a clear conscience “merit our respect—but as private individuals, not businessmen.” In other words, people who reject the rules of the game on ethical grounds are not true business professionals, because if they were, they would play by the rules. “From time to time every businessman, like every poker player, is offered a choice between certain loss or bluffing within the legal rules of the game. If he is not resigned to losing, if he wants to rise in his company and industry, then in such a crisis he will bluff—and bluff hard.” Carr further writes, “Whatever the form of the bluff, it is an integral part of the game, and the executive who does not master its techniques is not likely to accumulate much money or power.”

Carr is undoubtedly right that scrupulous knowledge of the rules of the game can help someone accumulate money and power. But the foundation of his argument is that those things are desirable in and of themselves, and that we cannot change the rules—and, while both of those views are correct in some ways, they’re also fundamentally incomplete.

In reality, Carr’s attitude is one of extreme naïveté and willful obliviousness. The poker analogy fails because, at many levels of business, the chips at the table represent not one’s own money but the money, health, livelihoods, and futures of others. The question Carr asks is, will bluffing help me win this hand, or this whole game? But the most important ethical question, which Carr apparently could not grasp, is whether it is ethical on any grounds to bluff with those kinds of chips in the first place. In that game—in the business game as it really is, not as we wish it to be in order to cleanse our conscience—a loss means much more than a financial hit or getting booted from the table.

At the same time, another childish naïveté haunts the opposite extreme, which is the idea that ethical principles can be generated, refined, and applied without regard for that same business reality. They can’t. The principles we’ve discussed in this book as well as others are and ought to be conditioned by the business environment in which we operate. It’s also foolish to think that every business bluff, or every instance of less-than-totally honest behavior, risks life and financial ruin. Not all do; most don’t.

Our job, therefore, is to discover and navigate the ethical middle ground that Carr was blind to. Between the rules of the business game and the perfectly ideal business ethics lies reality, the non-ideal place in which we do business. It is our responsibility to appreciate our middle position and there to apply our ethics, with an approach that’s both practical and principle-based. From general principles and values we derive specific applications that guide our behavior. We implement our applications judiciously, with neither a naïve view only to what is legal nor a naïve idealism that ignores our role in a market.

Discovering and holding the ethical middle ground is neither straightforward nor easy. But there is no reason we cannot do it. We praise the artist, the inventor, the entrepreneur, for their creativity and the way they break ground we didn’t think was possible before. Why can’t the same innovation happen in ethics?
With this thought in mind, let’s turn to specific ethical issues in marketing.

sidebar.title: Case Study: Buy-or-Bury
sidebar.para: In 2021 the Federal Trade Commission filed a complaint against Facebook, alleging that the company used a “buy-or-bury” scheme to maintain its market-leading position in social media on mobile platforms.Federal Trade Commission, “FTC Alleges Facebook Resorted to Illegal Buy-or-Bury Scheme to Crush Competition After String of Failed Attempts to Innovate,” news release, August 19, 2021, . The buy-or-bury strategy was simple: when Facebook faced a competitor with a product that they could not match or duplicate, Facebook did one of two things. It either bought the competitor and made the competitor’s product part of its own offerings; or it buried the competitor by allowing it to use Facebook’s platform—which allowed Facebook to study how the product worked and then bury the technology beneath the sea of other technologies that make up Facebook online.

Both practices are illegal, according to the FTC. Facebook’s strong-armed purchases of competitors created a monopoly that violated antitrust laws, and its burying “degraded the social network experience, subjecting users to lower levels of privacy and data protections and more intrusive ads.”

The FTC’s complaint alleges that Facebook resorted to its buy-or-bury scheme because it was unable to keep up with the rapid pace of mobile software development. Said Holly Vedova, FT Bureau of Competition Acting Director, “Facebook lacked the business acumen and technical talent to survive the transition to mobile. After failing to compete with new innovators, Facebook illegally bought or buried them when their popularity became an existential threat.”
As of mid-2023, a trial date for the FTC’s court case against Facebook was still undetermined.

listitem.para: Is the “buy” part of Facebook’s strategy just part of the rules of the business game, or is it actually unethical? Why?
Is the “bury” part of Facebook’s strategy just part of the rules of the business game, or is it actually unethical? Why?
Are antitrust and competitive-regulation laws founded on ethical principles? Or is their primary motivation financial and economic? Why?
Part of Facebook’s “bury” strategy involved manipulating the way competitors’ software functioned on its own platform. To what extent should Facebook be able to control how such software functions?
How does business ethics change when companies are large enough to influence or even create the laws that govern how they operate?

section.title: False Advertising and Deception
section.para: In the early 2020’s, various boxes of Cheerios cereal carried messages about the health benefits of the oat-based breakfast: “From Our ♡ to yours,” with a Cheerio cereal piece for the capital O; “Can help lower cholesterol as part of a heart healthy diet;” “100% whole grain oats your heart will thank you for.” General Mills, the maker for Cheerios, also started producing the cereal in heart shapes, meaning that someone who buys Cheerios gets a box covered with messages about how healthy they are, then pours literal hearts into a bowl (which could itself be heart-shaped, as the images on many of the Cheerios boxes will remind us).

Cheerios aren’t an unhealthy food; they have very little fat, no cholesterol, and very little sugar. But are they in fact beneficial for your heart? Do you know? Do you know whether it’s been studied? If you bought a box of Cheerios, would you read the fine print after the asterisk in order to figure out how General Mills qualifies all the statements it makes about health?

section.title: What Is False Advertising?
section.para: Depending on how we understand them, the claims made by Cheerios boxes may be examples of false advertisingAny attempt to induce a customer to buy a product by means that aren’t completely honest. . In general, false advertising is any attempt to induce a customer to buy a product by means that aren’t completely honest .As soon as we try to define the term, though, we run into the problems we mentioned in the previous section. Are companies really required to be completely honest? Why or why not? If they aren’t, what can they lie or mislead about, and how much can they lie or mislead? What makes an advertisement “false,” anyway—does it have to be proven false? Is the advertising all right if its claim hasn’t yet been shown to be false?

The ways we answer these questions reveal our judgments about false advertising, but they also reveal even more about what we think of the “rules of the game” discussed in the previous section. If false advertising, deceiving customers, and other practices are just part of the rules of the game, then treating this issue in a business ethics book is going to seem like a pointless thing to do. It would be better treated in a book about how to succeed in business or entrepreneurship, since it would just be one more tool for figuring out how to profit.

From this perspective, then, let’s do a little ethical investigation into the topic of false advertising. We’ll look at some examples and do some reflecting in order to see whether we can derive any general ethical principles about truth-telling in advertising.

We can begin by observing generally that, if false advertising is going to be interesting as a topic in ethics at all, then it must be able to include more than just outright lies. Everyone would agree that marketing a sugar pill as a cure for cancer is unethical because it’s dishonest—it’s an open lie. But cases of open lies are easy to make judgments about it because they’re obviously false and because we can see the harm they would do.

Consider a contrasting example: plyometric strength shoes. Strength shoes are special pieces of footwear designed to help with jump training and to increase the wearer’s vertical leap. They usually have a large circular platform attached to the front of the shoe at the bottom, forcing wearers to walk on the balls of their feet. The idea is that walking and exercising that way develops the muscles involved in jumping, which over time would (supposedly) lead to a higher vertical leap.

With that in mind, imagine that your company is ready to release a new line of plyometric strength shoes, the X-Plodes. You are deciding on marketing materials for an X-Plodes internet campaign. You’re looking at a few different possible claims:

listitem.para: X-Plodes will make you dunk like Michael Jordan!
X-Plodes will increase your vertical leap by 25%!
X-Plodes will increase your vertical leap!
X-Plodes can increase your vertical leap!
X-Plodes can help increase your vertical leap!

section.para: We’ve arranged these statements in descending order: the first are the boldest, the last the weakest. Now, read the items again, and for each one, ask yourself, would marketing the X-Plodes with this tagline be false advertising?
Statement 1 would have to be; no matter what most people do, they aren’t going to be dunking like Michael Jordan. Selling our shoes this way is just a lie.

Statement 2 might not necessarily be a lie, but it commits a clear marketing error: it attaches a measurable value to something. Someone who bought the X-Plodes and trained with them but saw their vertical leap increase by only 17% would therefore have grounds to think that our advertising campaign was false.

Statement 3 says the same thing as statement 2, but avoids naming a measurable value. Yet here we see another marketing error: the language reads like a guarantee—the shoes will increase your vertical leap. A guarantee isn’t what we want to give because someone training with them might not see any improvement, and then our tagline would be false.

Statement 4 is looking like it might be better, at least in terms of false advertising—the X-Plodes can increase your vertical leap, sure. Many things can happen; can statements are cheap. The X-Plodes can also get you cast in a movie—if you happen to be wearing them when a casting director walks by and she’s looking for a person wearing goofy shoes, for example.

Statement 5 is the weakest of all, for it won’t even commit to saying that the X-Plodes might increase your vertical leap by themselves—it uses the word “help” to allow space for how other things might affect your training.

As you consider statements 1–5 above, where would you draw the line? Most people will think that statement 1 constitutes false advertising, while statement 5 can’t be false, because it’s so wide open. Which claims are or might be examples of false advertising, in your opinion, and which ones not? Why do you draw the line there, and not at some other place?

So far, though, we’ve been considering only actual claims or sentences communicated to an audience about a product. Marketing and advertising are so much more than the claims made; in fact, some of the most effective advertisements don’t need to make any claims at all, because their goal is to share a part of a lifestyle or present an image or feeling to a prospective buyer.

Many beer commercials are an example of this kind of advertising. It’s common for beer commercials to consist of nothing but panning shots of attractive people doing awesome things while a certain brand of beer keeps vigilant watch nearby. The point of such advertisements isn’t to make claims about the beer’s taste or value; it’s to get the consumer thinking that if they were drinking that beer, then they could have those incredible moments too. Here the actual product takes a back seat in the advertisement, and there aren’t any claims made. You’ll be able to think of many examples of this advertising style—it’s also common for cars, perfumes and colognes, clothing, and other products.

section.title: False Advertising versus Misleading Marketing
section.para: This discussion brings us to another general claim. The first was that false advertising, if it exists and is a topic worth discussing, must be about more than just open lying; the second is that the possibility of false advertising simply doesn’t apply to many ads. So many ads simply don’t make claims that could be evaluated as true or false either way; they just put a product in an environment with people around, and let the consumer’s mind fill in the blanks. Since the ads don’t actually say anything about the product, they can’t come out false.

There are other common ways of misleading consumers in marketing materials. A retail outlet may offer last year’s products without telling customers that the current year’s lineup is already available; a store may mark up a product and then mark it down again as part of a “sale” in order to say that a product is now 50% off, instead of 25%; many dietary supplement and nutrition companies have only the very flimsiest “scientific” evidence to back up their claims, often in the form of “studies” that were funded and run by company representatives or researchers compensated by the company.

So what, then, is false advertising? If it’s unethical, we have to be able to explain what “it” is and a little about why it’s unethical; otherwise we have no objective basis for calling an advertisement false. Can we define it unambiguously?

The Federal Trade Commission or FTC is the government agency responsible for protecting consumers in the United States. The FTC’s website says the following about truth in advertising: “When consumers see or hear an advertisement, whether it’s on the Internet, radio or television, or anywhere else, federal law says that ad must be truthful, not misleading, and, when appropriate, backed by scientific evidence.”“Truth in Advertising,” Federal Trade Commission, accessed September 19, 2023, . This sounds great, but you might have noticed that it doesn’t actually give us an answer to our questions, because we’re now required to define what it is for a statement to be “truthful,” “not misleading,” or “backed” by scientific evidence. In the context of marketing and advertising, those are not going to be straightforward definitions.
The FTC’s website also contains recent examples of false-advertising claims it has prosecuted. The following list shows a few:

listitem.para: An aloe vera–based supplement company that claimed its products could treat chronic pain, diabetes, and acid reflux. “NatureCity, LLC,” Federal Trade Commission, updated May 26, 2020, .
An online marketing company that sold fake social media influence and fake reviews on retail websites.“Devumi, LLC,” Federal Trade Commission, updated February 26, 2021, .
A bath and beauty company that falsely claimed its products were “100% organic” and “certified organic” by the USDA.“Truly Organic Inc.,” Federal Trade Commission, updated September 19, 2019,

An online lending company that claimed to offer “objective” and “unbiased” information about financial products, when in reality the company rated paid partners more highly than others.“LendEDU, et. al., In the Matter of,” Federal Trade Commission, updated May 28, 2020, .

The maker of a dietary supplement called “Nobetes” that the company claimed could treat diabetes. These claims were not scientifically substantiated.“Nobetes Corp,” Federal Trade Commission, updated August 21, 2019, ; Federal Trade Commission, “FTC Refunds Consumers Who Bought Deceptively Marketed and Advertised “Nobetes” Diabetes Treatment Supplement,” press release, August 21, 2019, .

section.para: These are just a few cases; there are countless others. The FTC prosecutes dozens of cases every year.

Now, it is good that the FTC exists and that it can put a stop to false advertising. But if we’re interested in false advertising as an ethical problem, rather than a legal one, the FTC probably doesn’t have much to offer us. All the example cases cited here, and all the others on its website, are clear examples of ads using open lies to deceive consumers. But no one would dispute that such tactics are instances of false advertising, and everyone would agree that they’re unethical. The FTC exists to take obvious cases to court but making fine ethical decisions is beyond its purview.

And that, in itself, is the fundamental ethical challenge of false advertising. As long as marketers are careful with their language, it is virtually impossible to prove that their advertising copy is false. It is just too easy for companies to defend themselves against allegations of these kinds, because there are so many ways to explain what their advertisements mean.

In light of these facts, is it possible to find an ethical principle that can govern behavior in the truth of advertising? I suggest that it is—but to get there, we have to turn away from the strict truth or falsity of the advertising claims in order to look at the intentions behind them. I suggest the principle instructs us in our creation of advertisements and claims about products, rather than helping us identify which ones are false.
