We can state this ethical principle in terms of a question: if you had insider knowledge about what a product could actually do and how it was produced, but you had no connection to the company producing it and no financial stake in the product’s success, would you believe that advertisements about it were lies? If you would, then there’s a good chance that the claims you are making about the product constitute false advertising—not in the legal, prosecutable-by-the-FTC sense, but in the ethical sense.

This question asks us to imagine that we know a great deal about the product but we ourselves are not affected by what happens to it. From that vantage point—which is about as independent as we can be, in many cases—we can judge whether an advertisement is false or not. We add in the bit about “insider knowledge,” because whether someone deems something a lie depends on how much knowledge that person has—someone with more knowledge about a topic is better able to detect lies about it. The vantage point for our judgments, then, involves knowledge that normal people wouldn’t have, which makes us able to discern what is true about something from what is false.

This question and the ethical principle behind it are not perfect. There will still be borderline cases; the available ethical problems always outstrip the principles we’ve come up with so far. But this principle is a guide for ethical behavior that we can apply to real-world situations, and that’s about as good as we can do here. As with so many things in this chapter, the principle will sometimes go against the rules of the game. But ethics, in this case and others, is about human life and human values, which the “rules of the game” do a very poor job of capturing.

sidebar.title: Case Study: Truth in Advertising
sidebar.para: You work for Yummy Morning Inc., a breakfast cereal start-up that views itself as a “health-conscious” choice for parents. You’re part of Yummy Morning’s marketing team, and you’re trying to figure out how to present a new product.

The cereal you’re working with is called Yummy O’s. The food scientists at Yummy Morning have explained to you that Yummy O’s contains a great deal more sugar than other offerings in the product line, but still has less sugar than other major brands; “For example,” they say, “Yummy O’s has less sugar than Honey Smacks, Cocoa Puffs, and Golden Crisp.” Being a cereal aficionado yourself, though, you happen to know that those three cereals are all in the top five most sugary cereals generally.
You call your marketing team together for an initial strategy meeting about how you will try to sell Yummy O’s to consumers.

listitem.para: The food scientists at Yummy Morning never actually told you exactly how much sugar Yummy O’s contains. As the person leading the product’s marketing campaign, do you have an ethical responsibility to find out? Why or why not?
If you don’t find out, are you more justified in making possibly false claims about the cereal, given that you don’t really know its sugar content?

Your team decides that the phrase “Part of a balanced breakfast” should appear on Yummy O’s boxes and in Yummy O’s advertisements. Is it actually true, though, that a bowl of Yummy O’s is “part of a balanced breakfast”? How could you tell?

Yummy O’s are made with whole grain, and diets high in whole grains have been linked to lower incidences of chronic conditions like diabetes and heart disease. Is this enough evidence for you to market Yummy O’s as a “heart-healthy” cereal? Why or why not?

Reflect on this case with the ethical principle proposed in the section on false advertising: “If you had insider knowledge about what a product could actually do and how it was produced, but you had no connection to the company producing it and no financial stake in the product’s success, would you believe advertisements about it were lies?” Would claims about the health benefits of Yummy O’s pass this test? Why or why not?

section.title: Disclosure of Information
section.para: The ethics of deceptive advertising relate closely to the issue of the disclosure of information. The driving question here is, what information, in general, needs to be disclosed in marketing? In other words, what information must be shared in the process of marketing the product and in the media materials used to do so, and why must that information be shared?

You will note that this topic is also related to the one from the previous chapter on informed consent in buying. Although there is some overlap between the two, we’ll focus here on marketing in particular, without focusing on the point of sale or issues of informed consent during an actual exchange.

Perhaps you’ve had something like the following experience: you see a commercial on TV for a medication, and the voiceover instructs you to find an advertisement for the medication in a magazine. You get a copy of the magazine, find the ad, and see that the front page uses bright pictures and flashy text to tout the medication’s benefits. Then you flip the page over and you’re greeted by an entire page of tiny text giving you minute details in scientific language about everything that could go wrong with the product.

The two parts of an ad like this one couldn’t be more different: on the front, everything is just great, and you should definitely buy the product; on the back, everything isn’t great after all, but you need a PhD in biochemistry to figure out why.

An ad like that one is an example of advertising that’s attempting to comply with laws about the disclosure of informationThe practice of including in marketing materials further information about a product, either by law or voluntarily, that would be useful for the consumer to know as they consider it. . “Disclosure of information” refers to the practice of including in marketing materials further information about a product, either by law or voluntarily, that would be useful for the consumer to know as they consider it. Disclosure of information isn’t about what the company wants you to know—what they want you to know is in the advertisement itself. Disclosure of information is about what the company is legally or ethically obligated to tell you about the product.

For example, it’s common to find ads on TV and the internet for antidepressant and other mood-altering drugs. Because of the imprecise way in which such drugs can sometimes work, they may produce harmful side-effects—drugs for treating severe depression can sometimes worsen depression or cause suicidal thoughts. These and other side effects are so serious that companies must be open about them in their marketing materials. They are required to disclose the information about side effects so that consumers have better information to use in making a decision.

Let’s think about this issue from an ethical perspective: what kind of information should be disclosed, and why? Potentially harmful health effects are obvious ones for disclosure requirements. So are potentially harmful financial effects, such as for loan products. In general, a good principle to start reasoning from would be that companies ought to disclose any information regarding predictable harms that might result to a consumer in the course of the normal use of a product.

A principle like this one seems to govern marketing laws about disclosure of information, but the principle faces two significant problems. First, the principle is very unevenly applied to marketing practices from industry to industry. For example, there are detailed laws about what and how to disclose information for medications and other products with a direct relation to health. It’s easy to see the ethical basis for these laws, and other products, like cigarettes, are subject to some of the same requirements—seemingly in the hope that the shock value of the disclosed information will be enough to dissuade some consumers from purchasing them.

But other fields, even ones with implications for health, do not face these same requirements, despite our ethical principle suggesting that they ought to. The best example is food. High-calorie, high-fat, and high-sugar foods are major contributors to obesity, and obesity itself is a potentially serious health condition that by some metrics is worse for overall health outcomes than smoking.Roland Sturm and Kenneth B. Wells, The Health Risks of Obesity: Worse Than Smoking, Drinking or Poverty, (Santa Monica, CA: RAND Corporation, 2002,) . Given these potentially harmful effects, shouldn’t unhealthy foods require a disclosure of information? It seems silly to consider, but a fast-food restaurant could set up information disclosures near the lines to order, so that consumers could review them as they decided what to eat. Again, this sounds silly, and it wouldn’t happen, because no companies would agree to do it. But the question isn’t whether they would do it, it’s whether they ought to do it—what is the ethical thing to do, when it comes to information disclosures?

In your opinion, what information about a product should be disclosed in marketing materials, and why? What ethical duty do companies have to share with consumers the potential harms of their products? Is there other information they ought to disclose?

So the first problem for our proposed principle about information disclosure is that it isn’t applied uniformly across industries. Note that this is a problem not with the ethical basis of the principle, but with its implementation. We could overcome this problem by making disclosures more regularly—but would the resulting marketing materials and interactions with products be desirable? Would the good done by greater or more comprehensive information disclosures be worth it? What do you think?

The second problem with our principle is that it tells us nothing about which ways of disclosing information are ethical. For example, is it ethical to use very fine print to make disclosures? Is it ethical to use fonts whose letters are difficult to decipher, or to use yellow ink to print them? Is it ethical to bury the disclosures behind five links on a website that’s already difficult to navigate, or to speak the disclosures so fast in a radio ad that you can barely understand them?

In 2013, partly in response to this problem, the FTC issued a document called “.com Disclosures: How to Make Effective Disclosures in Digital Advertising.”Federal Trade Commission, .com Disclosures: How to Make Effective Disclosures in Digital Advertising, (March 2013), . Although the document focuses on digital media, especially websites, this resource will still be valuable for us to look at.

According to the FTC, “required disclosures must be clear and conspicuous.” The key notion of “clear and conspicuous” tells us that the information must be clear—easily comprehensible; and conspicuous—easily noticeable.FTC, .com Disclosures, i. A later passage gives the following list of features to look for when evaluating whether a particular disclosure has succeeded at being clear and conspicuous:

listitem.para: the placement of the disclosure in the advertisement and its proximity to the claim it is qualifying;
the prominence of the disclosure;
whether the disclosure is unavoidable;
the extent to which items in other parts of the advertisement might distract attention from the disclosure;

whether the disclosure needs to be repeated several times in order to be effectively communicated, or because consumers may enter the site at different locations or travel through the site on paths that cause them to miss the disclosure;
whether disclosures in audio messages are presented in an adequate volume and cadence and visual disclosures appear for a sufficient duration; and
whether the language of the disclosure is understandable to the intended audience.FTC, .com Disclosures, 7.

section.para: In other words, we can use these seven criteria to figure out whether a company has disclosed information properly. Our ethical principle from earlier tells us what should be disclosed—any information regarding predictable harms that might result to a consumer in the course of the normal use of a product. These points from the FTC help us understand how.
As you read each item on the list, ask yourself: what ethical difference would it make if a company failed to comply with this item? What possible effect could that failure have on a consumer?

Let us examine the final item on the list in a bit more detail. This is a requirement regarding language used, which falls under the idea of clarity. Without this requirement, companies could bury a disclosure in technical jargon that most people wouldn’t be able to understand, thereby complying with a demand to make the disclosure without actually communicating anything useful to the consumer.
The FTC expands on the point about language later in its discussion:
section.blockquote: For disclosures to be effective, consumers must be able to understand them. Advertisers should use clear language and syntax and avoid legalese or technical jargon. Disclosures should be as simple and straightforward as possible. Icons and abbreviations are not adequate to prevent a claim from being misleading if a significant minority of consumers do not understand their meaning. Incorporating extraneous material into the disclosure also may diminish communication of the message to consumers.FTC, .com Disclosures, 21.
section.para: This statement makes three points. First, the words and ways of connecting them should be accessible to most readers. Second, the disclosures shouldn’t include any information that isn’t relevant to the disclosure. And third, disclosures shouldn’t use unfamiliar images or abbreviations.

Here the FTC’s discussion does seem to reach the ethical principle behind why disclosures matter in the first place. Their whole purpose is informing customers of information about harms or other possible effects of a product; doing so with exclusively scientific language or arcane legal terms actually makes it harder for consumers to understand those effects. For example, in social media marketing, using the hashtag “#Affiliate” does not meet the FTC’s requirements for disclosures, because many people don’t know that “affiliate” is a newer term for internet-based brand partnerships.

Here are some examples of disclosures that have appeared in print and digital media. Using the principles we’ve discussed and the FTC’s requirements for clear and conspicuous disclosures, ask yourself: is this disclosure ethical? Why? Where does it succeed, and where does it fail? What ethical implications does its failure have for consumers?

listitem.para: On a NerdWallet blog post entitled “11 Things to Know Before Getting Your First Credit Card”: a longer disclosure appears as a hyperlink above the title of the blog post. You must click to access it. The following shorter disclosure appears below an image near the top of the screen: “Many or all of the products featured here are from our partners who compensate us. This influences which products we write about and where and how the product appears on a page. However, this does not influence our evaluations. Our opinions are our own. Here is a list of our partners and here's how we make money.”Claire Tsosie, “11 Things to Know before Getting Your First Credit Card,” NerdWallet, updated May 9, 2022, .

On the home page of Zoloft, an antidepressant medication, in the middle of the page but not viewable without scrolling: “ZOLOFT and other antidepressant medicines may increase suicidal thoughts or actions in some people 24 years of age and younger, especially within the first few months of treatment or when the dose is changed. Watch for these changes and call your healthcare provider right away if you notice new or sudden changes in mood, behavior, actions, thoughts, or feelings, especially if severe. Pay particular attention to such changes when ZOLOFT is started or when the dose is changed.”“Zoloft,” Viatris Inc., accessed September 19, 2023, .

On the website babycribscentral.com, a disclosure available by a link on the website’s upper navigation bar: “Baby Cribs Central does not always test the products reviewed here. When we don’t buy and test the product ourselves, we rely on the integrity of the feedback and reviews provided by real customers, product experts and the product details and specification provided by the manufacturer/supplier which means that the accuracy of every review is directly dependent upon the data a company chooses to share. Sometimes they may share outdated or incorrect details and specifications about their products and in the case when we don’t do a hands-on review, we bear no responsibility for the accuracy details that the manufacturer shares with us or that’s publicly accessible.”“Disclaimer & Disclosure,” Baby Cribs Central, accessed September 19, 2023, .

On Kylie Jenner’s Instagram account, a post with a picture of her appearing to drink a Glow beverage, captioned with the text, “baby it’s cold @drinkglow #GlowPartner.”Kylie Jenner (@kyliejenner), Instagram photo, December 21, 2022, .

section.para: Reflect on this section and on your experience with marketing materials for potentially harmful produces and services. In your view, what information ought to be disclosed? How should it be done? Do the principles we’ve proposed in this chapter give us a way to clearly handle difficult situations regarding product disclosures? Why or why not?

sidebar.title: Case Study: Preferred Brands
sidebar.para: Jackson runs a tire store called Jackson’s Tire. Jackson’s Tire supplies tires and other parts and services to customers in a large but sparsely populated area. Although his business has a good reputation, most customers in the area choose Jackson’s mainly because it would take too much time or would be too much trouble to drive to another tire store.

Jackson’s Tire sells six different brands of tires and can order many other varieties as well; the store receives two deliveries per week from a large distributor several hours away, and so the longest that customers ever go without their car is two or three days.

The six regular brands of tires that Jackson offers all sell for different amounts, but they all have roughly the same markup—Jackson earns around the same price for each tire he sells, no matter the brand. For this reason he has always felt he’s been able to give unbiased advice to different customers, since for most of his business’s history it has not mattered to him which tire he actually sells.

That is changing, now that a longtime friend of his, Nathan, has begun selling his tire out of Jackson’s main distributor. Nathan’s brand is called SureTire. Nathan tells Jackson that he will give him a deal: he will allow Jackson to order SureTire tires from the distributor at a steep discount, which means that Jackson will earn much more money on each SureTire sold than he would on any other tire sale. In exchange, Nathan wants Jackson to market SureTire inside Jackson’s Tire as the store’s preferred brand: there will be more displays, signage, and other marketing materials posted in the store for SureTire, and the mechanics and salespeople at Jackson’s Tire will begin recommending SureTire when asked.

Jackson isn’t sure what to do. He knows the extra money would be nice, but worries that he will lose the freedom he has to give advice. He has tested SureTires himself, and believes that they offer an average but not outstanding combination of quality and value.

listitem.para: If Jackson signed an agreement with SureTire, would it be misleading for his company to describe SureTires as the “preferred” brand, when all that meant was that the company had signed an agreement?
Suppose Jackson signs an agreement with SureTire. Is this agreement something that needs to be disclosed to customers when Jackson’s Tire mechanics make recommendations? Why or why not?
Does Jackson’s Tire need to reveal that it’s able to sell SureTires for higher profit than other tires? Would it make a difference to a customer if she had that information?

If a customer asks for a tire recommendation and a salesperson says, “I recommend the SureTire brand” even though she actually believes that SureTires are inferior, has she lied to the customer? Why or why not?
What would you do, if you were Jackson? Why?

section.title: Direct Marketing to Experts
section.para: This section of the chapter will be a bit different from the others. In the previous three, we have been considering the ethics of various marketing practices, such as business bluffing and false advertising. Although we haven’t made this explicit, we’ve been thinking about cases where the marketing channel goes from the marketing or selling company directly to the prospective consumer. The ethical principles we’ve considered have had those cases in mind.

In all this discussion, however, we’ve never asked whether marketing ought to be allowed at all. We’ve always assumed that marketing, at least in some basic form, is ethically permissible; the ethical questions have all been about specific activities or specific ways of performing an activity, and whether those are ethical or not.

This section will change course by focusing on a specific form of marketing activity and asking, should that activity be allowed at all? It may be that it’s so contentious and so potentially harmful that no variation of it could be ethically permissible.
That activity is direct marketing to experts, and we’ll use doctors as an example.

As regular consumers, we see advertisements in many different media for many different medications. We’ve given some examples in previous sections. But these direct-to-consumer advertisements are not the only form of marketing for medications; in fact, they probably aren’t the most important, either. Drug and other companies also market their products directly to the doctors—for doctors and other medical professionals are ultimately the ones who recommend and prescribe the drugs to patients. Direct marketing to experts, then, represents a way of trying to increase market share without doing any advertising to the people who will ultimately use the product itself.

James Hamblin and Art Van Zee have written in detail about the promotion and marketing of OxyContin,James Hamblin, “The Opioid Reckoning Will Not Be Just,” Health, Atlantic, August 29, 2019,: ; Art Van Zee, “The Promotion and Marketing of OxyContin: Commercial Triumph, Public Health Tragedy,” American Journal of Public Health 99, no. 2 (February 2009): 221–227, . an opioid painkiller part of a drug epidemic responsible for the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people in the United States alone. Purdue Pharma developed OxyContin in the early 1990s and introduced it to the market it 1996. In just five years its sales exploded from $48 million in 1996 to over $1 billion in 2000. These sales tracked a growing addiction as well, and in 2004 OxyContin was the most abused drug in the United States.

Normally, when a product sees such a rapid rise in sales, we assume that it must just be the best-available or best-priced product on the market—what else could explain the rise? For OxyContin, however, this isn’t the case. As Van Zee details, oxycodone-based preparations like OxyContin had no particular advantages over other strong opioid medications. According to the FDA itself, in reviewing Purdue’s new drug application, the only advantage of OxyContin over other drugs was that its sustained-release mechanism meant that patients took fewer pills per day. It was not more effective than other drugs in treating pain.
So what explains the meteoric sales growth? Direct marketing to doctors in order to inform them of the drug and get them to prescribe it, as Van Zee explains:
section.blockquote: From 1996 to 2001, Purdue conducted more than 40 national pain-management and speaker-training conferences at resorts in Florida, Arizona, and California. More than 5000 physicians, pharmacists, and nurses attended these all-expenses-paid symposia, where they were recruited and trained for Purdue’s national speaker bureau. . . .
One of the cornerstones of Purdue’s marketing plan was the use of sophisticated marketing data to influence physicians’ prescribing. . . .

A lucrative bonus system encouraged sales representatives to increase sales of OxyContin in their territories, resulting in a large number of visits to physicians with high rates of opioid prescriptions, as well as a multifaceted information campaign aimed at them. In 2001, in addition to the average sales representative’s annual salary of $55 000, annual bonuses averaged $71 500, with a range of $15 000 to nearly $240 000. Purdue paid $40 million in sales incentive bonuses to its sales representatives that year. . . .

Purdue promoted among primary care physicians a more liberal use of opioids, particularly sustained-release opioids. Primary care physicians began to use more of the increasingly popular OxyContin; by 2003, nearly half of all physicians prescribing OxyContin were primary care physicians. Van Dee, “Promotion and Marketing,” 221–222.
section.para: To market OxyContin, Purdue Pharma went straight to the source and spoke not to medical patients but to doctors themselves. They invited doctors to resorts, showered them with food, gifts, and other perks, and educated them on how they could prescribe more OxyContin to their patients for a wider variety of conditions. Part of Purdue’s strategy was to normalize the use of OxyContin for pain unrelated to cancer treatments, such as chronic back pain or other conditions. Since patients with those conditions are fairly common, convincing doctors to prescribe OxyContin to treat their patients’ pain would open up an entirely new market and lead to a huge increase in sales.
This effort required a massive marketing budget:
section.blockquote: The extraordinary amount of money spent in promoting a sustained-release opioid was unprecedented. During OxyContin’s first 6 years on the market, Purdue spent approximately 6 to 12 times more on promoting it than the company had spent on promoting MS Contin, or than Janssen Pharmaceutical Products LP had spent on Duragesic, one of OxyContin’s competitors. Although OxyContin has not been shown to be superior to other available potent opioid preparations, by 2001 it had become the most frequently prescribed brand-name opioid in the United States for treating moderate to severe pain.Van Dee, “Promotion and Marketing,” 225.
section.para: As we’ve seen, a great deal of this effort went toward marketing directly to doctors, rather than to patients.

To be clear, doctors did not receive the trips and perks in exchange for agreeing to prescribe OxyContin; the Purdue seminars were informational, and participating in them carried no obligation for doctors to prescribe or even suggest OxyContin to their patients. In addition, doctors, as all people do, imagine themselves immune to subtle persuasion and assume that they will always make treatment recommendations based on what is best for their patients, regardless of which corporate retreat they’ve just returned from.

This thinking, however, is false. It is well established that Purdue’s seminars and other retreat-based direct marketing activities do influence the way doctors prescribe drugs, independently of how good the drugs themselves are.James P. Orlowski and Leon Wateska, “The Effects of Pharmaceutical Firm Enticements on Physician Prescribing Patterns,” Chest 120, no. 1 (July 1992): 270–273, . In other words, Purdue’s marketing efforts worked, and doctors began prescribing the drug in large numbers, way out of proportion to its usefulness and in a market with many other pain-control options. But other pain-control options weren’t throwing fun and free corporate retreats in California.

Purdue had already had experience with some of its previous drugs becoming widely addictive, so another pillar in its marketing campaign was to minimize the perceived risk of addiction to OxyContin. According to Van Dee, “in much of its promotional campaign—in literature and audiotapes for physicians, brochures and videotapes for patients, and its ‘Partners Against Pain’ Web site—Purdue claimed that the risk of addiction from OxyContin was extremely small.”Van Dee, “Promotion and Marketing,” 223.

Purdue also instructed sales reps to tell doctors that the drug was addictive only to those with an “addictive personality,” insinuating that most normal people would be at no risk of addiction. Arthur Gale, “Sacklers Sacked but Purdue Still Caused Opioid Epidemic,” Missouri Medicine 119, no. 2 (Mar–Apr 2022): 109, .
These claims were lies, as was suspected at the time and is widely known now:
section.blockquote: The remarkable commercial success of OxyContin, however, was stained by increasing rates of abuse and addiction. Drug abusers learned how to simply crush the controlled-release tablet and swallow, inhale, or inject the high-potency opioid for an intense morphinelike high. . . .

From 1995 to 2001, the number of patients treated for opioid abuse in Maine increased 460%, and from 1997 to 1999 the state had a 400% increase in the number of chronic hepatitis C cases reported. In eastern Kentucky from 1995 to 2001, there was a 500% increase in the number of patients entering methadone maintenance treatment programs, about 75% of whom were OxyContin dependent. . . .

The increasing OxyContin abuse problem was an integral part of the escalating national prescription opioid abuse problem. Liberalization of the use of opioids, particularly for the treatment of chronic non–cancer-related pain, increased the availability of all opioids as well as their abuse.
section.para: Outside of alcohol and marijuana abuse, painkiller and oxycodone abuse is the most widespread drug problem in the United States today.

Take a moment to reflect on this story, which features a company whose sales doubled many times over and which made its founding family, the Sacklers, over $10 billion in profit. The Sacklers made direct marketing to experts Purdue Pharma’s primary marketing strategy, and the result was unbelievable financial success—but the drug, the family, and the company are also responsible for many thousands of deaths. Given the numbers involved, there is no question that the marketing effort focused on doctors is itself responsible for many of those deaths, since without that campaign, OxyContin would not have been prescribed nor used as much as it was. What seemed like a triumph of marketing turned out to have deadly consequences that are both long-lasting and potentially ineliminable.

It is from this perspective that we can appreciate the question with which we started this section: should this kind direct marketing to experts be allowed at all? Given that, despite what doctors think, marketing efforts do influence prescription decisions, should retreats like Purdue’s speaker seminars be ethically permissible?

It is tempting to answer with an immediate “no,” but the situation is more complicated than it may seem at first. In fields that rely on expert opinion—medicine is one, but there are many, since most people don’t know enough to solve their own plumbing, electrical, automotive, or computer problems, among other issues—patients and consumers rely on experts to help make decisions. Doctors, for example, spend many years in medical school and residency programs to become experts on particular systems of the body. If patients already knew everything that doctors knew, they wouldn’t need to see doctors in the first place, and so they must necessarily rely on expert opinion to know what to do.

For this reason, the issue of direct marketing to experts is a difficult ethical challenge. If such direct marketing were deemed unethical and outlawed entirely, then doctors would not receive as much new information about drugs or other products that really could help their patients. On the other hand, when the company doing the marketing has no interest other than sales, doctors may not be receiving the whole truth about a drug’s effectiveness or its side effects.

Our first conclusion, then, seems to be that direct marketing is ethically permissible, but only with certain bounds; no company should be able to do what Purdue Pharma did, for we know the consequences of that approach.
So what are the “bounds”? What limitations should apply to the way companies market their products directly to expert recommenders?

One industry that may require more stringent ethical principles is medicine, simply because it deals with human health. Your car mechanic may be upselling you on a tire or brake pad, but if those products work, the only harm done is that you paid more than you otherwise might have. The effects for products like computers are similar, and while they may be worse when we involve experts like construction managers or electricians, the harmful effects still are nothing like those seen in medicine. You don’t get addicted and ruin your life when buy a more expensive marble countertop.

What do you think? What ethical restrictions should there be on direct marketing to experts? How should these restrictions be put into law? Should medicine be a special case? Is it the only special case? If not, why not?

Another factor to consider is how laws about marketing practices come to exist in the first place. In many cases, industry lobbyists help create the legislation that their companies must then follow. Experience shows that it’s doubtful they’re crafting laws with consumers’ best interests in mind. Purdue Pharma itself spent over a million dollars on lobbying efforts, and the pharmaceutical industry as a whole spends over a hundred million dollars every year.

We’ll come back to this issue in a future chapter, but for now we can ask, is this kind of influence ethically acceptable? Why or why not? Should companies working in high-risk fields like medicine be allowed to help write the laws that they are supposed to obey in order to protect consumers?

Direct marketing to experts is not wholly responsible for the tragedy of the opioid epidemic, and there are other industries where direct marketing may not be ethically objectionable at all. But with medicine it is, and while we might still think that direct marketing is ethically permissible, it’s clear that we need additional principles to help us navigate the tricky ethical landscape of this difficult issue.
We’ve suggested some of those additional ethical principles here. What others would you add, and why?

sidebar.title: Case Study: Experts as Brand Representatives
sidebar.para: Dr. Cynthia Clyde works as a general practitioner in a rural health center that is part of a larger regional healthcare network. She sees many patients for many different types of conditions. Although she often refers patients to specialists, she finishes the care on her own for many of them, both diagnosing illnesses and making treatment recommendations or prescriptions.

Dr. Clyde’s own husband has had pretty severe health problems of his own in the last few years, and despite her large salary, she and her husband are facing a significant amount of medical debt. In addition, Dr. Clyde has had to cut back on her hours some in order to care for her husband. With less work she’s also earning less than she’s used to.

Last week she was approached by some representatives for a pharmaceutical company with an offer to be a brand representative for a new painkiller the company has developed. If she accepts, she would visit hospitals and healthcare centers in the area to tell them about the new drug, answer questions, and offer samples. The offer from the drug company includes very generous financial compensation, which would make a major different to Dr. Clyde and her family.

The representatives from the drug company left her with information about the drug as well as links to papers about drug trials online. When Dr. Clyde tried to access them, she had trouble understanding the results of the trials and the statistical analyses used to reach conclusions. Dr. Clyde wasn’t ever one for research; she preferred to work with patients, which was why she moved to a rural area in the first place. After being unable to make sense of the drug company’s materials, she asked her colleague, Dr. Winscott, for help, but he wasn’t able to understand the drug’s effectiveness either.
The drug company is pushing her for a response. She knows that if she declines, the company will just find someone else to take the position.

listitem.para: To what extent is Dr. Clyde ethically obligated to understand the drug herself before joining the company as a brand ambassador?
To what extent is Dr. Clyde ethically obligated to understand the drug herself before recommending it to patients?
Are your answers to questions 1 and 2 the same? If they aren’t, do different standards apply? Why?
Does Dr. Clyde have a professional or ethical responsibility to remain current on the scientific literature relevant to her areas of medicine?
What would you do, if you were Dr. Clyde?

section.title: Creating Needs and Negotiating Sales
section.para: The final section in this chapter fits itself in between marketing and the ethics of exchange. We’ll be considering the ethics of marketing to create needs and the resulting sales negotiations themselves.

To begin, let’s think about the purpose of marketing a product. At first glance, the purpose of marketing may seem to be to inform the customer about the product. After all, if a customer doesn’t know anything about a product, it’s extremely unlikely that they’ll ever consider buying it, much less actually make a purchase. Marketing would then be the mechanism by which companies inform consumers of what they offer for sale.

This explanation of marketing’s purpose works pretty well, but we can bring out some ethical issues by looking for a bit more nuance. In general, in order for a customer to buy something, an awareness of a product must be combined with a need which that product could fulfill, along with a desire to actually fulfill that need. If either the need or the desire is lacking, there won’t be a sale—someone could need something without desiring to fulfill that need, such as when you feel hungry but are trying to watch what you eat.

To go a bit deeper with the purpose of marketing, then, we could say that it is not only to inform audiences about a product, but to inform them specifically about what need the product can fulfill, along with why consumers should have a desire to fulfill that need with a specific product. If an ad for our restaurant convinces someone to go out to eat for dinner, but doesn’t convince them to come to our restaurant, then we’ve left a gap between informing them about our product and connecting the product to their need and desire.

section.title: Creating a Need
section.para: Think about this, though: what about when marketing creates a need, where no need existed before? Could there be an ethical issue here?

So perhaps I’m scrolling through my social media feeds, where carefully targeted advertisements make me aware of deficiencies in my appearance that had never occurred to me before. Prior to seeing the ads I felt good about myself and the way I look and dress; after seeing the ads, I sense a sudden desire to make serious changes. You might have experienced something like this before, and it happens with many other kinds of ads as well. The purpose of the marketing is to close the connection between product, need, and desire by creating a new need and desire where none existed before. The product in the ad then becomes associated with the new need and desire, such that a consumer now wishes to fulfill the need in a particular way.

The question here is, is this an ethical thing to do? Is it ethically permissible for marketing to create a need where there wasn’t one before? Is it ethically permissible for marketers to make consumers feel bad about themselves in order to make them aware of new desires to buy a good or service?

The answer to these questions seems to be “yes,” simply on the grounds that, most of the time, consumers can just choose not to look at an advertisement; in addition, consumers can just choose not to buy a product if they don’t want to buy it. This is a fairly powerful justification for the idea that certain marketing practices are not in fact unethical—as long as a person can just choose to do otherwise, they aren’t being forced to make a choice and so there may seem to be nothing wrong with the marketing.

Perhaps the principle here is that the only unethical thing would be if a consumer were acting on desires that were not their desires. As long as a consumer is acting on their own desire, they are acting autonomously and enjoying the human dignity that accompanies such an action.

This principle, however, raises the question of what it means for a desire to be “ours.” After all, we get desires for things from other people all the time—friends make movie or book recommendations, magazines make food recommendations, and podcasts make website recommendations. Any one of these recommendations can give rise to a desire in us. In what sense is such a desire “ours”?

We may also consider some other ethical questions related to these points. Do the ethical principles governing marketing and the creation of desires differ from those that govern person-to-person interactions? Do they need to differ? Why? Should businesses be prevented from doing things to manipulate thought or behavior that individual people do to each other all the time? Why? What makes the business’s ethical duty different from the duties we have to each other?

section.title: Sales Negotiations
section.para: It is here that we can understand why sales negotiations might be a place fraught with ethical problems. In most buying and selling exchanges, there’s a price already fixed by the seller, and the buyer can accept that price or walk away. But in certain kinds of exchanges, it is understood that the sticker price is not actually the price, and the buyer is free to do what they can to negotiate a lower final price.

We will deal here with three ethical problems arising from sales negotiations. First, what about buyers who don’t know they’re in a situation of negotiation? Second, does fairness matter for these exchanges? Third, are there any tactics of negotiation that aren’t ethically permissible?
In our discussion, we’ll follow an example of negotiations about the price of a car at a car dealership.

The first potential ethical problem for sales negotiations is that not all buyers may realize that they are in a situation of negotiation in the first place. It is common knowledge, for example, that the list price of a car in an advertisement or on the window is not the price for which the dealership actually expects to sell the car. The dealership expects buyers to haggle over the price and is usually willing to sell the car for up to thousands of dollars less than the list price.

Saying that something is “common knowledge,” however, doesn’t mean that everyone knows it; first-time car buyers especially may not know that the dealership expects negotiation. This ignorance may be completely innocent or accidental, too—it’s not like there’s a class one can take before buying a car. The result is that those with this special bit of knowledge will receive a far lower price than those without it, which may be unfair.

Is this an ethical problem? Or is this just an example of caveat emptor, “let the buyer beware,” as we discussed in the previous chapter? Is it unfair that a bit of knowledge that someone may happen not to have could make such a difference in the final price? Would we tolerate such price discrepancies in other kinds of exchanges? Why or why not? When selling cars, would it be better to stick to a list price with no room for negotiation?

The second potential ethical problem in sales negotiations concerns the broader question of whether fairness matters at all. We saw a bit of this in the first problem, but even in cases where buyers know that they are expected to negotiate, among those buying there are wide ranges of both ability to negotiate and willingness to negotiate. Should these differences matter? Suppose I’m bad at negotiation, for example—should my inability to do it well cost me $2,000 that the dealership would have taken off the price of the car, if I were better? Is it fair to penalize me $2,000? Or is the language of “penalties” not the right way to describe this situation? If it isn’t, the question of fairness may not arise at all.

A related issue concerns people who simply don’t want to negotiate. Negotiation is, by its nature, an adversarial interaction between two people with more or less incompatible goals; some people find such interactions uncomfortable or even hostile. Should that matter? Should a person be required to pay more because they don’t want to negotiate, even though they could? Is that another penalty? Or is it just a part of the way certain sales environments work? Are there other sales environments that work similarly? Do ethical issues arise there, or is this not an ethical issue at all?

The final potential ethical issue is what sales tactics, if any, are ethically impermissible. Here we’re excluding cases of actual violence or otherwise forcing someone to make a purchase—of course those actions would be unethical. For this potential problem, we’re more concerned with whether it’s permissible for salespeople to pressure buyers in different ways, such as by making buyers feel like they owe the salespeople for their time, refusing to take no for an answer, using short time limits to restrict offers, obligating someone to buy a product blindly (without seeing the actual product that will be sold), or appealing to buyers’ emotions or fear of missing out.

One reason to think that such tactics are unethical is that they look like bullying or manipulation. It’s easy to think that buyers ought to be resistant to things like that, since they can always walk away, but not everyone has the same awareness or fortitude for dealing with pressure. Should salespeople be able to take advantage of those who aren’t as able to handle it? Why should they be rewarded for that? If they’re bullying or pressuring someone into buying, aren’t they violating that person’s autonomy?

On the other hand, interpersonal interactions outside of sales are full of manipulation and pressure; sometimes it’s subtle, other times it’s overt, but it’s often there. Given that this sort of behavior happens all the time outside a situation of exchange, should it be unethical when someone might be buying something? Do the ethical rules governing normal human interactions change when sales are involved? Why or why not?

As with previous issues, there are many possible answers to these questions, and our answers will probably depend on a particular context. Nevertheless, it’s important to sharpen our skills for identifying potential ethical issues and analyzing them, in order to understand useful ethical principles to guide our behavior. Marketing, more than many other areas of business, presents us with these issues.

sidebar.title: Case Study: Direct-Mail Prizes
sidebar.para: It’s New To You Cars is a used-car dealership outside of a major population center in the western United States. The dealership has many acres of available lot space and at any given time has between 1,000 and 1,500 vehicles for sale.

In response to growing pressure from other dealerships, It’s New To You has adopted a new strategy for getting customers to walk in the door. They’ve noticed that even as their sales tactics vary, the percentage of customers who enter the dealership and buy a car is fairly constant. They therefore conclude that the way to increase sales is to get more people inside the dealership.

Here’s their new strategy. It’s New To You sends direct-mail advertisements and other marketing materials to consumers at their homes. Part of the advertisement is a scratch-off card that looks like a lottery ticket. By scratching off different combinations of boxes, consumers can win a free car, cash, or a vacation to Hawaii. Once they’ve scratched, they just bring the card into the dealership.

The strategy doesn’t end there, though. It’s New To You has instructed its salespeople to ignore the fact that a customer appears to have won a vacation and instead take them to tour a selection of vehicles for sale. The salespeople engage the customers in conversation about their families and their work, then try to steer them toward an area of the dealership with vehicles that would fit their needs. They continue to do this even if the customer says that they aren’t interested in buying a car and would just like to redeem the scratch-off card.

The dealership’s internal rule is that a customer must request redemption of the scratch-off card eight times before the salesperson begins the process of redeeming the prize. Anything less than eight times, and the salesperson is to continue focusing on selling a car.

The “vacation” prize, by far the most common prize on the scratch-off cards, isn’t worth a whole vacation. It’s a two-night stay at an unspecified hotel and is only good during off-peak travel times. The marketing materials sent in the mail make it appear as though the prize is an all-expenses paid trip, but customers only find out it’s not after pushing eight or more times to redeem the prize.

listitem.para: Is It’s New to You’s new marketing strategy ethically permissible? That is, is it ethically permissible to draw customers into the dealership on the misleading grounds that they have won a prize, only to try to sell them a car?

Some customers who weren’t interested in buying a car when they walked into the dealership end up buying one. Is it ethical for the dealership to try to convince them to do so, even if their stated intention is to not do it? Or should customers just know what they are getting themselves into when they walk into the dealership?
Do marketing materials that seem to offer a prize of a full vacation constitute false advertising if the actual prize is just a stay at a hotel? Why or why not?
Are sales negotiations a situation that requires a set of ethical principles to govern the behavior of companies and customers? Why or why not?

section.title: Introduction to Accounting and Finance Ethics

listitem.para: Be able to explain the idea behind GAAP, or generally accepted accounting principles.
Recognize situations where accounting and financial decisions create ethically problematic issues.
Understand the the morality of different kinds of punishment for financial crimes.

section.title: Accounting Ethics
section.para: As we’ve learned in this course, business ethics is a very broad field—it includes many problems, concepts, and principles. But in addition to those things, it also includes many “subfields,” or fields within a field—narrow areas of study that pertain to a single domain of business or business practice. So far, the two most prominent subfields we’ve studied have been corporate responsibility and marketing ethics.

This chapter will introduce and discuss two other subfields of business ethics, along with the problems, concepts, and principles belonging to them. The first is accounting ethics, and the second is finance ethics. We’ve chosen these subfields because they’re some of the largest in business ethics and because the ethical issues in them are, in some cases, so wide-reaching and famous that even people outside of business or business ethics know about them. After discussing each subfield, we’ll then dedicate one section to complicity and one to the usual punishments associated with fraud and other white-collar crimes.
Let’s begin with accounting ethics.

AccountingThe area of business focused on the proper creation and use of financial records. is the area of business focused on the proper creation and use of financial records. Every business needs an accountant—even if the business is so small that it has a single employee, that person would be the firm’s accountant, since no business will live long without accurate records.

Accounting ethicsThe study of the ethical issues, problems, principles, and concepts that arise in accounting. , then, is the study of the ethical issues, problems, principles, and concepts that arise in accounting.

We could dedicate an entire course to accounting ethics, and there are many textbooks that cover that topic alone.Levine, Accounting Ethics: A Practical Approach; Klein, Ethics in Accounting: A Decision-Making Approach; Duska, Duska, and Kury, Accounting Ethics; Pakaluk and Cheffers, Accounting Ethics; Costa and Pinheiro, Accounting Ethics Education; etc. We can cover only a small fraction of that material here, so we’ll focus on just a few basic issues with some practical implications.

The first is why accounting ethics is important. Like other areas of business ethics, there’s lots to reason and think about in accounting ethics. But there are several reasons why the ethics of accounting practice is particularly important. One is what we mentioned earlier—every business, regardless of its size, must do some form of accounting; this makes some parts of accounting ethics almost universal in their reach across different domains of business.

Another reason accounting ethics is so important is that, in many ways, financial records are the only real window that many people have into the health of a business: basic metrics like profit, revenue, and others tell us how well a business is doing and represent a business’s efforts to accomplish some of its most fundamental purposes. Therefore, ethical issues arising from lying about those records cut to the heart of the purpose of many firms and to how they interact with other firms and individuals in a marketplace.
A third reason for the importance of business ethics is the far-reaching consequences that accounting ethics can have, not only for a business but also for an entire market or a whole economy.

The greatest examples are the Enron and WorldCom accounting scandals of the first decade of the 2000’s. We’ve mentioned these briefly in previous chapters—at the time it declared bankruptcy, Enron held more than 60 billion dollars in assets, and had seen its stock price drop from a one-time high of over $90 per share to less than one dollar. Such massive financial losses could not help but have ripple effects both inside and outside an industry. WorldCom, a long-distance telephone company, was just as large: when it filed for bankruptcy in summer 2002, just under a year after Enron, it had forged more than $3.8 billion worth of false financial records and was overstating its assets by more than $11 billion. Both companies were enormous, and their toppling had powerful effects in the domestic and world economies.

So accounting ethics is important for many reasons. But what is it, and how does it happen? There are countless variations and methods, but the most straightforward is simply the misclassifying or misreporting of financial data. We’ll look here at an example involving WorldCom, and then we will see a much more common case in our case study.

To auditTo review financial records for accuracy and to examine the way different pots of money have been allocated to different parts of a business’s operation. financial records is to review them for accuracy and to examine the way different pots of money have been allocated to different parts of a business’s operation. An internal auditor is an accountant who works for a company and scrutinizes the financial records of that same company; an external auditor works for some other company. The lead internal auditor at WorldCom was Cynthia Cooper, who held both a bachelor’s and master’s degree in accounting. As such, Cooper was a WorldCom employee, and it was her job to review WorldCom’s own financial records.The following account is drawn from Cooper’s own version of events in her book, Extraordinary Circumstances: The Journey of a Corporate Whistleblower, (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, Inc., 2008).

Based on a tip she received from a member of her auditing team, Cooper began to look into a classification known in WorldCom’s financial system as “prepaid capacity.” WorldCom was a telecommunications company and so could have had an actual expenditure account for “prepaid capacity”—the problem was that no one in the company seemed to know what “prepaid capacity” was. Cooper asked her supervisors and other high-ranking employees, but no one could explain it, including people who had themselves made entries into the financial records with that designation.

Cooper continued to poke around but started to receive pushback: she began to receive emails telling her to stop her audit. At around the same time, she and her team discovered that, were it not for the unexplained “prepaid capacity” records, WorldCom’s profits in early 2002 would have dropped by over 500 million dollars. Cooper came to realize that something illegal seemed to be happening, and began to question the accountants responsible for the entries; at each turn, no one could provide justification for the questionable classifications. Later, in a meeting with an external auditor, two executives made a now-famous remark about the irregularities in the records: they made sense “from a business perspective, but not an accounting perspective.”

Later on, Cooper’s work showed nearly 4 billion dollars in fraudulent transfers from expense accounts to assets. These transfers served to make the company appear more profitable, but in reality hid massive losses. The company was forced to refile its earnings reports for all of 2001 and the first quarter of 2002.

The story of WorldCom helps us understand one of the most basic ways that accounting fraud can occur: accountants, either knowingly or unknowingly, misclassify money. In the case of WorldCom, expenses were transferred from assets to hide the fact that the company wasn’t making any money. Although there are different kinds of accounting fraud, at the root of many cases are simple transfers like these, making one or more accounts appear larger or smaller than they actually are.

For this reason, the United States Securities and Exchange Commission, or SEC—the body responsible for regulating and investigating any form of market manipulation—supports a set of accounting standards known as GAAP, or the “generally accepted accounting principles” of the United States. As the name suggests, these are accounting norms that most experts agree on and that the SEC uses to inform its examination of public companies and their financial records.

The Financial Accounting Standards Board, or FASB, maintains an updated website with detailed discussions of GAAP. There are two main divisions of principles: those that are authoritative, and those that aren’t. As the FASB notes on its website, the Accounting Standards Codification is “the source of authoritative generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) recognized by the FASB to be applied by nongovernmental entities.”Financial Accounting Standards Board, Accounting Standards Codification, accessed September 25, 2023, 105-10-05-1. It later expounds on sources for nonauthoritative principles:

blockquote.para: Accounting and financial reporting practices not included in the Codification are nonauthoritative. Sources of nonauthoritative accounting guidance and literature include, for example, the following:

a. Practices that are widely recognized and prevalent either generally or in the industry
b. FASB Concepts Statements
c. American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) Issues Papers
d. International Financial Reporting Standards of the International Accounting Standards Board
e. Pronouncements of professional associations or regulatory agencies
f. Technical Information Service Inquiries and Replies included in AICPA Technical Practice Aids
g. Accounting textbooks, handbooks, and articles.

The appropriateness of other sources of accounting guidance depends on its relevance to particular circumstances, the specificity of the guidance, the general recognition of the issuer or author as an authority, and the extent of its use in practice.Financial Accounting Standards Board, Accounting Standards Codification, accessed September 25, 2023, 105-10-05-3.

section.para: GAAP provides systematic guidance to accountants, auditors, organizations, and other entities, and is a standard part of accounting education.

From our discussion so far, we can distill a simple ethical principle for issues of accounting: always follow GAAP. That principle is so simple that it’s almost laughable—and yet, if Enron and WorldCom had followed it, there wouldn’t have been any fraud. Those companies were making transfers that would never have been condoned under GAAP, because of how misleading and potentially damaging they were. GAAP would have stopped them.

For this reason, GAAP isn’t just a set of standards for keeping financial records—we could also consider it a set of ethical standards. If companies followed GAAP standards strictly, then accounting fraud would be much less common, and it would be easy to avoid at least some ethical problems in accounting practice.

Unfortunately, it isn’t always that easy. The accounting firm Arthur Andersen was the main provider of accounting services to both Enron and WorldCom, and so was supposed to oversee GAAP and other ethical accounting practices at both companies. But, as we read in the following discussion, Arthur Andersen and its employees were not exactly impartial judges of what was happening at those organizations:

blockquote.para: Auditors at Arthur Andersen misrepresented the financial status of companies such as Enron, WorldCom, Qwest, and Halliburton, merely because it was in their financial interest to do so. At the root of Andersen’s failure were conflicts of interest that undermined the independence of Andersen’s auditors and corrupted the independent auditing process. First, Andersen’s consulting business made much more money working for these individual companies than did the accounting unit at Andersen. To retain the lucrative consulting business, Andersen applied pressure to its auditors to ignore fraudulent practices. Second, companies such as Enron actively recruited employees from Andersen for well-compensated management positions within their organizations. Thus, in many cases the company being audited employed former Andersen employees. In addition, the prospect of obtaining such jobs in the future is alleged to have influenced the behavior of current Andersen employees, especially junior auditors.Denis Arnold, Tom Beauchamp, and Norman Bowie, Ethical Theory and Business, 9th ed. (Essex: Pearson, 2014), 336.

section.para: In other words, while Andersen’s accountants and auditors did fail in their responsibility to follow GAAP, the real problem was the fact that they could not be independent of the company they were auditing. Technically they were independent because they worked for another business—but the relationship between that business and its clients made true independence impossible. As a result, massive conflicts of interest distracted accountants from performing their professional and ethical duties.

On this basis we can observe another ethical principle for accounting. The first was about following GAAP—because of the role accounting plays in a business, its standards of professional competence and its ethical standards are virtually one and the same. This second principle separates professional competence and ethics, but it’s just as important: ethical accounting practices are only possible with the true independence of the accountant or auditor.

By “true independence,” we don’t just mean that the accountants don’t work for the company they’re reviewing. In fact, true independence can’t mean that, because internal auditors do work for the company they review, instead of some third-party auditor , and are still expected to be independent in the sense of unbiased and disinterested. True independence instead refers to both how the auditors see themselves and how they are treated by the people hiring them, paying them, and, in some cases, receiving their reports of potentially unethical behavior.

With these issues in mind, authors Ronald Duska and Brenda Duska have proposed four principles for evaluating the true independence of an auditor.Ronald Duska, Brenda Shay Duska, and Julie Ragatz, Accounting Ethics, 2nd ed. (Malden, MA: Wiley-Blackwell, 2011) 127–128. Here are their four principles, along with a short explanation they give for each:

blockquote.para: Principle 1. Assessing the level of independence risk. Independence decision makers should assess the level of independence risk by considering the types and significance of threats to auditor independence and the types and effectiveness of safeguards. . . .

Principle 2. Determining the acceptability of the level of independence risk. After assessing the level of risk the auditor needs to determine whether the level of independence is at an acceptable position on the independence risk continuum.

Principle 3. Considering benefits and costs. Independence decision makers should ensure that the benefits resulting from reducing independence risk by imposing additional safeguards exceed the costs of those safeguards.

Principle 4. Considering interested parties’ views in addressing auditor independence issues. Independence decision makers should consider the views of investors, other users and others with an interest in the integrity of financial reporting when addressing issues related to auditor independence and should resolve those issues based on the decision makers’ judgment about how best to meet the goal of auditor independence.

section.para: By using these guidelines, we can evaluate the independence of an auditor. Arthur Andersen’s relationships with Enron and WorldCom were at one end of a continuum—we probably won’t encounter such obvious and thorough wrongdoing very often. But the guidelines can help us with trickier cases as well.
Taken together, our two principles—follow GAAP, and maintain true independence—are two of the most important foundations of ethics in accounting.

sidebar.title: Case Study: Accepted Accounting Principles
sidebar.para: Salantha is an accountant for Johnny’s Sporting Goods. She keeps the books for the store and also handles all its interactions with the bank and other lending partners.

Two months from now the store is due to make a large payment on a loan. In order to continue to receive favorable terms, Johnny’s must demonstrate that it’s growing revenue at a rate above a minimum threshold.

To counteract some recent low sales numbers, Salantha’s boss has asked her to log sales that will occur after the loan is due as though they occurred before it. The contracts for those sales have already been signed, and Johnny’s will receive the money for them—the only thing Salantha would be doing would be to misrepresent the dates at which the sales took place. Since the next date for evaluating their revenue growth won’t come around for another six months, the store will have plenty of time to make up the difference later on, her boss says.

listitem.para: Salantha is worried that, if she doesn’t agree to classify the future revenue as revenue they’ve already received, her boss will just do it anyway. Who should she speak to about this problem, and why?

If Salantha doesn’t misrepresent the sales dates, Johnny’s will likely default on its loan, and the store might have to close. Many people would lose their jobs. Does this make a difference in what Salantha ought to do? Why or why not?

Salantha also knows about other sales the company is likely to make several months after the loan due date, and they will provide the company with even more revenue. Her boss suggests that, if she wants to, she could classify those sales as occurring before the target date as well. Does the number of times Salantha makes this misrepresentation matter to the ethics of the situation? Why or why not?
What would you do, if you were Salantha? Why?

section.title: Finance Ethics
section.para: Like our previous section on accounting ethics, finance ethics is also too broad a topic to cover in any significant detail here. The goal of this section will be to introduce some of the major ethical issues with an invitation to greater study.

By “finance,” in the term “finance ethics,” we mean all aspects of business having to do with funding, fundraising, saving, investing, lending, and other related activities. Based on that description, it looks like finance ethics cannot be completely separated from accounting ethics. That is true—there is some overlap between these areas. But finance ethics includes other issues as well.

That it includes these additional issues, however, may not be apparent from the way that the finance industry actually runs. For example, author Jay Walker published a 1987 book called The Complete Book of Wall Street Ethics, which was an attempt to cover the industry’s basic ethical principles. Walker apparently didn’t have much trouble doing so, and in fact was able to accomplish the goal quite succinctly: every page in the book is blank.

Now, while Walker’s book makes for a good joke gift, it raises again an issue that we’ve seen other times in our study of business ethics: can there really be an ethics for an industry whose entire goal is to make more money, no matter what? If it is true, as Walker suggests, that there are no ethical principles governing behavior in finance, then what’s the point of studying it? Why bother, if professionals in the field are just going to do whatever they can to succeed anyway?

Here, as elsewhere, we must hold on to the distinction between how things do actually work and how things should work, given the ethical principles we arrive at. The fact that they don’t work according to these principles—or even that it would be extremely difficult to get them to work that way—doesn’t say anything about the value of the principles. We would all be better off if there were no burglaries, for example; and even though burglaries aren’t going to disappear, it would still be worthwhile for us to push in that direction. The same is true for finance ethics. Investment banks, private investors, and other major players in the finance industry are some of the most powerful entities in the world; in some ways they are more powerful than heads of government. But that doesn’t mean we can’t be aware of how they should be acting, or that we can’t understand how it would be better for them to do different things in different circumstances.

Business ethicist John Boatright identified three of these circumstances in the ethical issues of deception, churning, and suitability.John Boatright, “Ethical Issues in Financial Services,” in Ethical Theory and Business, ed. Denis Arnold, Tom Beauchamp, and Norman Bowie (Essex: Pearson, 2014) 357–359. We’ll cover these three issues briefly, and then finish the section with a discussion on insider trading.

DeceptionThe way that the sellers of financial products do or don’t disclose information to clients. refers to the way that the sellers of financial products do or don’t disclose information to clients. Financial advisers are in fact salespeople, who make a living by selling products to consumers, usually in the form of insurance, loans, or investments. No such product is without risk, and many of them require a potential buyer to have specialized knowledge to understand how they actually work. The crucial question about deception therefore becomes what information a salesperson is ethically obligated to share with a potential customer before making a sale.

Many pieces of information are relevant to making a decision about an investment or loan, such as the projected return, the level of risk, or the interest rate. Take health insurance as another example—until the beginning of 2022, it was legal and even expected for health insurance brokers and agents to not disclose their commissions to clients. Even though commissions are how brokers and agents get paid, and even though their commissions are built into the premiums, they did not need to inform clients of these fees nor make it clear that the clients would be responsible for them. This changed with the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2021, which required these salespeople to make their commissions apparent.

This law seems like a good change, as information about fee structures and payments is relevant to most people. We might ask, however—if avoiding deception in this way is an ethical thing to do, why wasn’t the industry doing it before? Why did it take a law to institute this particular ethical practice? The most obvious response is that it is in the interest of the salespeople to withhold information about what they sell. This motivation is even stronger in an industry where larger products, such as more expansive insurance policies, generate more commissions.

We’ve covered various aspects of deception in and , and the points we made there apply to the ethics of finance as well. To take a more principled stance, we can ask ourselves the following question about deception: If we had insider knowledge about what a product could actually do and how it was produced, but we had no connection to the company producing it and no financial stake in the product’s success, would we believe that the information about it that is available to consumers is sufficient to make a well-informed choice? If the answer is yes, we’ve gone a long way toward not deceiving; if no, then we may need to think more about how to better disclose what is really going on.

section.title: Churning
section.para: The second of Boatright’s issues is churning. ChurningThe very frequent buying and selling of stocks on behalf of a client in order to generate more commissions. refers to the very frequent buying and selling of stocks on behalf of a client in order to generate more commissions. Many stock brokers and other financial representatives are compensated on commissions from each sale, and so the more sales they make, the greater compensation they’ll receive. This gives them an incentive to trade in a way that may not meet a client’s investment goals—and even when the trades are in line with what a client wants, the excessive number still piles on the fees.

Because stock trading is such a specialized profession, it’s difficult to know whether a given set of trades constitutes churning. It may be that a professional used her best judgment, with the client’s best interests in mind, in making the trades; it would be hard for anyone on the outside to prove her wrong. The ethical issue of churning, then, boils down to trust and whether a broker is respecting her fiduciary duty to a client. For many clients at least, a smaller number of trades would be optimal, in part because it would mean paying fewer commissions to the broker. Therefore the way of handling this ethical issue lies almost entirely in the hands of the finance professionals, as they balance many pressures in deciding how to fulfill their duty.

section.title: Suitability
section.para: The third ethical issue Boatright mentions is suitability. SuitabilityHow appropriate a financial product is for a certain client. refers to how appropriate a financial product is for a certain client. Younger clients with young families, for example, might prefer slow-growth investments with lower risk; wealthier clients in the mood to gamble, however, might prefer something with a greater potential for both growth and loss. Clients like these and others require financial products that are suitable to their needs, and once again, the judgment of what is “suitable” lies in the hands of the finance professionals. Like churning, the ethical issue of suitability must be understood on the basis of that judgment as well as the professionals’ fiduciary duties to clients.

Deception, churning, and suitability are ethical issues that arise in the close relationship between a financial adviser and a customer. On the other hand, finance ethics includes a broader and more public ethical issue: insider trading. At its most basic, insider tradingThe buying and selling of stocks or other securities on the basis of “insider” information, or information that isn’t otherwise available to most customers. is the buying and selling of stocks or other securities on the basis of “insider” information, or information that isn’t otherwise available to most customers. We’ll give an example below, but as you read, you should ask yourself: is insider trading unethical? If it is, why, or on what basis? If not, why not?

A classic example of insider trading is the case that sent lifestyle guru Martha Stewart to prison in 2004. A broker named Peter Bacanovic managed Stewart’s investment portfolio, and Bacanovic had received information about a company called ImClone. ImClone was preparing to market a new cancer drug, Erbitux, but found out that the Food and Drug Administration in the United States would not be approving the drug. The CEO of ImClone, Samuel Waksal, shared this information with various acquaintances, including Bacanovic. Bacanovic then sold Stewart’s shares in the company, netting her a modest profit and, eventually, five months of house arrest.

Another classic case of insider trading is SEC v. Texas Gulf Sulphur Co., a court case from 1967–1968. Texas Gulf Sulphur had discovered mineral deposits in exploratory digs in Canada, and on the basis of that information, a number of employees bought stock or received stock options without sharing their reasons for doing so. They were found guilty of insider trading.
One of the primary laws governing insider trading is SEC Rule 10b-5, on the “Employment of Manipulative and Deceptive Practices.” The rule states,

blockquote.para: It shall be unlawful for any person, directly or indirectly, by the use of any means or instrumentality of interstate commerce, or of the mails or of any facility of any national securities exchange,

(a) To employ any device, scheme, or artifice to defraud,
(b) To make any untrue statement of a material fact or to omit to state a material fact necessary in order to make the statements made, in the light of the circumstances under which they were made, not misleading, or
(c) To engage in any act, practice, or course of business which operates or would operate as a fraud or deceit upon any person,
in connection with the purchase or sale of any security.17 C.F.R. § 240.10b-5 2023.

section.para: This rule requires a great deal of interpretation in order to apply it to particular cases; much of the debate in Texas Sulphur, for example, concerns what does or doesn’t count as a “material fact.” In part to help with these issues of interpretation, the SEC adopted Rule 10b5-1 in 2000, which clarifies earlier rules and adds additional information.

The question for us, though, is an ethical one: is insider trading ethical? If it is ethical, it might follow that it ought to be legal as well. What, then, are the arguments for and against the ethics of insider trading?

There are two primary arguments in favor of insider trading as an ethical practice. The first is that insider trading is merely an expression of an overall laissez-faire free-market approach to financial regulation.
