If this approach to regulation is ethical, then insider trading will likely be ethical as well, since it’s no more nor less than one’s ability to use one’s best information to make decisions. The second argument in favor of insider trading as ethical is that it is difficult to identify who, if anyone, is actually harmed by insider trading. In addition, even if there is some harm, the harm will by nature be limited, since insider trading is by definition done by a small number of people. On this way of thinking, insider trading isn’t different from many other financial practices, and could therefore be considered ethical.

On the other hand, there are several powerful arguments that conclude that insider trading is unethical. In a 1990 paper, for example, Jennifer Moore argued that insider trading is unethical because it “undermines the fiduciary relationship that lies at the heart of American business.”Jennifer Moore, “What Is Really Unethical about Insider Trading?” Journal of Business Ethics 9, no. 3, (March 1990), 171–182, . Moore’s claim is that the fiduciary relationship—in which one person acts with an inviolable duty to uphold the best interests of another—is fundamental to business in America and thus to the finance industry. Insider trading necessarily involves a breach of this duty, where those supposed to watch over those best interests turn against them in favor of their own interests. For this reason, according to Moore, insider trading is unethical.

Alan Strudler adds three more arguments to Moore’s in favor of the unethical status of insider trading.Alan Strudler, “Insider Trading: A Moral Problem,” Philosophy and Public Policy Quarterly 29 no. 3–4 (Summer–Fall, 2009): 12–16. First, Strudler claims that, although identifying specific individuals harmed by insider trading may be difficult, the practice also causes harms at the level of society—by making it impossible to “attain optimal social welfare or social good.” In particular, Strudler believes that insider trading may deter investments. It’s also possible, however, that insider trading creates some social goods, and so it isn’t clear how far the harm argument will get us.

Strudler’s second argument is that insider trading involves deception, and is unethical on those grounds. We discussed this issue earlier in this section, when we considered deception as an ethical problem in finance. The same points we made there could apply here as well.

Strudler’s third argument is that insider trading is unfair. Those who trade on information that isn’t publicly available aren’t playing on the same field as everyone else; a free-market approach to economic regulation assumes that everyone plays on the same field, and so insider trading could be unethical for this reason. Looking at insider trading from the outside, we as members of a society would not sanction agreements that allowed inequalities like disparate levels of information in buying and selling. Therefore, insider trading is unethical.
Strudler finishes his presentation of these arguments with these remarks:

blockquote.para: The problem with allowing insider trading, then, is not simply in the harm it might cause, but in the exploitative relations it fosters. We as a society have no more reason to facilitate the exploitative relations in insider trading than to facilitate exploitative labor practices, even if some people are willing to gamble that they will prosper under exploitation. Insider trading is wrong as a matter of principle.Strudler, “Insider Trading,” 16.

section.para: In light of what you’ve read, what is your view? Do you believe insider trading is unethical? (Remember the difference between what is illegal and what is unethical.) If you do, why is it unethical? If not, why not? What laws should govern the use of private information in trading stocks and securities?

sidebar.title: Case Study: Insider Trading
sidebar.para: Ryan Kerrigan is a janitor who works the night shift at a large office park. Normally he works in building D, but as a favor to a coworker, he works a night in building B. One of the occupants of building B is a tech company named Megafone. Megafone is developing products for enhancing cellular phone service in outlying areas of the United States.

While cleaning Megafone’s office, Ryan comes across a pile of loose papers in a conference room. He puts them into a bin for recycling, but something catches his attention and he starts reading them. The papers are records of a meeting Megafone recently held with investors who wish to receive the first opportunity to buy Megafone stocks when the company goes public. Ryan also learns that Megafone’s technology has been wildly successful in secret product testing in remote areas in Montana and Wyoming, and the investors believe that the company’s products will soon be adopted by every major cellular carrier in the western world.
Later that night, Ryan dumps the papers in the recycling bin, thinking about what he’s read. Ryan never intended to find information about Megafone.

listitem.para: As a janitor in an office park, does Ryan have a fiduciary duty to anyone? Why or why not?
Do scattered office memos and notes constitute “public information”? Do they constitute “material facts” on which someone could make an investment decision?
In buying Megafone stock when it goes public some weeks later, has Ryan done something unethical? Why or why not?
Before Megafone goes public, Ryan shares what he learned about the company with friends, one of whom is a banker. In sharing this information, has Ryan done something unethical? Why or why not?

section.title: The Ethics of Complicity
section.para: In the previous two sections of this chapter we discussed accounting ethics and finance ethics. Both accounting and finance are professions in themselves, and while we only covered some of the more prominent ethical issues, we were able to get a grasp on the sorts of challenges that professionals in those fields face.

An important thing to note about both accounting and finance is that the professionals carrying out those roles in an organization may be doing unethical things without fully realizing what they are doing. This could also be true of other topics we’ve discussed in other chapters, like false advertising or informed consent in buying, but the issue is particularly prominent in accounting and finance. Lower-level accountants or finance managers may be instructed by managers or executives to perform their jobs in certain ways—but if those ways are illegal or unethical, then the lower-level employees become responsible for what has happened, at least indirectly.
How should we think about and handle the ethics of such cases? This question leads us to discuss the ethics of complicity.

Complicity is the term we use to describe a situation where one person is involved in something illegal or unethical. To be complicitTo be one of the people perpetrating a crime or a violation of some ethical standard. is to be one of the people perpetrating a crime or a violation of some ethical standard. In most cases, “complicity” and “complicit” suggest that the person spoken of is not the mastermind or primary cause of the unethical action, but instead is playing only a minor or outside role.

For example, in previous sections we read about how lower-level accountants at Arthur Andersen faced pressure to look the other way on accounting issues with Enron and WorldCom. Because of conflicts of interest and consulting relationships between the accounting firm and its clients, some accountants may have noticed oddities or other irregularities that, in other cases, they would have investigated in more detail. But they didn’t—and this inaction made them complicit in illegal and unethical activities.

Complicity usually involves some level of knowledge of the illegal or unethical action, but not always. It’s possible to be complicit without realizing it or knowing that something unethical is happening in the first place.

It’s in being complicit that we find the greatest potential ethical risk for most accountants and finance professionals. The stories of Enron and WorldCom are famous and appear in almost every textbook on business ethics because they involve such massive failures of ethical standards. Most business professionals, however, will never work in positions where their decisions can affect billions of dollars in capital, nor will they ever have the opportunity to mastermind an accounting fraud that tanks the stock market when discovered. At one time or another, however, many accounts and other finance workers will face a situation in which they begin to have reason to believe that something unethical is taking place. It may be impossible for them to know for sure—if they don’t have access to the right records, for example, or if they don’t know enough about what others are doing. But the ethics of those situations will require them to understand principles and make choices about their level of complicity in what they suspect is going on.

Along with Deloittte, EY, and KPMG, PricewaterhouseCoopers is one of the Big Four accounting firms that handles accounting, financial, and other professional services for many large companies around the world. Their code of conduct“Living Our Purpose and Values: PWC’s Code of Conduct,” PwC, April 2021, . speaks to the issue of complicity and its relationship to the ethical issues we’ve been discussing.
The introduction acknowledges the significant challenges that employees face in their industry:

blockquote.para: The trust that our clients, communities and our people place in PwC, and our high standards of ethical behaviour, are fundamental to everything we do. As we go about our work it’s important we have a frame of reference for the decisions we make every day. Our Code of Conduct (Code) can guide us, no matter where we are or what we do. It’s how we do business.

The Code reinforces the importance of conducting business within the framework of professional standards, laws, and regulations, together with our own policies, values, and standards, even as we work across borders. It outlines the values and behaviours that define how we do business. It holds us accountable to be open-minded and responsive and to give our best.

section.para: Then the Code deals with the issue of complicity:

blockquote.para: If we come across a situation that is inconsistent with our Code, we speak up. We value the courage it takes to raise concerns. Remember, investigations into allegations of misconduct are handled discretely and with sensitivity and we do not tolerate retaliation. When in doubt or facing a dilemma, we ask for help. There are local and network resources available to help us.

section.para: This passage suggests that the ethical principle operating in questions of complicity is very simple: those who suspect something ought to speak up about it. Speaking about their suspicions is their ethical duty, and this ethical principle urges them to do so. Of course, this is made most realistic when a company takes suspicions seriously and doesn’t fire or otherwise take revenge on employees who actually speak up. Part of the company’s ethical responsibility is to create that environment, so that individual employees can then fulfill their ethical responsibility not to be complicit in fraud or other unethical practices.

In a section at the beginning of the code, this focus continues, and for good reason—for lower-level employees in accounting and finance, the most significant ethical problem they will likely face is whether to share information when they suspect wrongdoing. If they don’t, they risk becoming complicit, even if they understand that the behavior is unethical or illegal.
We’ll finish by quoting the Speak Up section of the PwC code, as it’s a powerful statement of the ideal ethical situation in accounting and finance:

blockquote.para: Speak Up

Speaking up is crucial to our culture and our long term results—it is a living example of our values. Speaking up when something doesn’t seem right demonstrates our integrity and that we have the courage to do the right thing. Speaking up helps to prevent mistakes and misconduct and foster innovation. Speaking up shows that we care about each other and our business. And speaking up to get things right or keep them on track helps us live up to our commitment to deliver high quality outcomes.
Something doesn’t seem right? Facing a dilemma? Have a question that leads to more difficult questions? Need advice?
Consult. Pick up the phone. Send an email. Set up a meeting. Speak up.

Each of us, no matter what our level or role, is empowered to speak up when dealing with behaviour or facing a situation that doesn’t seem right. Each of us has a responsibility to report and express our concerns, and to do so fairly, honestly, and professionally.
Do not ignore it. Do not stay silent.

Collaboration means we consult with our colleagues in matters large and small, and we know that our concerns are heard and addressed in an open and professional manner, including that an investigation will take place when warranted. We consult with our supervisors, coaches, partners/principals, ethics teams, Risk and Quality teams, Office of the General Counsel, Human Capital representatives, or others at PwC, particularly those in reporting lines. These people are responsible for addressing or escalating as necessary the issues brought to their attention. We raise issues using formal and informal methods as appropriate: in person, over the phone, and/or electronically.

We protect against retaliation. In being true to the values of integrity and care—if you report a concern, it will be handled with appropriate confidentiality and discussed with others only as needed or advisable under the circumstances. Exercising professional scepticism, applying common sense, and knowing and applying the Code as well as the local supplementary guidance, will help each of us know when to speak up through whichever channel we are most comfortable.

sidebar.title: Case Study: Failure to Disclose Investments
sidebar.para: In February 2023, the Securities and Exchange Commission of the United States (SEC) announced charges against Ensign Peak Advisers, a non-profit investment manager operated by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, “SEC Charges The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and Its Investment Management Company for Disclosure Failures and Misstated Filings,” press release no. 2023-35, February 21, 2023, . The SEC claimed that Ensign Peak, on behalf of the church, failed to adequately disclose the content and extent of its investment portfolio, thereby misleading investors and the market about its holdings.

More specifically, the SEC found that Ensign Peak had helped to set up shell companies which received assets from the church’s portfolio. As part of this arrangement, investment managers ought to have disclosed the relationship between Ensign Peak and those companies, but chose not to do so from 1997 until 2019.

According to the SEC, the church’s motivation in not disclosing their relationship to the shell companies was to obscure the size of its large portfolio, which by 2018 had grown to around $32 billion. The SEC alleged that the church feared it would receive negative public attention for having a portfolio so large and so decided to make it seem as though it was smaller by funneling the money to other groups and not reporting the portfolio as a whole. Gurbir Grewal, a director in the SEC, said that “We allege that the LDS Church’s investment manager, with the Church’s knowledge, went to great lengths to avoid disclosing the Church’s investments, depriving the Commission and the investing public of accurate market information.”

In a press release near the end of February 2023, the church stated, “Since 2000, Ensign Peak received and relied upon legal counsel regarding how to comply with its reporting obligations while attempting to maintain the privacy of the portfolio. As a result, Ensign Peak established separate companies (LLCs) that each filed Forms 13F instead of a single aggregated filing. Ensign Peak and the Church believe that all securities required to be reported were included in the filings by the separate companies.” They also reported, “We reached resolution with the SEC. We affirm our commitment to comply with the law, regret mistakes made, and now consider this matter closed.”

listitem.para: In a case such as this one, how might ethical principles go beyond what is required by the law, or by SEC regulations?
Do you believe the LDS church did anything unethical in their approach to regulatory filings? Why or why not?
Who, if anyone, ought to be punished or otherwise held responsible for these violations?
Should companies or other entities have a right to keep their investment portfolios private?

Suppose an organization believes that the quantity of its assets will attract negative public attention. If that organization then deliberately, but legally, misleads the public about what it owns, has the organization done anything unethical? Why or why not?

section.title: The Ethics of White-Collar Punishment
section.para: Richard Fuld was the last CEO of Lehman Brothers, a bank and financial services provider. Under his supervision, the company began its involvement in using subprime mortgages as bonds to sell to investors. This decision, among others, made a major contribution to the 2008 financial meltdown in the US economy.
Fuld was never charged with a crime, and made over $400 million during his time at Lehman Brothers.

Standard & Poor’s president Kathleen Corbet ran the organization at a time that it received payments from companies even though it was supposed to be rating the riskiness of their investment products. After she left, S&P had to pay a $1.5 billion fine as part of the meltdown.
Corbet was never charged with a crime.

Stan O’Neal was in charge of Merrill Lynch, and during his tenure the bank bought many subprime mortgage bonds. Although he left the company in 2007, Merrill Lynch eventually went into financial troubles in 2008.
O’Neal received a $160 million retirement payout when he left the bank, and was never charged with a crime.

The 2008 financial crisis—brought on in large part due to the actions of people like Fuld, Corbet, and O’Neal—caused the largest recession in the United States since World War II. Eight million homes were foreclosed on; more than eight million jobs were lost; the stock market took enormous hits, and trillions of dollars of household wealth were lost.Caleb Silver, “Lessons from the 2008 Financial Crisis,” Investopedia, September 12, 2023, .
Yet none of the people responsible ever went to prison, and in fact many received golden parachutes when they left their companies and still operate financial service firms today.

These stories would fit into many discussions of business ethics, for we could analyze the many decisions which led to the crisis in order to discover what ethical principles might have better governed those choices. Rather than take on that task here, though, we’ll focus instead on an ethical issue that sometimes goes unnoticed: the fact that none of the people involved were ever held responsible for what they did.
Is that an ethical, fair outcome? If it isn’t ethical or fair that no one was ever punished, what could we do to change things?

Let’s deal with the first question first. What ethical principles should guide us in holding people responsible for their actions? Here we face a tension between two things we’ve seen many times so far in this book: what is legal, and what is ethical. Not all or even many of the actions taken by corporate leaders in the lead-up to the 2008 crisis were illegal. However, given the risks involved, there is no question that many of them were unethical, and also led to massive damage, both economic and otherwise.
However, the legal system in the United States is not designed to hold people accountable for what is unethical; it’s only designed to hold them accountable for what is illegal.

On the one hand we should be glad that this is true. The fact that laws must be passed by legislators and then codified with criteria of application is a good thing; part of the rule of law is that we can only be held responsible for laws that were actually made through legal processes.

On the other hand, the current system also allows for the situations described at the beginning of this section: large-scale risky and unethical behaviors that did incalculable damage to individuals and the economy as a whole, and yet there is literally nothing that regular people can do to change it. In addition, the very people who we want to hold accountable are, in some cases, the ones lobbying Congress to create the laws that they will then be expected to follow. Can we really believe that they will create laws that go against their own future interests, or the interests of their companies or business associates? To believe that would be to go against many decades of observations on how the US economy is regulated.

The problem with white-collar punishment gets even worse when we compare it to other sorts of crimes. For example, arson, or the deliberate burning of property, is a crime with potentially serious consequences for human life. But someone can also be charged with arson even though no one is physically harmed in the fire. While sentencing guidelines vary by state and the details of each crime, it is unusual for those convicted of arson to receive a sentence of less than a few years in prison.Joseph Fawbush, “How Much Time Will I Serve for Arsen?” LawInfo, accessed October 11, 2023, . Thus, between unethical white-collar behaviors and arson, we see an enormous discrepancy in both our ability to hold perpetrators accountable and our ability to charge them with crimes.

The immediate explanation for this discrepancy is that unethical white-collar behaviors are not illegal, while arson is. But this is exactly the point. If unethical white-collar behaviors cause such massive damage—and there is no question that some of them cause damage far more serious than the burning of a building—then those behaviors ought to be illegal, exactly so we can hold people responsible for them. Ethical principles demand that we hold people accountable for their behavior, but we cannot effectively do so without meaningful legal regulation. When there are no laws, ethical principles have no teeth.

Our strategy in this book has been to taken a practical approach to business ethics. This means that we’re looking to apply what we learn and to work with principles that we can actually use. As we’ve seen, large-scale applications and changes driven by what we’ve covered are not possible for a single person to carry out; in fact, given the way the economy and the government work in the United States, large-scale changes of the ethical landscape for businesses may not even be possible.

None of this changes the fact, though, that we make our own choices about what is ethical, and hold ourselves to ethical standards of our choosing. We are ultimately the only business ethicists that matter, since we’re driving our choices and careers in the direction that we choose.

sidebar.title: Case Study: Regulations for Finance Industries
sidebar.para: Suppose you are a lawmaker who is working on a committee with other lawmakers to redesign regulations for the accounting and finance industries. Your recommendations will become the backbone for a new set of rules that citizens and the government hope will lead to more ethical and accountable behavior in these fields.
For the following issues, what ethical principles would be most fundamental to your new regulations, and why?

listitem.para: Conflicts of interest between accounting firms and clients
Conflicts of interest between lobbyists and government regulators
Regulations governing the sale of risky investment products
Punishment of those who are complicit in financial crimes
Government bailouts

chapter.title: Business, the Law, and Political Influence

section.title: Introduction to Business, the Law, and Political Influence

listitem.para: Identify the ethical aspects of the relationship between business and the law.
Be able to apply the difference between what is ethical and what is legal in analyzing how businesses interact with the government.

section.title: Corporate Lobbying and Political Donation
section.para: While many of the issues we’ve discussed in this book involve not only business but society as well, this chapter will deal with the relationship between business and society in particular. Our focus will be on the relationship between business and the law—lawmakers, the government, and the courts.

Let’s begin by talking about lobbying. LobbyingCommunicating directly or soliciting others to communicate with any public servant with the purpose of influencing legislative action or administrative action. , as defined in the Arkansas state code, “means communicating directly or soliciting others to communicate with any public servant with the purpose of influencing legislative action or administrative action.”Communicating directly or soliciting others to communicate with any public servant with the purpose of influencing legislative action or administrative action. A “lobbyist” is one who lobbies, or more specifically, a person who receives pay in exchange for trying to influence legislators and other public servants.

Most states define a “lobbyist” as someone whose job it is to influence lawmakers. The idea that lobbyists receive pay for their work is important because we would not consider an ordinary citizen speaking to a state or federal legislator as a lobbyist. California, for example, defines a lobbyist as “any individual who receives $2,000 or more in economic consideration in a calendar month, other than reimbursement for reasonable travel expenses, or whose principal duties as an employee are, to communicate directly or through his or her agents with any elective state official, agency official, or legislative official for the purpose of influencing legislative or administrative action.”Cal. Gov. Code § 82039.

Less formally, then, lobbyists are people who try to influence lawmakers in a certain direction. It’s most common for lobbyists to be employed either by large corporations or by industry organizations, in order to advocate for laws that would benefit either the corporation paying them or the industry as a whole. In 2022, one estimate of money spent on lobbying by different industries looked as follows:“Industries,” OpenSecrets, accessed May 30, 2023, .

In other words, in 2022, the pharmaceutical and health industry spent $375 million on lobbying—that’s money spent on paying lobbyists and on working with politicians and others in government. The electronics industry spent over two hundred million dollars. In total, these five industries, the highest-spending industries on lobbying in 2022, shelled out more than one billion dollars. Nine other industries spent more than one hundred million dollars in 2022 alone.

What does all that money go to? Some of it goes to pay the lobbyists for their work, of course. But a large portion goes to the politicians themselves. To be clear, the channels have to be indirect—direct donations from corporations to legislators are illegal. But there are so many loopholes that the law has virtually no effect here.

The most common way of paying lawmakers for influence is to organize a fundraiser. While corporations cannot donate directly, they can hire lobbyists, who then organize events and raise money by selling spots at a fancy dinner or a meet-and-greet with an election candidate. Then, all the money raised by means of the lobbyists and the fundraiser goes to the lawmaker. The outcome is the same—a corporation has engineered a transfer of funds that they control to funds that the politician controls. But because this method is technically legal, no laws have been broken.

For a look at the results, here are the top five recipients of lobbyist contributions among members of Congress in 2022, along with the amounts they received.“Top Recipients of Contributions from Lobbyists, 2022 Cycle,” OpenSecrets, accessed October 26, 2023, .

One of the most important ethical questions surrounding lobbying, then, is whether it ought to happen in the first place. The fundraiser method and other roundabout ways of giving money to politicians allow wealthy companies to have a powerful influence in the way laws are written and implemented in the United States. Should companies be able to have that say? Is it ethical for them to have such a powerful influence?

On the one hand, the immediate answer seems to be, what’s the problem? The United States is a democracy, after all, and everyone, both citizens and groups, are free to express opinions about whatever they would like. We might see lobbyist donations and other tactics simply as ways of expressing those opinions and communicating to politicians the issues that are important to a company or group.

On the other hand, when we see the actual effect this lobbying has, we might see things differently. According to one study, between 2007 and 2012, 200 of the most lobbyist-active corporations spent nearly six billion dollars on lobbying and campaign contributions. In return, however, they received over four trillion dollars in federal business, contracts, and other forms of financial support.Bill Allison and Sarah Harkins, “Fixed Fortunes: Biggest Corporate Political Interests Spend Billions, Get Trillions,” Sunlight Foundation, November 17, 2014, .

Perhaps if it were possible for corporations to donate to politicians without unduly influencing their views or actions, then lobbying and corporate donations wouldn’t be unethical. If their voice counted for as much as everyone else’s voice, then regardless of the company’s wealth, lobbying might not be that bad. It wouldn’t have to lead to the kind of outsize influence we see corporations having on government.

This, at least, was the thought behind the reasoning in the Supreme Court case Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, a landmark case argued in 2009 and decided in 2010. Citizens United was a political action group who, among other things, challenged a federal law restricting large campaign contributions. They argued that the law violated the First Amendment rights of corporations. In a 5–4 decision, the Supreme Court agreed and removed campaign contribution limits funded by corporate interests.

In defense of the prior restrictions, the government had argued that “corporate political speech can be banned to prevent corruption or its appearance.” The Court ruled, in contrast, that “independent expenditures, including those made by corporations, do not give rise to corruption or the appearance of corruption. That speakers may have influence over or access to elected officials does not mean that those officials are corrupt. And the appearance of influence or access will not cause the electorate to lose faith in this democracy.”558 U.S. 310, (2010).

Though many will find it difficult to share the Court’s hope, whether their prediction turns out true remains to be seen. It would be difficult to know whether the Citizens United decision had any impact on public faith in democracy—according to most measures of trust in government, those who belong to the party controlling the presidency tend to have higher trust while those in the opposite party have lower trust, regardless of party affiliation.“Public Trust in Government: 1958–2023,” Pew Research Center, September 19, 2023, .

One thing that has already been seen is the effect the Supreme Court’s 2010 decision has had on political donations, as corporate campaign spending rose nearly 500% in some areas between 2008 and 2016, a window that included the Citizens United decision.Karl Evers-Hillstrom, “More Money, Less Transparency: A Decade under Citizens United,” January 14, 2020, . In 2020, more than one billion dollars in “dark money”—money whose source isn’t clear because the donations come from nondescript political organizations or shell companies—was spent on election funding.Anna Massoglia and Karl Evers-Hillstrom, “ ‘Dark Money’ Topped $1 Billion in 2020, Largely Boosting Democrats,” Open Secrets, March 17, 2021, .

To what extent are these contributions ethical? We must be careful here, as elsewhere, to distinguish what is legal from what is ethical. Yes, corporate campaign contributions are legal. That fact says absolutely nothing about whether they are ethical; that they are legal just means that certain lawmakers were willing to allow them to exist and certain judges voted to keep the laws. Whether they are ethical is another matter entirely, one for which we could have serious doubts.

Perhaps the most obvious ethical problem with corporate lobbying and political donation is that it gives the most powerful voices to companies, and in particular, to wealthy companies. It’s true that individual citizens must still vote to elect someone, but it takes an enormous amount of money to win a federal-level election. Receiving corporate donations may actually be a practical necessity for candidates, because they could not generate enough money any other way. But why should we believe that the money those candidates receive has no effect on them after they are elected? Do we have any real reason to side with the Supreme Court’s view of possible corruption? Note here that our political party affiliation is irrelevant. In both parties, the ones with the most powerful voices are the wealthy, regardless of politics or position. What incentive do politicians have to listen to normal citizens, when those citizens can’t provide the politicians with any of the resources they need to get elected? United States senators have six years in office, and American voters have short memories—something that happens near the beginning of a senator’s tenure may be so far away by their next election that voters no longer either know nor care. But companies care, since senators set the rules in which companies operate. Is it ethical for business organizations to be able to have the influence they already have on senators and other representatives?

Another ethical issue is the role of business in society more broadly. What should businesses be able to do to protect their interests? It seems reasonable for them to advocate for changes that will benefit them, their employees, or their industry. But what restrictions should they have to abide by as they do so? Is it ethical for them to spend billions when they receive trillions in return? Is it ethical for government representatives to have such close ties to businesses when they are supposed to represent all their constituents equally?

There is probably room for a variety of positions on these issues. What we cannot disagree about is the power of corporate lobbying and other kinds of corporate-financed political influence. The amount of money American companies spend on lobbying will likely continue to increase, and the associated ethical issues will likely become more stark. They wouldn’t be spending so much money on lobbying if it weren’t working.
We’ll see a final ethical issue regarding lobbying in the next case study.

sidebar.title: Case Study: Lobbying
sidebar.para: One of the challenges politicians face is that they must know a great deal about a great many different topics. After all, they are tasked with writing laws about every conceivable topic, from environmental policy to cybercrime to divorce to everything else.

It is here we see another ethical issue stemming from corporate lobbying: the fact that political influence allows companies to write the laws that will govern how they must act—and not just figuratively.

Corporations would only spend money on lobbying if it worked, and one of the ways it works is by giving those companies or their representatives access to the law-making process. There is a somewhat innocent angle to this access. Industry representatives probably know a lot more about the issues relating to the laws than politicians do, since the operation of companies within that industry relies on expert knowledge. With access to lawmakers who are drafting legislation, they could provide some of this expert knowledge, which may be more than a minor contribution.

But sometimes access is more than just access. In 2013, for example, lobbyists from the banking industry helped write legislation that amended prior laws restricting certain kinds of securities trading. In some cases the corporate- and lobbyist-approved language was used without alteration, according to the New York Times:

blockquote.para: One bill that sailed through the House Financial Services Committee this month—over the objections of the Treasury Department—was essentially Citigroup’s, according to e-mails reviewed by The New York Times. The bill would exempt broad swathes of trades from new regulation.

In a sign of Wall Street’s resurgent influence in Washington, Citigroup’s recommendations were reflected in more than 70 lines of the House committee’s 85-line bill. Two crucial paragraphs, prepared by Citigroup in conjunction with other Wall Street banks, were copied nearly word for word. (Lawmakers changed two words to make them plural.)Eric Lipton and Ben Protess, “Banks’ Lobbyists Help in Drafting Financial Bills,” New York Times, May 32, 2013, .

sidebar.para: Thus, in this case as in others, the corporations that will be required to obey the laws are literally writing those laws.

listitem.para: Should anyone other than elected lawmakers be allowed to write the actual laws? Why or why not?

If others besides elected representatives were allowed to write laws, should companies or representatives of companies be allowed to do so, when they would be writing legislation that would apply to their own operations?

According to the New York Times article quoted above, “Industry officials acknowledged that they played a role in drafting the legislation, but argued that the practice was common in Washington.” Does this make the situation better or worse? Why?

section.title: Government Assistance to Businesses
section.para: In and in various other places in this book, we discussed the ethics of regulations imposed on businesses by governments. There is much more to say about this topic, however, for the relationship between government and business has many facets, each with its own ethical dimension. Here we will take up one of those facets in exploring the issue of government financial assistance to businesses and the ethical implications of giving taxpayer money to for-profit companies.

In relation to business, the term “government assistance” could mean many different things, from tax breaks to farmer subsidies to payments made during the COVID-19 pandemic. But one of the most prominent and ethically controversial forms of government assistance is the “bailout,” or large payments made by the government to distressed companies. Ostensibly these payments are made in order to avoid widespread economic catastrophe.

The most significant examples of government bailouts took place during the recession of 2008. Due to poor investment decisions as well as many other factors—we discussed some of them in an earlier chapter, but understanding the ethics of the recession would take a book on its own—many banks, both large and small, found themselves in precarious financial positions. In order to prop up the banks and strengthen their position to lend and manage large amounts of capital, the United States government began bailing them out by lending large sums of money under an initiative called TARP, or “Troubled Assets Relief Program.” The money began to be distributed as part of TARP in October 2008. Over the next year and two months, the government would distribute over $200 billion to hundreds of banks, with the largest payments ($25 billion each) going to Wells Fargo, Citigroup, and JPMorgan Chase; some others, such as Bank of America, Morgan Stanley, and Goldman Sachs, received at least $10 billion each.

There are many ethical questions that we can and ought to ask about these bailout payments, and we’ll discuss some of them below. But first we must ask, were the bailouts effective in avoiding greater damage to a US economy that had already been racked by a recession? Unfortunately, it is very difficult to answer this question either way. For one, we don’t have a good comparison, or another time in recent history when the government considered bailing out large banks but chose not to. If we had such a large-scale event, we’d be able to compare what happened when the government didn’t bail banks out versus when they did, and perhaps we’d be able to draw some conclusions about whether the move was effective. But we don’t have this comparison.

Another reason that it’s difficult to know whether the bailouts were effective is simply the inexact nature of economic analysis. Physics is the gold standard for the sciences in being able to make exact, quantitative predictions about what we can expect to happen in the future, but economics cannot do this. The phenomena that economics studies are simply too complex to allow for consistently reliable predictions. Both dire and rosy forecasts of future large-scale economic activity often turn out to be false. As such, while the government and many economists believed that the bailouts were necessary to avert further damage, we must admit that those predictions were only as exact as the science of economics allows—which is to say, not very exact. For this reason it is difficult to tell whether the bailouts accomplished their goals.

The uncertainty we face in our knowledge on these issues complicates the way we analyze them ethically. If the bailouts truly were the only way to stop a total economic collapse, then there would be strong reasons, particularly from a utilitarian perspective, to make them happen. As we review some ethical points below, we must keep our uncertainty on these matters in mind.

The most pressing ethical question about the bailouts is also the overarching one: is it ethical for the government to bail out for-profit public companies at all? From a perspective of American mostly-hands-off capitalism, bailouts are unusual—after all, shouldn’t companies that make poor decisions just fail? Why should the government step in to save them when they’ve shown that they are no longer viable in a competitive economy? Many small businesses fail all the time, for example, without receiving government assistance. What is the difference here? What could justify such a stark violation of the spirit behind an economic system that usually seeks less government regulation, rather than more?

That last point is worth exploring a little. As we discussed in the previous section, banks and other financial institutions are usually interested in lobbying the government for less regulation, so that they are freer to conduct their business however they want. But giving companies taxpayer money is as much a government interference in business as a law that makes insider trading illegal. What justifies this interference?

In the case of the 2008 bailouts, the answer was the size of the banks. Wells Fargo, Bank of America, Citigroup, and others were so large that their financial health and continued operation were thought to be absolutely integral to the overall economy: lose them, and something really, really bad would happen. This was the justification given at the time, at least, and it seems to be the only one possible, for the term “government bailout” is just a roundabout way of describing a transaction where money from American taxpayers is given to businesses.

The question then becomes, do the banks’ size and their possible essential connection to the overall economy justify giving them the money of regular citizens? It’s tempting to answer with an emphatic “Yes!” or “No!” depending on one’s political or economic views, but we must stress again how uncertain our knowledge is about these situations. If the alternatives were bad enough, the answer would almost certainly be yes. But we just don’t know.

There are other ethical issues involved too. For example, Citigroup, one of the banks receiving bailout money, paid out over $5 billion in employee bonuses in 2008. The bank made these payments despite the company losing over $18 billion overall in that same year. Given the bank’s performance—very, very bad—it is hard to believe that these bonuses represented compensation for effective employees. The bulk of the bonuses went to high-ranking employees, as well, with 738 people receiving at least one million dollars in additional compensation.ABC News, “Bailed-Out Banks Gave Millions in Exec Bonuses, NY AG Report Shows,” July 30, 2009, .

Is it ethical for companies such as Citigroup to give bonuses after receiving taxpayer money? If the bonuses themselves are ethical, what about the amounts? Are there ethical reasons to allow the government to restrict employee compensation programs when the government has played a role in helping a company remain solvent? From an ethical perspective, what should the companies have done with the taxpayer money, anyway?

The 2008–2009 bailouts raise an issue that has come up again and again in this book: the fact that something is a certain way, or is legal according to current laws, does not automatically mean that it is ethical. It is common for business professionals and many others simply to take what happens with big business and large-scale economic decisions as a given, a baseline that forms the background in which they must work and live. And when we treat something as given, or as a fixed feature of the background, we almost never question anything about it; the law of gravity is always in the background of our life on Earth, and who could question that?

But we must remember that, in business ethics, everything is up for ethical analysis—including and even especially those features of the economy that we usually think of as the background. The fact that a business or government did something, the fact that it happened and had an effect, does not mean that it was an ethical thing to do. This idea is obvious when we see starkly unethical behavior like Enron, WorldCom, Napster, and other bad actors. We must make a conscious effort, however, to keep in mind that the very nature of an economy, the very way it is set up from the beginning, is a target that we can and must ethically analyze.

If we don’t analyze these deeper institutions and practices, we make business ethics both boring and useless. We make it boring because we just read and discuss problem cases that no reasonable person could disagree about. But we also make it useless because we stay at a surface level and never produce any results that could really move us to make meaningful changes in how we see the world and how we act.

Business ethics has the power to do so much more than give a superficial look at what is obviously wrong. But in order to make that happen, we ourselves must be willing to go beyond the obviously wrong to see and appreciate the features of business practice that we normally don’t consider from an ethical perspective. That’s where the real meat of business ethics is—but it’s up to us to get there.

sidebar.title: Case Study: Businesses and Gvernment Regulation
sidebar.para: In late 2018 and early 2019, two major airline disasters shone a light on the relationship between businesses and the government, and in particular, on how companies implement the regulation that the government is supposed to enforce.

In October 2018, Lion Air Flight 610 took off in Indonesia but crashed into the Java Sea just 13 minutes after takeoff. All 189 people on board, both passengers and crew, lost their lives. A few months later, in March 2019, Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 departed from Ethiopia with a destination in Kenya, but crashed shortly after takeoff as well. In that crash, 157 people died.

These disasters had a number of things in common, but the most important was that they both involved the Boeing 737 MAX aircraft, a relatively recent addition to Boeing’s lineup of planes. The MAX included a piece of autopilot software called MCAS, short for “Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System.” MCAS played a crucial role in both the Lion Air and Ethiopian Airlines crashes. The pilots of both planes were unfamiliar with how the software functioned, and based on flight recorder data, did not understand why the aircraft were behaving as they did. As a result the pilots were unable to control their planes.

The pilots were unfamiliar with MCAS because it was a new addition to the functioning of the MAX. One of Boeing’s primary selling points for the new aircraft, however, was that pilots trained on older 737 planes would not need additional training to fly the MAX. Additional training would have been expensive and time consuming for companies interested in the aircraft, and buying new planes without needing training was a major advantage. In fact, this was more than just a selling point for Boeing—it was a part of the MAX’s development program that Boeing refused to change. In March 2017, the company’s chief technical pilot, Mark Forkner, wrote the following to colleagues: “I want to stress the importance of holding firm that there will not be any type of simulator training required to transition from 737 NG to MAX. Boeing will not allow that to happen. We’ll go face to face with any regulator who tries to make that a requirement.”Jon Ostrower, “Boeing’s MCAS on the 737 Max May Not Have Been Needed At All,” The Air Current, January 10, 2021, .

Forkner’s comment underscores the unusual relationship between the company and the Federal Aviation Administration, the government agency tasked with regulating and approving aircraft in the United States. For many years prior to the MAX crashes, the FAA had outsourced much of its oversight and regulation for Boeing—to the company itself. In other words, Boeing had been allowed to “self-certify” some of its products and practices by determining on its own, without the government’s involvement, whether it was properly complying with federal law and FAA regulations for aircraft. Boeing therefore did most of the certification of the MCAS software itself, and was primarily responsible for the decision to sell the MAX as a plane that experienced 737 pilots would not need additional training for.

The arrangement Boeing had with the FAA was not unusual. According to later testimony from FAA officials, around the time of the MAX crashes, more than 80 companies helped certify their products by overseeing their own compliance with federal regulations. The acting administrator of the FAA, Daniel Elwell, said that this arrangement was necessary, given the agency’s limited resources. According to his remarks, the FAA would require 10,000 additional employees and an increase of almost two billion dollars to its budget to be solely responsible for overseeing regulation throughout the industry.Sinéad Baker, “FAA Boss Says It Let Boeing Partly Self-Regulate the Software Thought to Be Behind Both Fatal 737 Max Crashes,” Insider, March 28, 2019, .

All MAX aircraft worldwide were grounded after the second crash and remained so for 20 more months. Starting in December 2020 a few began to fly again, and now almost 1000 of them are in active service.

listitem.para: How should a company be held responsible for an event like an airline crash, which involves such significant loss of life? What punishments should it face, and what actions should it have to take?
How, if at all, should individual people be held responsible in a case such as this one?

Is it ethical for companies to self-certify their products and processes? Should it be allowed in a case where the malfunctioning of a product, such as an airplane, could lead to significant loss of life?
What is the proper role of a government regulator in overseeing the development of new products? What are the regulator’s responsibilities, and how should the regulator fulfill them?
To what extent should companies have a say in the regulations that their products will be expected to comply with?

section.title: Business and the Courts
section.para: We’ll finish this chapter with a discussion of business and the court system. Our focus will be on two key Supreme Court cases: Ford Motor Co. v. Montana Eighth Judicial District Court, and Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores. Both cases concern the ethical duties and accountability that businesses have to consumers and employees.

We’ll begin with Ford Motor Co. v. Montana Eighth Judicial District Court. In 2015 Markkaya Jean Gullett, a resident of Superior, Montana, was driving her Ford Explorer on I-90 near Alberton. One of the tires failed and so the vehicle hit the median and rolled into a ditch. According to a state trooper, Gullett was not wearing a seatbelt. As a result of her injuries, she died at the scene.Associated Press, “Officials ID Superior Woman Killed in Alberton Crash,” Great Falls Tribune, My 27, 2015, .

Following her death, representatives of Gullett’s estate filed a lawsuit against Ford, the vehicle’s manufacturer. The lawsuit claimed that Ford was responsible for the tire failure and accused the company of various violations of law, including design defects, a failure-to-warn, and negligence.Ford Motor Co. v. Montana Eighth Jud. Dist. Ct., 141 S. Ct. 1017, (2021).

Ford in turn filed a motion to dismiss the claims. Gullett’s estate had filed the lawsuit in Montana state court, and Ford argued that the state did not have the proper jurisdiction over the company; the company could therefore not be held liable by members of the state, whether or not it had done anything wrong. Ford’s headquarters are in Dearborn, Michigan.

The question of jurisdiction in a case like this one is a complicated legal issue that traces back to the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. This clause states that no one can be “deprived of life, liberty, or property without due process of law.” Ford’s claim about jurisdiction was that allowing a state-level lawsuit to proceed in Montana would violate its own protections as guaranteed by the amendment. None of Ford’s interests within the state were directly or even indirectly responsible for Gullett’s accident—her vehicle had been assembled in Kentucky, transported to a dealership in Washington state, and sold to a resident of Oregon. That resident then sold it to someone else who eventually brought it to Montana.

In short, and without the legal language, Ford’s claim was that they couldn’t be held responsible for the accident, because none of their actual activities within the state had had anything to do with what happened. On the other hand, the lawsuit claimed that Ford as a company was responsible and could be held legally accountable, whether or not its activities within Montana had caused the damage.

In 2021 the Supreme Court ruled that the Montana state court did in fact have jurisdiction over Ford. It granted that none of the company’s interests within the state had caused the accident, but because of Ford’s business activities within the state of Montana, the company could be held liable for what happened with its products inside the state. The Court also said that there was no requirement of “causation,” or direct link, from what Ford had done inside Montana to the accident. All that was required in order for the company to be held liable was that it regularly conducted business in the state through advertising, selling, and servicing its vehicles.

That’s the legal case; now let’s think about it from an ethical perspective. The fundamental ethical issue is whether and how companies can be held responsible for the performance of their products. In this case, a tire failure caused an accident, which caused a death, and the estate of the deceased filed a lawsuit. Ford’s argument was not necessarily that it wasn’t responsible for what happened—the argument was that the state-level court did not have jurisdiction to hold it legally responsible.

The Supreme Court’s decision, therefore, was not about whether Ford’s actions caused the accident. The decision was about whether Ford could even be charged with causing the accident in the first place. To answer the question of whether Ford caused the accident, we’d have to look at things like tires, wheels, the condition of Gullett’s vehicle at the time of the crash, and so on. But the question of whether Ford can be held responsible at all is not something we can answer by looking at cars, because it’s an ethical issue.

To decide the issue, we have to decide whether we believe companies ought to be able to be held responsible in the way that Gullett’s estate was trying to hold Ford responsible. In making this decision we say nothing about whether Ford actually did anything that caused Gullett’s death. We instead are only trying to resolve the fundamental ethical issue of Ford’s accountability.
In light of this case, then, consider the following discussion questions:

listitem.para: Can Ford be held responsible for the performance of its vehicles and their parts? Why or why not?
If Ford can be held responsible, should a state-level court be the entity holding the company responsible? Why or why not?

How much responsibility do courts have to make legal action accessible to the citizens over whom they have jurisdiction? For example, if the Gullet estate had not been able to sue Ford in Montana state court, they would have had to file suit in another state or in federal court. Could that be considered an undue burden on someone who intends to try to hold a company responsible for its actions?

section.para: The second case we’ll discuss here is Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores. After the Affordable Care Act was passed by Congress in 2010, the government could begin requiring businesses to offer certain kinds of coverage in health insurance packages. One of the things they could require was coverage for birth control—because of the ACA, companies were required to provide health care plans that covered certain kinds of approved contraceptive methods.

Hobby Lobby, as a for-profit company, was not exempt from this requirement. The owners of the chain, however, felt that their ability to run their business according to Biblical rules was compromised by the law: since they thought that various birth control methods were immoral, they did not want to offer them in their health insurance. Hobby Lobby sued the government and eventually a court of appeals ruled that the corporation was a “person” for the purposes of evaluating its ability to exercise its religious freedom. The case then went to the Supreme Court.

The Court voted 5–4 in favor of supporting the decision from the court of appeals, thus effectively making the Hobby Lobby corporation a “person” as far as its religious freedom. The company was allowed to reject that part of the Affordable Care Act which otherwise would have required it to provide contraception in its health insurance packages.

We’ve previously discussed the fraught issue of whether corporations ought to be considered “persons,” and that issue is front and center here. Whatever the court’s motivation, the ruling creates a very strong sense in which a corporation is a person—because it operates through people who wish to exercise their religious freedom, a corporation may also be understood as an entity that can exercise religious freedom as well.

From the perspective of business ethics, one of the fundamental questions about this case is whether corporations really ought to be considered “persons” in this strong sense. We can set that one aside, though, for another: should companies, even in the “exercise” of their “freedom of religion,” be allowed to deny employees benefits that they would have had if the companies had different “religious beliefs”?

The choice of whether to use birth control is a personal one, but the choice of whether birth control should be available is one that the Affordable Care Act sought to fix. Hobby Lobby’s exemption from that requirement, however, necessarily forces all of its employees to be exempt as well, in that they are no longer eligible for the benefits of a law that other people are eligible for. By refusing to provide contraceptive coverage in its health insurance packages, Hobby Lobby seems as though it may be compelling its employees to share in its religious views—not in the sense of actually sharing them as authentic beliefs, but in the sense of having to act as though they also didn’t want birth control as part of their health care plan. For regardless of the employees’ desires, the company is not obligated to provide it.

Thus the primary ethical issue here has to do with how a company relates to its employees and what sort of obligations it owes them. Suppose, for example, that an employee of Hobby Lobby had a sincerely-held religious belief that required them to use birth control. That employee would therefore not be able to exercise that freedom. Does the company owe the employee anything in such a case? If the company severed ties with that employee over the issue of contraception, could the employee bring a lawsuit on grounds of religious discrimination?

In answering these hypothetical questions, we ought to resist the immediate response which many people leap to: “Tell the employee to get a different job.” This may in fact be the correct response, but if it is correct, there must be actual reasons in favor of it, and we must be able to identify them. One of the major ethical problems with responses like “If you don’t like it, then don’t work there” is that they assume that the decision-making power ought to be in the hands of corporations, rather than individual employees. Although it’s particularly common in America and other western countries to make this assumption, this is exactly the kind of background view that we should learn to see and question. Again, the right answer to these ethical dilemmas may actually be for the employees to get other jobs. But we must appreciate that that response is itself a deserving target of ethical analysis.

The Hobby Lobby case also opens the door for many other exercises of corporate “freedom of religion.” What might some of those be, and what potential harms could come of them? What about potential benefits?
To wrap up our analysis, consider the following discussion questions:

listitem.para: Should companies be required to subsidize employees’ health insurance? Why or why not?
If companies do subsidize health insurance, who gets to decide what services are covered, and why?
Should a for-profit company be able to opt out or otherwise receive a religious exemption from federal law? Why or why not?
If a company can exercise religious freedom, what other freedoms does it have? Are they protected by law in the same way that the freedoms of an individual person are protected?
How do we balance conflicts between competing instances of religious freedom?

section.title: Introduction to Business, the Environment, and Sustainability

listitem.para: Recognize both short- and long-term ethical problems in the interaction between businesses and the environment.
Identify applications for the concept of “sustainability” in modern business practice.
Understand the most important issues stopping businesses from changing their relationship to the environment.

section.title: Business Ethics and the Environment
section.para: In our last chapter we considered the ethical issues arising from the relationship between businesses and society in general. We'll continue with this general look at ethical issues, but the relationship we’ll focus on next is that between businesses and the environment.

By the term environmentThe natural world, including all kinds of living organisms, the atmosphere, and the earth., we mean the natural world—and that term includes all of what we see in the world around us, from local plants and animals to the Amazon rain forests to the oceans and the atmosphere and everything else in- between, including all kinds of living organisms. Humans are also part of the natural world, and therefore part of the environment, understood in this broad way. As we’ll see, many of the effects businesses have on the environment affect both non-human animals and humans alike.

It isn’t difficult to find the ethical issues in the relationship between business operations and the environment. The most obvious and perhaps most pressing of all these issues is climate change, and especially the marked increase in the average global temperature since the early twentieth century. According to data gathered by US government agencies, 2023 was the warmest year ever recorded.https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/climate-change-global-temperature In the next section, we will explore climate change in greater detail.

Apart from climate change, though, we also find ethical issues concerning business and the environment on other scales. Some of these have to do with specific events brought about by the actions of specific companies or corporations, such as when, in 1989, the oil tanker Exxon Valdez ran aground in Prince William Sound on the southern coast of Alaska. The accident released an estimated 11 million gallons of oil into the water and surrounding coastlands, resulting in the deaths of hundreds of thousands of birds, thousands of otters and seals, billions of fish eggs, and thousands of other animals. https://darrp.noaa.gov/oil-spills/exxon-valdez

Another facet of the relationship between business and the environment is government regulation of business activities. While we’ve discussed government regulation before, here we’ll see how it targets specific industries and specific industry practices in order to reduce, eliminate, or penalize environmental damage. For example, partly in response to what happened in Prince William Sound, the US government passed the Oil Pollution Act (OPA) in 1990.Texthttps://darrp.noaa.gov/oil-pollution-act-opa This legislation governs the liability companies have for polluting water with oil. It involves provisions for oil recovery and foreign businesses, as well as for the associated financial liabilities. A passage early in the OPA stipulates that “each responsible party for a vessel or a facility from which oil is discharged, or which poses the substantial threat of a discharge of oil, into or upon the navigable waters or adjoining shorelines or the exclusive economic zone is liable for the removal costs and damages...that result from such incident.”https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?path=/prelim@title33/chapter40

While such catastrophic environmental damage is, at least for now, an exceptional case, the Exxon Valdez spill and related regulation prompt several of the crucial ethical questions we’ll ask in this chapter. These include:

listitem.para: What obligation do businesses have to protect the environment?
What obligation do businesses have to make amends for environmental damage they cause?
What obligation do businesses have to prevent possible environment damage in the future?
What is the proper role of government in regulating how business activities affect the environment?

section.para: These questions and others all belong to a broad area of moral concern: the place of humans in the natural world, and their treatment of that world. The natural world is a living world, and what businesses do, both locally and globally, affects all life. These are moral and ethical issues, in addition to being business and resource management issues. Sometimes the effects of business operations are direct, as in the case of the Exxon Valdez incident, while other times the effects are indirect. But they all have moral dimensions, and ought to be an important part of how businesses think about what they do now and what they intend to do in the future.

Some of the environment-related ethical issues for businesses arise due to conflicts between certain profit-seeking activities, along with the environmental consequences associated with them, and more environmentally friendly ways of doing business, which often increase costs. We have seen similar issues before: in chapter 7, for example, we covered the issue of fast fashion, and discussed how many clothing companies opt to have their products made in countries such as Bangladesh, where they will be able to pay lesser wages to workers who labor in worse conditions. These companies save money on production costs, which leads to greater profits, but contribute to an ethical problem elsewhere.

The same thing can happen in relation to the environment. The United States has certain regulations to govern the amount of pollutants or other waste that companies can generate in their production processes. But other countries don’t necessarily follow the same regulations—and so, just as some companies have done in Bangladesh, an American manufacturing operation could choose to base itself in another country, where weaker oversight will make it both cheaper and easier to turn a profit. If such a company then pollutes much more than it otherwise would if it were based in America, then we see a conflict between an ethically dubious action—significant amounts of pollution—and a company’s primary goal, which is to make money.

The possibility of a situation like this sometimes leads to a race to the bottomA competition in which the players “win” by making increasingly greater concessions.. A race to the bottom is a competition in which the players “win” by making increasingly greater concessions. Suppose that an American company is looking to build a new manufacturing facility overseas, in a country with fewer environmental regulations. In order to lure the business and secure the resulting jobs and taxes, countries may vie against each other by agreeing to successively lower amounts of oversight or regulation. The “winner” of this competition is the country that gets the contract and the new facility, but at the cost of allowing greater pollution or environmental contamination than another country would have allowed. The race to the bottom can have catastrophic effects in different industries, as we’ll see.

Racing to the bottom over environmental issues is one manifestation of a more general phenomenon known as collective action problems. A collective action problem is one where a group as a whole would benefit if each of its members performed a certain action, but the individual actions themselves make little difference to the outcome. Only the coordinated efforts of many group members can bring about a change, and individual actions taken in isolation do almost nothing. As a result, individual group members have little reason to change their behavior, both because their individual actions accomplish so little and because it is unlikely that other people will change their behavior.

A race to the bottom is a collective action problem because it would be better if environmental regulations were in place throughout the world—but individual countries have little incentive to adopt those regulations, because doing so would make it difficult to lure business operations.

More generally, many ethical problems of the environment and business are also collective action problems. Yes, it would be better if all American businesses agreed to even higher standards of clean manufacturing and environmental care—but individual companies have little incentive to take that path, because doing so would cost more money and put them at a disadvantage relative to their competitors. Similarly, the country would be better off if more people recycled and chose more sustainable materials and products—but individual people have little incentive to do so, because many other people will not and because an individual person’s recycling habits make no difference at all to large-scale sustainability issues.

We’ll return to the topic of races to the bottom in the next chapter, but throughout this current one we’ll see the ethics of collective action problems again and again. As we do, we must remember that, for any given collective action problem, there is a limited amount of time that group members have to take a collective action. If the problem grows too large, it may not be possible for group coordination to solve it.
The issue of collective action problems also raises another question about environmental ethics and business: who, specifically, bears the responsibility for taking care of the environment?

This question has various possible answers. The first and most obvious is that individual people have the responsibility of caring for the environment. And in a sense this is true, since the only organisms on our planet that can make long-term plans to care for the environment are humans. It is therefore our responsibility to do so. But it is also true that the individual actions we take make virtually no impact on the environmental causes we care about.

We can put the point more sharply by asking, how can I be responsible for taking care of the environment, when my actions make no difference to the outcome? That is, how can I carry the ethical obligation to recycle or use less water or electricity, when what I do won’t change anything? And, to be clear, it won’t: while me not recycling might cause bottles to pile up in my house, actually recycling them makes no measurable difference to the overall amount of reusable material available in the future.

There are two other obvious answers to the question about who bears responsibility for the environment: businesses and governments. Businesses may bear this responsibility because of their size—if they produce more, then they use and pollute more, and are therefore able to make more impactful changes than individual people. Governments can also take more impactful action, either by setting up infrastructure to responsibly use resources or by regulating the way businesses interact with the environment.

We will focus on the business side of this responsibility here. There is a strong case to be made for seeing businesses as the entities primarily responsible for caring for the environment; if they do have that responsibility, then environmental concerns ought to be some of their most important priorities.

As you explore the ethical issues of business and the environment in this chapter, keep these questions in mind: who is responsible, and why? What can those responsible do about these problems, and how should they best act?

sidebar.title: Case Study
sidebar.para: Durham, North Carolina, has experienced growing concern over water use as climate change and population growth strain regional water supplies. The Washington Duke Golf Club, a prestigious establishment located on Duke University’s campus, is often in the spotlight for its water consumption. Golf courses, known for their sprawling green landscapes, require significant amounts of water for maintenance: while their water use depends on the course style and region, some courses may use more than 500,000 gallons of water per day. For comparison, the average American family uses around 300 gallons of water per day. This discrepancy raises ethical questions about resource use in a time of environmental uncertainty.

Evelyn, a local environmental advocate and Duke alumna, recently moved back to Durham and has joined a civic group focused on water conservation. The group is lobbying for stricter regulations on water use, particularly for businesses like golf courses. Evelyn’s participation in the group prompts her to reflect on her personal responsibility in conserving water at home while grappling with how much accountability should rest on large water consumers like the Washington Duke Golf Club.

Evelyn enjoys golfing occasionally and recognizes the value the club provides as a community asset, hosting charity events and university gatherings. However, she wonders whether her efforts to reduce water usage—by installing low-flow fixtures and limiting outdoor watering—are meaningful when compared to the club’s vast consumption.

Advocates of individual responsibility argue that small actions can collectively make a difference. If everyone in Durham adopted water-saving habits, the cumulative effect could relieve pressure on water resources. Evelyn wrestles with whether it’s enough to lead by example and encourage others to do the same or if she needs to focus on influencing larger entities like the golf club.

On the other side of the debate, critics argue that high-impact users like the Washington Duke Golf Club bear greater ethical responsibility. They believe the club should invest in innovative water-saving technologies, such as rainwater harvesting systems or drought-resistant grass, even if these measures increase operating costs.

The club’s management, however, argues they already take measures to conserve water, such as using advanced irrigation systems and recycling water from nearby reservoirs. Evelyn considers whether these efforts are sufficient or if more stringent standards should be applied to businesses consuming water at scale.

listitem.para: Should individual households be held to the same water-saving standards as large entities like the golf club, or should regulations be weighted based on consumption?
How should Evelyn balance the benefits the Washington Duke Golf Club provides to the community against its environmental costs?
Is Evelyn’s focus on her own water conservation practices an effective way to inspire broader change, or is it a distraction from targeting high-consumption entities?
Who should bear the financial burden of implementing water-saving technologies—businesses, individuals, or the government?
Discuss the broader implications of this case for environmental ethics. What principles should guide decisions about shared resources in communities?
Who bears greater responsibility for protecting the environment: corporations, or individual people? Why?

section.title: Business Operations and Environmental Effects
section.para: Before moving on, it will be helpful to have a clearer picture of how business operations can affect the environment. We sometimes have a tendency to see this issue only in terms of climate change, and while rising global temperatures are a major ethical issue, they are far from the only one.

Let’s consider first the issue of resource extraction and depletion. In many cases, extracting natural resources from the environment is a difficult and expensive process, requiring lots of time and sophisticated equipment. And many of the resources are not located within the countries that carry out the extraction processes. For example, removing rare earth elements and metals, such as lanthanum, erbium, and ytterbium, from the earth’s outer surface is an arduous process. Despite the name, these elements and minerals are not actually “rare”; they are in fact abundant, but because they are almost always found mixed with other materials, they must be separated from those materials first before they can be used. The two primary methods for mining and purifying these elements are: removing topsoil by pit mining, or drill mining and then adding chemicals to the drilled holes.
